title: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
summary: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region are preparing for the end of a localized ceasefire
story: Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region are preparing for the end of a localized ceasefire

KHERSON, Ukraine -- Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago.

The White House said that U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce, which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday.

“The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace.”

An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers weren't released after the evacuation.

At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy.
But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems before winter.
Hundreds of thousands of families were left without power overnight as Moscow sought to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.
“The intensity of the strikes is extremely high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said in a post on X.
Residents in the Ukrainian city of Kherson remained calm Sunday, despite knowing that the quiet of the localized ceasefire would soon end.
“Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert.

The theater performs every Saturday and Sunday. This weekend’s shows fell during the ceasefire, but the company plans to perform next weekend as usual, even as local officials warn that Russian forces have brought in more weapons and personnel and some residents expect shelling to intensify.

“Of course, we want peace to finally come,” Knyha said. But “we’ve been working on the front line for four years,” he added, referring to Kherson itself, and the theater has never canceled a performance.
“Whatever happens, the show is not canceled,” he said.
The company now performs in a basement and is equipping an additional bomb shelter. About 100 of the theater’s 120 staff members work in Kherson, and none has evacuated.
Costume maker Alla Vasylenko, 58, said that the silence of the brief truce still frightens her.
“Nothing will change,” she said. “Everything will go back to how it was before the ceasefire, because believing the Russians means not believing yourself.”
Vasylenko has no plans to leave.
“I have 10 dogs, so I can’t leave,” she said. “They urge us to leave, but you need somewhere to go and the means to get there.”
The trip alone would cost 30,000 to 50,000 hryvnias ($650 to $1,080), a significant sum for her, she said.
“Until we liberate the left bank, we have no certainty this will end,” Vasylenko said, referring to the Russia-occupied part of the region.
For many in Kherson, a city that itself lived through Russian occupation, that belief is the reason they stay.
Knyha is from Oleshky, on the occupied left bank, and used to commute from there to work in Kherson. He hasn’t given up hope of returning home.
“That’s also what keeps me here,” he said.

On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater staged a concert built around a “musical map of Ukraine,” with songs from the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, to the Carpathian mountains in Ukraine's southwest.
“This is also our job — to unite people and give them hope,” Knyha said.

Elsewhere, a Russian attack killed three people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Ukrainian region of Vinnytsia when a drone hit the grounds of a vocational school, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. Four others were wounded, including two 5-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy.

Russian drone attacks also continued to target Ukraine’s Kyiv region for a second consecutive day, wounding a woman and damaging homes, energy infrastructure and a retail establishment, regional authorities said.
In its daily report Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said that Moscow's forces attacked Ukraine with 433 drones overnight, of which 371 were destroyed or suppressed.
Elsewhere, more than 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the skies of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow, local Gov. Gleb Nikitin said Sunday.

Nikitin said an industrial building in the town of Kstovo had sustained “significant damage,” but didn't give further details. Russian media outlets later reported that the attack sparked a blaze at the Kstovo oil refinery, sharing images of black plumes of smoke over the horizon.

Local officials later placed limits on gasoline sales in the region after lines appeared at gas stations, Russian media outlets reported, citing Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government. Diesel sales weren't affected, they said.
Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv had also struck a factory used to make missile components and air defense facilities inside Russia’s southern Rostov region.
“We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capability to continue it,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Katie Marie Davies contributed to this report from Manchester, England.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Owner of private Serbian bank detained and accused of siphoning money
summary: Serbian authorities have detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender
story: Serbian authorities have detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender

BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbian authorities Monday detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender that was used for some public utility payments during the previous government of former President Aleksandar Vucic.

Alta Bank rose to prominence under the rule of Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party that was ousted from power in a parliamentary election last week. The bank has handled all electricity payments by millions of users in the capital Belgrade, as well as public parking accounts.

On Saturday, Serbia’s Central Bank revoked Alta Bank’s operating license and launched bankruptcy proceedings to protect the bank’s depositors, saying that its liquidity “has deteriorated significantly” and “could worsen further."
Serbia’s Deposit Insurance Agency, which guarantees deposits of up to 50,000 euros ($56,000), will act as Alta Bank's bankruptcy administrator, the central bank said.
Davor Macura, the bank owner who initially owned an exchange office before becoming a prominent banker, was given a 48-hour detention on Monday, prosecutors said.

Macura’s lawyers told local media he was present at the bank headquarters in Belgrade and fully cooperated during an hourslong police search over the weekend. Lawyers added that Macura will be questioned by the public prosecutor on Tuesday.

Macura, whose businesses also span retail and construction, is suspected of illegally moving 45 billion dinars ($428 million) out of Alta Bank’s vault. Two other persons were also held for aiding and abetting the crime.

The moves against Alta Bank and its owner came as part of a wave of changes triggered by Vucic’s defeat in the Oct. 25 election that also included resignations in the state-run media, arrests of several officials and an announced review of long-standing corruption cases.

Former central bank governor Kori Udovicki on Sunday criticized the Serbian Central Bank moves as too slow. She said on RTS television that the central bank “lost a week in which it could have limited the bank’s ability to transfer the money abroad or to the connected individuals.”

Alta Bank is a rare Serbian lender that allowed tens of thousands of Russian émigrés to open personal and business accounts. Scores of Russians have moved to Russia-friendly Serbia since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Alta Bank's troubles resonated outside Serbia. The Central Bank of North Macedonia put Alta Bank’s subsidiary into temporary administration and limited cash withdrawals to 160 euros ($179) per week, while Montenegro's banking regulator shut down payment processing company Alta Pay.
In Serbia, armed police could be seen guarding the bank's offices in Belgrade after dozens of customers stood in long lines over the weekend trying to withdraw their savings.

Serbian investigative outlets in the past have described Macura as a tycoon whose political connections to Vucic and his SNS helped him win lucrative contracts with state agencies and public enterprises.

In 2024, Macura’s Alta Group came under scrutiny by the European Central Bank, or ECB, when it attempted to acquire a 20% stake in Austria’s Addiko Group through two connected firms to avoid triggering the ECB’s approval requirement. The ECB spotted this and stopped the deal. It also questioned the anti-money laundering controls and the source of funds in Macura's network.
The Association of Serbian Banks called Alta Bank's collapse “an individual issue” and said it would not affect other banks.

The SNS, which has governed Serbia since 2012, lost the parliamentary election to the student-led Student List movement. The outgoing authorities remain in control until a formal transition of power, expected to take several weeks.

Critics say the SNS has steadily taken control of state institutions since it came to power. It has been accused of corruption, cronyism, links to organized crime and pressure on the judiciary, police and media. The party has denied the accusations.

title: Asian shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices retreat
summary: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran
story: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran
HONG KONG -- Asian shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped technology- and artificial intelligence-related stocks.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3% to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell.
Shares of OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 1.6%. Japanese memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings plunged 15.8% as its earnings forecasts disappointed some analysts and investors.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2% to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8%.
Technology stocks have been volatile as investors worry that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble.

Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped.
While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note.
Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole.
“Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.”
Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than 7% and the Kospi dropped more than 16%.
Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7% lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7%.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.5% to 23,411.49. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1% to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contraction territory in October indicating that the economic momentum may have slowed.

China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions Monday to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen 14.6% in the past year.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.6% to 8,856.50.
India’s Sensex rose 1.3%.
On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 fell 1.8% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1%.

Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections. Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centers, along with inflation and other key issues.
Oil prices dropped more than 2% early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 2.8% to $110.24 per barrel. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 3.1%, to $100.85 a barrel.

Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S.
The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said.
In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.83 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1186, up from $1.1160.

title: Volkswagen posts $6.5 billion quarterly loss amid China slump, Porsche writedown
summary: Volkswagen has posted a $6.5 billion after-tax loss for the July-September quarter
story: Volkswagen has posted a $6.5 billion after-tax loss for the July-September quarter

FRANKFURT, Germany -- FRANKFURT, Germany (AP) — Automaker Volkswagen posted a 5.8 billion euro ($6.5 billion) after-tax loss for the July-September quarter as large one-time charges piled on top of weak demand in China, U.S. tariffs and lower profits from electric vehicles.

The results announced Thursday underline the challenges facing the company as it seeks to cut costs through a restructuring that could mean the loss of up to 100,000 jobs and the closure of four German plants.
Chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a statement that the company's results so far this year mean that “we cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively.”

Sales revenue decreased 6.3% to 80.3 billion euros from the year-earlier quarter. Earnings also suffered from a 6.4 billion euro reduction to account for the fallen value of Volkswagen's stake in luxury carmaker Porsche.

China was once a key profit center for Volkswagen, but now the company faces declining demand for cars there on top of fierce price competition from local carmakers. U.S. tariffs, or import taxes, imposed by President Donald Trump have also weighed on profits, as has the increasing share of electric vehicles, which earn less per vehicle than internal combustion models.

title: Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure
summary: Get ready to fall back
story: Get ready to fall back

WASHINGTON -- The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don’t like having to change their clocks twice a year.

As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.

“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark.

Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump’s ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to “GET IT DONE!” But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard.
Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it.
“You’d be sending kids to school in the dark,” said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds.

Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and “CRIMINALS DON’T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT."
He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that “United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it.”

An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when “you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings.”
Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that “nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year."

The president’s arguments don’t appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump's pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won’t come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election.

Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it’s his understanding that the House bill is a “non-starter” for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon.
“No way,” Moreno said.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn’t weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past.

In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark.
Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day.

An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen.

“I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them,” Scott said.
Several Democrats are on board, as well.

“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets.”
Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed to this report.

title: Hong Kong's housing minister resigns after fire investigation finds inadequate oversight
summary: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight
story: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight

HONG KONG -- Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out last November engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.

Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were then undergoing building maintenance work.

At the opening of the news conference, Lee and seven other top officials bowed in apology. Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho “should bear political responsibility," although no personal wrongdoing was found. He said Ho had resigned Wednesday.

An independent committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit failed in its duties supervising the maintenance work. Lee said the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labor Department had shortcomings in supervision over fire hazards of the apartment complex.
He said a three-month investigation will be conducted into the four government agencies to determine whether staff were derelict in their duties.
Officials also proposed a series of measures, including criminalizing bid rigging.

The committee's report said evidence pointed to a lighted cigarette being the cause of the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House. The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, including on the scaffolding, while a few cigarette butts and some partially burnt materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, among other factors, the report said.

A majority of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation rather than burns. The replacement of some staircase windows with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience allowed smoke to infiltrate residents’ escape routes. Opaque foam boards that covered the apartments’ windows blocked residents’ views, delaying evacuation. The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll.

The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Company, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor on the project, had cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.

It said the evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber-stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee. The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.

“However ... deception succeeded because the regulators’ own practices enabled it,” the report said. “In each case, the regulator’s reliance on the good faith of the regulated parties left obvious fire hazards uninvestigated.”

The committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit and the Buildings Department, as the two agencies primarily responsible for supervising the execution of the maintenance work at Wang Fuk Court, had failed in their supervisory duties in ensuring the safety of such work.

Among the shortcomings were the lack of proper investigations into the use of the foam boards and the fire-retardant quality of the scaffolding nets despite multiple complaints. The Independent Checking Unit should be criticized for adopting the practice of giving prenotification to consultants and contractors about site inspections, it added.

The committee's work is separate from criminal investigations in which seven people and two companies, Will Power and Prestige, were charged with offenses including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud over the fire.

Authorities alleged that the two companies and some defendants conspired together to defraud the apartment owners by concealing previous litigation records of the company later awarded the renovation project, a contract worth more than 300 million Hong Kong dollars (over $38 million).

title: CNN, MSNOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent
summary: Three news outlets are telling a federal court that the White House is defying a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump
story: Three news outlets are telling a federal court that the White House is defying a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump

Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press “pool.”

CNN, MSNOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president.

Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in “the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press,” Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets' attorney, said in a statement.
The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent.

At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is “viewpoint discrimination” forbidden by the First Amendment’s free-speech protections.

Trump insists that he doesn’t have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning.

“Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable," the outlets wrote in their filing, "and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government.”
The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him.

In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.

Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.
“Simply put,” Kelly wrote in the opinion, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.

title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
summary: FBI sys attack was tied to an entity known as TraderTraitor.
story: FBI sys attack was tied to an entity known as TraderTraitor.
New York -- The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.
The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.
The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.”

Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved.
“I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.

Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

“It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.”
He added: “It’s just this cat and mouse game.”

On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.
The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.
Associated Press writer Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed.

title: Airbnb pledges $500M to nonprofit, scaling emergency stays and raising questions over housing relief
summary: Airbnb is dedicating more than $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years
story: Airbnb is dedicating more than $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Airbnb plans to dedicate $500 million to its philanthropic arm over the next five years to increase temporary housing support for medical travelers and disaster survivors.

The short-term rental platform will fund the expansion by donating 10 cents from every booking and make up any shortfall, according to Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky. Airbnb.org, the independent nonprofit whose operating costs are already covered by the company, aims to scale up to eventually provide 1 million nights of free housing each year.

The pledge, announced Wednesday, arrives at an uncertain time for corporate philanthropy overall. Most companies reduced their giving over the past five years, according to a recent survey by Chief Executives for Corporate Purpose. Tax law changes have prompted businesses to reconsider their charitable strategies.

Airbnb.org's new funding model has resurfaced questions about the charitable endeavors of a corporation criticized by some affordable housing advocates for worsening the supply of lower-cost, residential housing. The affordable housing crisis — which critics say is exacerbated by Airbnb — means less housing is available for people displaced by disasters.

Should a for-profit enterprise use its philanthropy to offset less desirable business impacts? Leading artificial intelligence companies, currently sketching out plans to share some of their wealth, say yes.

For Chesky, the answer is emphatically “no.” He denied Airbnb is “the contributor of the reason cities are expensive” but acknowledged that some hosts take a small fraction of their area's housing off the market. This week's commitment is about doing the “right thing” with the company's “natural superpower,” he said.

“I don’t like this idea that somehow you create a nonprofit to make up for or apologize for your core business," Chesky told The Associated Press. "Our core business, independently, is gonna affect a lot more lives than this organization. And our core business needs to be responsible. And if we’re doing something that’s not responsible, we need to correct it.”

Many governments, including the country of Spain and the city of New York, have recently moved to curb short-term rentals. The company could use its growing philanthropic footprint to further ingrain its product into communities and legitimize the presence of short-term rentals as its model is contested, according to Ka­ro­lina Mikoła­jew­ska-Za­jąc, a postdoctoral fellow at Copenhagen Business School who researches the societal impacts of digital platforms. She cautioned the humanitarian sector against growing too dependent on commercial platforms.
Murray Cox, the founder of the data activist project Inside Airbnb, noted one “crisis” missing from the nonprofit's list of emergency housing interventions.

“There’s also the housing crisis that’s occurring around the world,” Cox said. “And, although they’re not causing the housing crisis, they’re contributing to it by taking millions of housing units -- residential houses -- off the housing market.”
Airbnb.org is squarely focused on short-term emergency housing.

Launched formally in 2020 as the San Francisco-based company went public, the nonprofit uses company-donated credits to book stays on its platform for those experiencing crises. Since then, the nonprofit reports having provided 1.6 million nights of free, temporary housing in nearly 140 countries. Fees are dropped and hosts are compensated. The nonprofit also provides credits for other relief organizations to book stays.

Beneficiaries include people recovering from natural disasters, families traveling for medical care and survivors escaping domestic violence. When Washington state wildfires forced tens of thousands of evacuations in August, Airbnb.org said it provided more than 1,400 nights of free housing in the disaster's early days.

Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org, compares the nonprofit to “the ambulance that'll get you to the hospital.” Short-term housing is a “great product-market fit," he said, because they're able to “house a lot of people very quickly with an enormous amount of flexibility to meet their particular needs.”
He emphasized that the new funding mechanism will provide a “lot more money” that the nonprofit can depend on each year. “It’s not just shuffling the deck chairs around,” he said.

The $500 million five-year injection would more than double the total contributions reported by Airbnb.org between 2021 and 2025. The company would have to register 5 billion bookings over the next five years to reach that figure through the sliver of each booking donated to the nonprofit.
Chesky emphasized that the commitment will be completed regardless of business outcomes.
“We felt like this is a responsible number where it’s sufficiently big to make a difference in the world," Chesky said. “But it’s also a number shareholders can be comfortable with.”

Short-term assistance from nonprofits such as Airbnb.org and government entities such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency are “key for preventing that initial displacement,” according to Noah Patton, the director of disaster recovery at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. That's especially so as an AP analysis showed President Donald Trump takes longer to approve disaster aid and denies a greater percentage of requests than his predecessors.
But Patton said there's a need for more lasting solutions so “folks have homes to return back to."
“It's a Band-Aid if you don't also focus on the long-term aspect of this,” he said.
Airbnb.org will also expand its medical stays program to 20 countries by the end of the year.

The nonprofit partners with medical relief organizations to provide housing for families traveling to get treatment. Airbnbs, according to Gorder, allow families to bring additional relatives and pets that some alternatives don't allow. Amenities such as kitchens, sometimes not available in hotels or hospital lodgings, give the option to cook patients' favorite foods.
“And then they just have a quiet place at the end of the day,” Gorder said. “So, it's a lot more than four walls and a roof.”

In Mexico, where the program was piloted last fall, Airbnb.org says it has housed medical travelers for nearly 1,500 nights. Its first partner, Vuela Fundación, supports children diagnosed with cancer. Many of the Mexico City-based organization's clients travel from poor rural towns and lack access to the country's social security system.

Diego Parada Herrera, the co-founder and CEO, said it's not uncommon to see families camping in tents or sleeping in parked cars outside of hospitals because they couldn't afford to stay anywhere else.
“The need was there. And we were conscious of it,” he said. “But we didn't know how to address it.”

Airbnb.org now provides his organization with credits that case managers use to complete bookings for families in need. Some hosts offer discounted rates, he said. Vuela Fundación stocks fridges with ready-to-cook food packages.

The challenge, he's found, is that many families aren't technologically savvy. Some aren't familiar with Airbnb's business model and struggle to grasp that they'll be staying in someone else's home. His nonprofit created instructional videos and shows them how to use the platform.
Chesky said the company will likely “keep going” based on how this expansion goes.
“Whatever people think of us, we’re doing this for decades,” he said. “It’s up to them to judge us and our motivations. And it’s up to us to have a commitment that’s a decade-long commitment.”

title: Average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month
WASHINGTON -- The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate declined for the second straight week, falling to its lowest level in more than a month.
The benchmark 30-year fixed-rate mortgage fell to 7.24% from 7.32% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.17%.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also fell this week. That average rate dipped to 6.60% from 6.68% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.41%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.
The yield was at 4.98% at midday on the bond market Thursday. It surged to more than 5.30% earlier this month and remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran.

title: Starbucks reports lower than expected revenue on softer international demand
summary: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
story: Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened
Starbucks reported lower than expected revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter as international traffic softened.

The Seattle coffee giant said global same-store sales rose 7.2% for the July-September period, which was higher than the 6% increase Wall Street was expecting, according to analysts polled by FactSet.

That was largely due to strong demand in the U.S., where same-store sales jumped 7.7%. International same-store sales rose less than 1%, and Starbucks noted a 2.8% decline in international store traffic.
Net revenue fell 4% for the quarter to $9.14 billion. That was lower than the $9.2 billion analysts were forecasting.

title: Man United fans bid to disrupt Champions League tie by hurling tennis balls
summary: Manchester United fans have attempted to disrupt the Champions League match against Roma by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch at Old Trafford
story: Manchester United fans have attempted to disrupt the Champions League match against Roma by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch at Old Trafford

MANCHESTER, England -- MANCHESTER, England (AP) — Manchester United fans attempted to disrupt the Champions League match against Roma on Tuesday by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch at Old Trafford.
United was 2-0 down inside 18 minutes, but the protest had been pre-planned and flagged on social media earlier in the day.
It ended up causing only a brief delay, with just a small number of balls being thrown from the Stretford End and quickly removed by players.
The protest was nothing like as disruptive as a similar demonstration by Celtic fans last year when trying to bring about a change in their club's hierarchy.
United supporters have long-tried to force regime change at their club with numerous protests against American owners the Glazer family.
Minority owner British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe has also come in for criticism in the face of the club's on-field problems and increased ticket prices.

Ratcliffe, the owner of petrochemical giant INEOS, assumed control of the soccer operations after buying an initial 25% stake for $1.3 billion in 2024. Since then the 20-time English champion has fired two coaches, while Michael Carrick's position is under intense scrutiny after a troubled start to the season.
The Glazers have been unpopular among fans since their leveraged buyout of the club in 2005.
The protest was timed for 21 minutes to mark 21 years of the Glazers' ownership.
United went into Tuesday's game on a nine-game winless run and was quickly behind against Roma when Matias Soule struck after 11 minutes.
Seven minutes later, Donyell Malen made it 2-0 with a penalty.
James Robson is at https://x.com/jamesalanrobson

title: NASCAR driver Hocevar suspended for season finale following actions at Martinsville
summary: Spire Motorsports has suspended NASCAR driver Carson Hocevar for Sunday’s season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, saying “racing at the Cup level is a privilege, and it comes with an expected level of professionalism.”
story: Spire Motorsports has suspended NASCAR driver Carson Hocevar for Sunday’s season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, saying “racing at the Cup level is a privilege, and it comes with an expected level of professionalism.”

CONCORD, N.C. -- Spire Motorsports has suspended NASCAR driver Carson Hocevar for Sunday's season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway, saying “racing at the Cup level is a privilege, and it comes with an expected level of professionalism.”
Hocevar was accused of intentionally brake-checking competitor Austin Cindric following a restart at Martinsville Speedway last Sunday. He denied doing it on purpose.

Cindric finished 36th, with his No. 2 Ford’s front end destroyed by multiple collisions with Hocevar, who seemed to slam on the brakes multiple times to initiate contact. Cindric declined interviews after leaving the care center, but he radioed his team that Hocevar “had a mental breakdown” in the incidents.
Hocevar, who has been involved in several run-ins this season, said he “got lost there for a second” and denied hitting Cindric intentionally.

Earlier in the race, Hocevar was accused of intentionally spinning his No. 77 Chevrolet to bring out a caution flag and potentially catch Christopher Bell and others on pit road, disrupting their race strategies.

“A decision like this has a lot of variables and a cascading effect across an organization like ours," Spire Motorsports co-owner Jeff Dickerson said in a statement. "The easy thing would have been to leave this in NASCAR's hands and let them decide what any penalty should be.
"To us, however, this isn't about money or points. We believe in respect. Our integrity matters. This is the right decision for Spire Motorsports.”
Justin Haley will replace Hocevar in the finale.

“This is an embarrassing day for me,” Hocevar said in a statement posted on social media. “I let the people down that gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to drive a Cup car. I also let down my team, sponsors and fans. I crossed the line with my on-track actions and gave Jeff and Spire Motorsports no option but to put someone else in the 77 car this weekend at Homestead.
"I’ll be rooting for the entire organization this weekend and look forward to coming back in 2027 as a better driver, competitor and teammate.”
Hocevar, driving in his third full season for Spire, made the 16-team playoff field but has since been eliminated from the championship chase. He currently ranks 12th.
“Everyone here loves working with Carson, and we've enjoyed watching him thrive alongside our team,” Dickerson said. "Sometimes the right decision for someone you care about hurts in the short term.

“The way Carson conducted himself at Martinsville doesn't meet the standard we set for our drives, team members or employees, and there are consequences for that. That doesn't mean we don't love him and support him.”

title: MLB proposes delaying salary cap implementation to 2028 in talks with players
summary: Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the start of a salary cap until 2028
story: Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the start of a salary cap until 2028

NEW YORK -- Major League Baseball proposed delaying the start of a salary cap until 2028, saying teams have too many commitments for next season that wouldn't allow them to reduce spending quickly enough.

A day after the start of free agent negotiations for the 2026-27 offseason, owners on Tuesday proposed to players the sport adopt a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028 and a floor of $180.2 million, using luxury tax payrolls with average annual values. A team would be allowed to remain as low as 90% of the floor in 2028, which would be $162.18 million, but would have to spend the entire amount of the floor over a three-year period.

“We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. “This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn.”

Baseball's five-year labor contract, reached in March 2022 on the 99th day of a lockout, expires Dec. 1 and management is expected to again lock out the union. MLB hadn't proposed a salary cap since the negotiations that led to a 7 1/2-month strike in 1994 that forced cancellation of the World Series for the first time in 90 years. The players’ association has said it never will accept a cap.

“Coming off another incredible season of baseball, MLB owners continue to propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values,” the union said in a statement. “Players stand ready to negotiate in good faith toward a new CBA that will capitalize on our sport’s unprecedented momentum and benefit players, clubs, and fans alike.”

Management's proposal is tied to a 50-50 split of revenue with players, and the union takes issue with management's definitions of revenue and expenses. Cap and floor figures would be lower if there is a work stoppage that causes MLB revenue to decline. Management's May proposal included a fixed $245.3 million figure for a cap and $171.2 million for a floor, also with the provision a club could be at only 90% of the floor.

“The projected salary cap and floor for 2028 continues to provide more money for major league players while leveling the playing field and giving more teams the ability to participate in the free agent market and retain their homegrown stars so that every fan believes their team has a fair chance to win it all,” Caplin said.

Management said eight teams would have to reduce current payroll by a combined $528 million to get under the 2028 cap: Boston, the Chicago Cubs, the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets and Yankees, Philadelphia, San Diego and Toronto.

Twelve teams would have to increase spending by $636 million to reach the floor: the Athletics, the Chicago White Sox, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Colorado, Miami, World Series champion Milwaukee, Minnesota, Pittsburgh, St. Louis, AL champion Tampa Bay and Washington.

MLB said it was willing to discuss phase-in timelines and procedures. It would keep the current luxury tax system and revenue-sharing plan for 2027 with the same thresholds and tax rates as in 2026, then centralize MLB media revenue for 2028.

Players claim the cap proposal would eliminate guaranteed contracts because of its escrow provision that would claw back salary money if the players' share of defined revenue in a year is above 50%. The union called the plan “replacement of market-based fundamentals with a zero-sum system that harms the middle class and pits player against player” and said the proposal would lead to “stripping current competitive advantages for smaller market teams." Players said the proposal would cause a $400 million reduction in amateur signing bonuses for 2027.

Owners said they would accept the union's proposal to reduce service time for free-agent eligibility from six seasons of service to five for players at least 30 years old but would give a player's team the right to make a qualifying offer as under the current free-agent rules. If a player rejects the qualifying offer, he would be eligible for salary arbitration.
MLB would accept the union's proposal to eliminate qualifying offers for other free agents.

Management would raise the minimum salary from $780,000 to $1 million for those with two years of service and $900,000 for others — those others would earn $100,000 more from the pre-arbitration bonus pool if they accrue a full year of service as long as they are not on the injured list for half a season or more. Minor league minimums would increase from $63,600 to $73,400 for initial big league deals and $127,100 to $146,700 for additional contracts.

MLB proposed a one-time bonus payment to players as part of the plan, using money from luxury tax proceeds the current labor agreement earmarks for players’ 401(k) accounts. The bonus would be based on 2026 service time, with those in the majors for at least 172 of the 187-day regular season getting $285,000. The bonus would be $213,400 for three-quarters of a year, $142,300 for half and $71,100 for a quarter.

MLB would increase the pre-arbitration bonus pool from $50 million in 2026 to $65 million in 2027, then up to $75 million over the term of a seven-year labor agreement through the 2033 season. It would include Prospect Promotion Incentive draft picks in the international draft MLB wants and would allow a player to earn his team two PPI picks, one in the amateur draft and the other in the international draft. MLB would accept the union's proposal to exclude foreign professionals, such as Japanese players, from the calculation if a player earns additional service time based on his finish in Rookie of the Year voting.

Owners would eliminate a player's fourth option year and reduce optional assignments per season from five to four. They would decrease the number of years by one for when a player must be protected from the Rule 5 draft and allow a player selected in the Rule 5 draft to be optioned.

title: U.S. star Balogun added to Monaco's squad for Conference League after scoring first goal this season
summary: U.S. striker Folarin Balogun has been added to Monaco’s squad for the Conference League having originally been left out amid uncertainty over his future
story: U.S. striker Folarin Balogun has been added to Monaco’s squad for the Conference League having originally been left out amid uncertainty over his future
MONACO -- U.S. striker Folarin Balogun has been added to Monaco's squad for the Conference League, having originally been left out amid uncertainty over his future.

In the squad list displayed on UEFA's website on Tuesday, Balogun's name now appears among the forwards. Ansu Fati, who was injured in an Oct. 25 match against Lille and — according to French daily L'Equipe — is sidelined for two months, is no longer on the list.
Balogun has only featured as a substitute this season for Monaco, playing in five games and scoring his first goal in a 3-1 loss at Paris FC on Sunday.

The striker was close to joining Everton for a reported 40 million pounds ($54 million) on the last day of the summer transfer window for most leagues in Europe — Sept. 1 — but pulled out of a deal because he felt uncomfortable that the English club raised doubts about his health in a medical examination.
Days later, Balogun was left out of Monaco's Conference League squad because the club still had the option of selling him to a league where the transfer window remained open. That didn't materialize.

All this came after a World Cup when Balogun — the star player for the U.S. team — was the subject of a major controversy following his red card during the round-of-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina.

His one-game suspension was deferred by FIFA after U.S. President Donald Trump intervened, calling Gianni Infantino — president of soccer’s world governing body — to see if the red card could be reviewed.
Balogun was allowed to play in the round of 16 and had a forgettable performance as the U.S lost to Belgium.

Monaco won its first two games in the Conference League — against CSKA Sofia and Freiburg — and has matches to come in the 36-club league phase against FC Nordsjælland on Thursday, then Hearts, Brighton and Lincoln Red Imps.

title: Djokovic overcomes scare late in 2nd set to beat Vacherot in Paris Masters 1st round
summary: Record seven-time champion Novak Djokovic has overcome a scare late in the second set to beat big-serving Valentin Vacherot 6-7, 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters
story: Record seven-time champion Novak Djokovic has overcome a scare late in the second set to beat big-serving Valentin Vacherot 6-7, 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters

PARIS -- PARIS (AP) — Record seven-time champion Novak Djokovic overcame a scare late in the second set to beat big-serving Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters on Tuesday.
The men's record 24-time Grand Slam winner is chasing a 103rd career title, which would move him level in second place with Roger Federer. Jimmy Connors leads in the Open era on 109.
But the 10th-seeded Serb could have gone out early in Paris.

Serving at 4-4 in the second set, he needed to save three break points to prevent Vacherot — who won the Swiss Indoors on Sunday and beat Djokovic in the Shanghai Masters semifinals last year — from serving for the match at the indoor tournament.

“His second serves are faster than my first serves, so it's very tough to play a guy in these conditions, which are really, really fast," Djokovic said. “Last year was very slow, this year is like ice.”
Djokovic was bamboozled by the Monaco player's “huge” serves and saw 22 aces fly past him.
“For a set and a half, I had difficulty reading his serve," Djokovic said. "Even if I guessed right, it was coming with some speed.”

After breaking Vacherot to level the match, he broke him at the start of the deciding set to seize the momentum. Djokovic won on his second match point with a fine two-handed backhand winner down the line from the back of the court.
Both players took a medical timeout during the second set, with Djokovic having some massage on his right shoulder and Vacherot having his left ankle strapped.
Also Tuesday, third-seeded Ben Shelton moved into the third round after beating fellow left hander Cameron Norrie 6-3, 6-4 to equal his season-best total with a 42nd win.

The American player has added Carlos Alcaraz’s former coach Juan Carlos Ferrero to his team for 2027. Shelton has already secured his spot in the Nov. 15-22 ATP Finals, along with top-ranked Alexander Zverev, seven-time major winner Alcaraz and Daniil Medvedev.

Djokovic is chasing a spot but is an outsider at 11th in the race. He needs to reach at least the semifinals here to stay in contention, the ATP said, with only an ATP250 event remaining in Stockholm after Paris.
No. 11-seeded Taylor Fritz, who is one place below Djokovic, won 3-6, 6-3, 6-4 against Benjamin Bonzi.

In other first-round matches Tuesday, French teenager Moïse Kouame — a fan favorite at the French Open this year — lost 6-3, 6-1 to Nuno Borges, and 2022 champion Holger Rune lost 7-5, 6-4 to No. 12-seeded Tommy Paul.
Rune is still finding his way back following an Achilles injury. The 23-year-old Dane returned to action in September and lost to Vacherot in the quarterfinals last week at the Swiss Indoors.

In the third round on Wednesday, Zverev faces mercurial Italian Lorenzo Musetti, Djokovic plays qualifier Rinky Hijikata while second-seeded Alcaraz takes on Alex Michelsen and No. 4 Medvedev plays Ignacio Buse.

title: Seattle Mariners hire Chicago Cubs farm director Jason Kanzler as manager
summary: The Seattle Mariners have hired Chicago Cubs farm director Jason Kanzler as manager
story: The Seattle Mariners have hired Chicago Cubs farm director Jason Kanzler as manager
SEATTLE -- The Seattle Mariners have hired Chicago Cubs farm director Jason Kanzler as manager, the team said Tuesday.

The 36-year-old Kanzler replaces Dan Wilson, who was fired after a disappointing 76-86 season that began with World Series aspirations. Seattle reached Game 7 of the American League Championship Series in 2025.

Kanzler was the Cubs' director of player development, leading the organization’s minor league system, players and coaching staff. A former minor league player and coach, Kanzler has not managed a club at any level. He was on the big league coaching staff for the Houston Astros in 2022-23, serving as assistant hitting coach in his final season.
He will be the second-youngest manager in baseball behind Washington’s 34-year-old skipper Blake Butera.

“I am thrilled to join the Mariners organization and I’m looking forward to hitting the ground running,” Kanzler said in a statement. “This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game, and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team’s full potential.”
Kanzler was a 20th-round pick by the Minnesota Twins in 2013 and played three minor league seasons as an outfielder.

After retiring as a player, he taught high school chemistry and physics in Katy, Texas, before Houston hired him in 2019 as hitting coach for High-A Fayetteville. He worked in a variety of roles within the organization over five seasons.
Seattle general manager Justin Hollander said in a statement the organization believes Kanzler can lead the club back to the postseason.

The Mariners won the AL West in 2025, their first division title in 24 years, and came within one victory of the franchise’s first World Series appearance. But a combination of injuries and regression by the bullpen and several of the team’s top offensive stars led to a 2026 season filled with disappointment.

Slugger Cal Raleigh batted .182 with 23 homers and 69 RBIs. Center fielder Julio Rodríguez and first baseman Josh Naylor also had career-worst seasons, and the Mariners scored just 664 runs — third-fewest in the majors.
Seattle is still the only major league team that’s never reached the World Series.
“Throughout the process, Jason consistently demonstrated elite leadership skills, high-end content and an ability to connect and partner with players, staff and front office," Hollander said.

title: Miami a good bet for No. 1 in the initial College Football Playoff rankings, but then what?
summary: Miami is undefeated and hard to deny as a team that deserves top seeding when the College Football Playoff selection committee releases its first set of rankings for the season
story: Miami is undefeated and hard to deny as a team that deserves top seeding when the College Football Playoff selection committee releases its first set of rankings for the season

AP No. 1 Miami is undefeated and hard to deny as a team that deserves top seeding when the College Football Playoff selection committee releases its first set of rankings for the season Tuesday night.
After that, who knows?

Will the 13 people on the panel take a harder look at the other two undefeated teams in — AP No. 3 Utah and No. 5 UCLA — and reward them for somehow avoiding a loss in a season that has produced nothing but upheaval in the upper reaches of the Associated Press Top 25?
Or will the committee follow the AP voters and place Georgia at No. 2 despite its loss last month to an unranked Auburn team that fell by 30 to Ole Miss just last weekend?

About the only guarantee for this reveal, which doubles as programming for ESPN — the network that's paying roughly $1.3 billion this year to televise the playoff, starting in December — is that somebody will end up unhappy.

This is the first of six weekly rankings for the playoff, culminating on Dec. 6, at which time the 12-team bracket will be announced. If college football fans learned anything from last season, it was that one week's decisions don't necessarily bleed into the next.

For weeks last year, the panel refused to elevate Miami ahead of Notre Dame even though they both had two losses and one of the Irish losses came against the Hurricanes on opening week in August. Then, when the bracket came out, the 'Canes were in and the Irish were out.
This season, those two programs don't face off until November — specifically, this upcoming Saturday, where the result will almost certainly dictate the first big shakeup in the rankings.

Notre Dame is ranked fourth in the AP poll — getting leapfrogged by Utah after a less-than-overwhelming 35-13 win over Navy. The rest of the Irish schedule is ranked 37th (only five spots below Miami's), meaning a second loss on the season could put them behind in some of the metrics the panel says it uses beyond wins and losses.
Another point of interest will be what the panel makes of the Southeastern Conferecen, which comes into Week 10 without a single undefeated team but with 10 teams ranked in the Top 25.

Alabama has lost to Tennessee, Tennessee has lost to Kentucky, Kentucky has lost (badly) to Alabama. Texas has lost to Florida and Oklahoma, but has beaten Ohio State and Ole Miss. Ole Miss beat LSU but also lost to Florida.

The list goes on, but someone in that league might be questioning whether the strength-of-schedule boost the SEC got from booking a ninth conference game starting this season is worth all these losses piling up. At least until the CFP doubles in size to make room.

No. 11 Ohio State has two losses and lost quarterback Julian Sayin, too. The loss last weekend to USC tumbled the Buckeyes out of the AP top 10 for the first time since 2021. They now look like the quintessential definition of a bubble team, with some of this depending on the weight the committee gives to Sayin's absence.

Meanwhile, defending national champion Indiana dropped two spots to AP No. 6 after an overtime win against Minnesota, its third less-than-dominating win in four weeks, sandwiched around a loss to Ohio State.

No. 20 Boise State and No. 22 New Mexico are the two Group of Six teams in the AP Top 25. The CFP's highest-ranked team among the G6 will earn one of 12 playoff spots. Will the committee size up the G6 the same way?
A couple new things for this, the second year of the 12-team bracket:
—Unlike last season, if Notre Dame is anywhere in the top 12 on Dec. 6, the Irish are guaranteed a spot and cannot be ousted by a conference champ ranked ahead of them, the way it happened last year.

—All four Power Four conference champions are guaranteed spots. Last year, automatic bids went to the four highest-ranked conference champions and James Madison of the Sun Belt beat out Duke of the ACC for the last spot.
—The G6 spot goes to the highest ranked team from that group, even if the team didn't win its conference.
—Don't get too comfortable with any of it. ESPN and the CFP apparently have a handshake agreement to expand the playoff to 24 teams beginning next year.
—The playoff starts on campus on Dec. 18-19, then winds through traditional bowl games over New Year's and Jan. 14-15. The title game will be in Las Vegas on Jan. 25.

title: Le Havre fans call for American owners to leave after coach's suspension and president's exit
summary: Le Havre fans are calling for the American owners the Blue Crow Sports Group to leave the club
story: Le Havre fans are calling for the American owners the Blue Crow Sports Group to leave the club
With their club in turmoil, Le Havre fan groups are calling for the American owners to leave.
Le Havre, founded in 1872 and considered the oldest club in French professional soccer, has plunged into a deep and unprecedented sporting crisis.
Languishing at the bottom of Ligue 1, and with relegation looming, the club started the week without a coach and a president.

Following a heavy 5-1 loss against leader Paris Saint-Germain over the weekend, Le Havre announced head coach Didier Digard had been suspended, and that the board members of owner Blue Crow Sports Group had accepted the resignation of president Jean-Michel Roussier.
Roussier’s resignation will be formally presented and ratified on Thursday, Le Havre said.
He's led the Normandy club since 2022 while Digard was appointed in the summer of 2024.
The exodus does not end there because French media have reported that sports director Demba Ba and goalkeeping coach Nicolas Douchez are also on their way out.
Blue Crow acquired Le Havre in July 2025, adding it to a portfolio of soccer clubs.

“In the space of just a few days, every individual who embodied this club, who helped bring it back to Ligue 1 (in 2023) and keep it there, has disappeared from its organizational structure,” three supporters groups said in a joint statement.
Le Havre has two points from nine matches and the fans blame the multi-club group based in Houston for the worrying situation.

“Blue Crow represents nothing in Le Havre,” they said. “Blue Crow Sports Group has dismantled (Le Havre) and demonstrates more clearly with each passing day its complete lack of understanding of how to run a football club, its history and its identity. The catastrophe that now looms is entirely their responsibility.”
Le Havre’s next game is against Lorient on Sunday.

“With this crucial match against Lorient approaching, the united front established between the players, the manager and the Kop (of supporters) following the match against PSG has been shattered,” the fan groups said.

A former Le Havre player, Digard managed to keep the team in the topflight over the past two seasons. He leaves the club with a record of 17 wins, 20 draws and 40 losses, according to Ligue 1 statistics.
The club has appointed Jaïr Karam, the academy director, as interim coach and said Yacine Alaoui would oversee administrative and sporting activities until a new chairman and CEO are appointed.

title: New York Liberty fire coach Chris DeMarco after one disappointing season
summary: The New York Liberty have fired coach Chris DeMarco after only one season
story: The New York Liberty have fired coach Chris DeMarco after only one season
NEW YORK -- The New York Liberty have fired coach Chris DeMarco after only one season, the franchise announced Tuesday.

DeMarco came to New York in December after serving for more than a decade as an assistant with the Golden State Warriors. He had no prior WNBA experience before guiding the Liberty to the eighth seed in the regular season. After an impressive first-round playoff sweep over the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx, the Liberty were ousted by the Atlanta Dream in three games.
The Liberty coaching staff made a crucial mistake in Game 2 of the series not knowing that they had a reset timeout left in overtime with the team trailing by three late in that game.
Now New York will be looking for its third coach in three seasons. General Manager Jonathan Kolb didn't retain Sandy Brondello after the 2025 season.
ESPN first reported DeMarco's departure.
After the final loss to Atlanta, none of the Liberty’s three star players — Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu and Jonquel Jones — offered a definitive vote of confidence of DeMarco.

“Of course, we want to win a championship every single time we step on the court, but it’s really hard in this league, and in order to do that, you need to be consistent for the full 44 games,” Stewart said when asked about DeMarco. “And I don’t think we were consistent throughout the season. I think that we started to show some life and peak a little bit towards the end and in the playoffs. But this is not like cramming for a test. You got to be ready and ready to go since the jump.”
Ionescu said DeMarco’s future was “not our decision.”

“We’re thankful for everything that he’s done this year,” Ionescu said. “Just focusing on the now, the way he’s poured into us and stayed positive, level-headed through the ups and downs of this season as well that didn’t go the way that he wanted either.”
DeMarco was under contract for next season. Now Kolb will lead his fourth coaching search since 2019.
New York had a disappointing regular season two years removed from winning the WNBA title. The Liberty finished eighth with a 26-18 record.

title: Spanish police investigating after soccer player dies following on-field collision
summary: Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team’s goalkeeper in a second-division match
story: Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team’s goalkeeper in a second-division match

BARCELONA, Spain -- Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team's goalkeeper in a second-division match.
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest following the on-field collision, his club said Tuesday. He was 30.

De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, who came running from the opposite direction in an apparent attempt to make a clearance. Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident, which happened in added time.
The country’s National Police said Tuesday that an investigation was opened. Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.
The club located on Spain's Canary Islands said it was “heartbroken.”
The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
The goalkeeper's Instagram account, which had nearly 30,000 followers, had been deactivated on Tuesday.
De Miguel, a Madrid native, began his senior career with Leganés B in 2015 and subsequently played for a number of lower-division clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.
Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter.

“There are no words of comfort,” the club statement read. “There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community.”
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Piqué, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
“We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace,” Andorra said in a statement.
Piqué said on X: “I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesús.”
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: “So much sadness. There are no words.”
Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: “There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends.”
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina matches scheduled for later on Tuesday.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun died from head injuries sustained in a collision during a match while playing for CSKA Moscow.
Malaga goalkeeper José Antonio Gallardo died in January 1987, more than three weeks after a collision with Celta Vigo forward Baltazar in a second-division game.
Azzoni contributed from Madrid.
