title: Book excerpt: "Frank Capra: A Life" by Sam Wasson
summary: Returning to movie screens after his service in World War II, Jimmy Stewart was nervous about appearing in Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life" – a film now acknowledged as one of his very best.
story: We may receive an affiliate commission from anything you buy from this article.

Returning to movie screens after his service in World War II, actor Jimmy Stewart was nervous about appearing in Frank Capra's "It's a Wonderful Life" – a film now acknowledged as one of his very best.

In his biography of the director, "Frank Capra: A Life" (published by Harper), Hollywood historian Sam Wasson writes of how Capra helped shepherd Stewart back into the public limelight in a role that was perfectly suited to Stewart's talents – and in the process created a timeless classic.
Read the excerpt below – and don't miss Lee Cowan's report on Jimmy Stewart's post-WWII experience on "CBS Sunday Morning" November 1!
Prefer to listen? Audible has a 30-day free trial available right now.

Unlike Capra, Stewart refused to promote his return to Hollywood. His contract with Liberty stipulated that he was not to be made to discuss his heroism. "In all advertising and publicity issues by the corporation, or under its control," the relevant clause read, "the corporation will not mention or cause to be mentioned the part taken by the artist in World War II as an officer in the U.S. Army."

By then, Stewart had read the script Capra had given him. George Bailey, the hero of the picture they would call It's a Wonderful Life, was the truest to his own life. Still, he was terrified. It was to be his first film in almost five years. Had he lost the audience? Had they forgotten about him? Leaving a department store in Beverly Hills, he was mistaken by a gaggle of bobby-soxers for MGM's new heartthrob Van Johnson. But more than tastes in movie stars had changed since Stewart went to war. At a Lux Radio Theatre performance of Destry Rides Again, the script he was holding shook so hard, they could see it from the control room.
"No sense running away," Stewart told his friends one night at Chasen's. "The truth is I'm scared as hell."

Scared, and also emotionally fried. "I don't think I'll ever get into an airplane again," he confessed. "I rolled two thousand hours overseas, and that'll just about do me." There was, one journalist observed in 1946, "a trace of weariness" about him now. To another, Stewart said, "It got pretty rough overseas at times."

What Capra would not have told Stewart was that he, the director, was the more frightened of the two. Without [Robert] Riskin, it had been the most chaotic script gestation of his career—a career that had never been more vulnerable. The script he had given Stewart was still changing, and where once he could have turned to [Jo] Swerling or Myles Connolly or Sidney Buchman to pitch in for a polish or, at least, talk story, friend to friend, none of them was available to him. Capra's loneliness was, for him, unprecedented, impossible to describe.

The night before his first day of filming, April 15, 1946, Stewart's worry intensified. He studied the scene, as if being word-perfect—never a requirement on a Capra set (in fact, a disadvantage)—would save him from disaster.

The first day of It's a Wonderful Life was also William Wyler's first day on The Best Years of Our Lives, which would be his last picture with Goldwyn before he joined Liberty. "Last one in is a rotten egg," Wyler had cabled Capra. With its hundreds of partying extras, that scene that first day—the first of several on location at Beverly Hills High School, where George and Mary fall into the swimming pool beneath the gymnasium floor while dancing—would open Capra's production on a happy note. Using his independence to the hilt, Capra would go to the trouble and expense of shooting It's a Wonderful Life, to the best of his ability, in sequence, as was his preference, but in his capacity as social director of a new filmmaking community, he understood that the best way to break the ice was with a bang—three days at a high school dance in Bedford Falls.
Cannily, he also knew it was the setting for the first adult meeting of George and Mary.

Rather than Jean Arthur, who would have added an unnecessary tinge of knowing sophistication to Mary Hatch, Capra cast the fresh-faced midwestern beauty Donna Reed, whom he had first seen opposite John Wayne in John Ford's 1945 They Were Expendable. It was a lucky break for the director who rarely needed luck when casting. One look at Reed grinning with unguarded devotion at the man she loves, and any audience would see just why Bailey, blind for so long, might see her face in the right light, at the right moment, and open his eyes to life.

It was true also of Jimmy Stewart that the first time he saw Donna Reed that day in the gym of Beverly Hills High, "I fell in love with her right off the bat. She just seemed to be everything. ... Everything just seemed to come out of her."
"Jimmy," Capra said, doing a bit of acting himself, "I meant to call you last night to tell you our first scene starts on page 31, not 33. Ready?"

Capra, directing without directing, had surely never intended to call Stewart the night before. But it got the actor just where Capra wanted him: off his guard, a little nervous, that is, to approach Donna Reed as Mary Hatch, for Stewart was meeting both for the first time, nervous enough to fumble his answer to her question—not in the script or finished film, but tossed in just moments before they shot, by Capra—"Are you going to walk me home tonight?"
Stewart didn't have to act the scene. He just did it, perfectly, gulping, "N– n– no."
"That's it," Capra said. "Cut!" He grinned at Stewart. One take was all they needed.

title: Notable Deaths in 2026
summary: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
story: A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.
By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery.

Sir Patrick Stewart (July 13, 1940-Oct. 28, 2026) spent decades performing Shakespeare, Shaw, Ibsen, Beckett and Stoppard, and had already earned a reputation for commanding performances in the classics, when he took what would become his most recognizable role: Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the science fiction TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation."

When asked by "Sunday Morning" in 2013 why he wanted to play Picard, Stewart replied that he was channeling his father, who was a professional soldier for much of his life — and a weekend alcoholic. As a young boy, Stewart tried to keep his father from violently abusing his mother, a textile worker. "Yes," Stewart said, "and I hated him for that. But I also wanted to adore him, too. And I know that a lot of what I did early on in my career — and still possibly what I do now — is somehow in some way to please him."

Stewart turned to acting as an escape; he began performing with local drama groups at the age of 12. As a teenager he quit school and worked at a local newspaper, but was fired for spending too much time at the theater. Then, in 1957, he was offered a place at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, paid for by a scholarship that usually went to students destined for Oxford or Cambridge. In the early 1960s he toured the world with the Old Vic Company, starring in works by Brecht and Shakespeare. In 1966 he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, where Ian McKellen was already playing the great parts. Stewart worshipped McKellen, though found him to be intimidating. (Years later they bonded on the set of "X-Men," in which Stewart played Professor Charles Xavier, and McKellen played Magneto.) In addition to stage roles, Stewart appeared on television in "I, Claudius," and "Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy," and in the movies "Excalibur," "Dune," "The Doctor and the Devils," and "Lady Jane."

In 1986, Stewart was touring U.S. colleges to lecture about theater when he was selected to be the lead in "Star Trek: The Next Generation." Stewart thought that it wouldn't last a season. But he told "CBS This Morning" in 2023 that taking the role of Picard, captain of a revamped U.S.S. Enterprise, changed his life. "There was nothing in my life that was not affected," he said.

Stewart played Picard for seven seasons of "The Next Generation" and in four movies. (He also returned to the character in the 2020 TV series "Star Trek: Picard.") Stewart's 24th-century captain was notable for his stoic command, intelligence and diplomacy, whether he was wrestling with the trickster character Q or resisting the Borg. He also played the flute. "I saw the impact that Star Trek could have on people and their lives, the diversity of the show, its belief in honesty, fair play, equality, all those elements which kind of get a little sketchy these days," he said.

But rather than have Picard define him for the remainder of his career, Stewart returned to the theater. "Well, that was, in a way, my escape," Stewart said. He performed "Macbeth" at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, where he met his third wife, Sunny Ozell, a singer-songwriter. McKellen officiated their 2013 wedding, shortly before he and Stewart starred on Broadway in "Waiting for Godot" and "No Man's Land."
Stewart was knighted in 2009.

When the COVID pandemic shut down theaters in 2020, Stewart gifted his audience with a daily reading of a Shakespearean sonnet, posted online from his home in Los Angeles. "I miss work," he explained. And so, he performed the Bard once again:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

title: Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
summary: Patrick Stewart starred on stage and screen across his decadeslong acting career. He died at his home on Wednesday.
story: Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.
Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.
Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.

Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.
In a 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart said "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry initially turned him away.
"He was talked into employing me by the other producers," Stewart said.

Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."

"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.

Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.
Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."
In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.
In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.

Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."

Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.
In that 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart reflected on what he believed made a successful relationship.

"I think it's being open and a good listener and to make connection," he said. "You don't have to be exactly the same but it's necessary that you can share – I think very important. So sharing and respecting."

Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: Google will block search access for schools that ban AI use
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other critics are accusing Google of trying to pressure U.S. schools to use AI.
story: Google said on Tuesday that it will turn off artificial intelligence in its educational apps for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators expressly enable it.
The Alphabet-owned search giant said that after surveying school administrators and teachers, it wants educational institutions to control students' access to various AI capabilities.

Access to Google's AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until "school administrators explicitly turn them on," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.
Schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available," Phillips told The New York Times.
While Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be turned off by default, schools can choose to turn on one, two or all three services, Google explained in a post on X Tuesday.
"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Phillips wrote in the post.
New policy prompts outcry

Google's new policy immediately prompted criticism that it is seeking to pressure schools to use its AI apps. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."
"No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech," he added.
A Google spokesperson declined to respond to Mamdani's remarks.

Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Google Classroom, and many students use school-provided Chromebooks, according to Google. Google drew backlash in August when it activated its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

In September, New York City schools said that AI would be banned until students reach high school and implemented a one-year delay on the use of generative AI for children in 2-K through eighth grade.
Lina Khan, who served as chair of the Federal Trade Commission from 2021 to 2025, said in a statement posted on X that Google is seeking to exploit its dominance in internet search.

"This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service," said Khan, who now chairs the board of the New York City Economic Development Corporation, a nonprofit group that promotes economic growth and investment in New York.

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," she added. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to "strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire." He said Google's technology in schools is not about learning but about "developing lifetime brand loyalty" for its products.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, accused Google of putting its business interests ahead of education. "Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether," she said in a statement.

title: JetBlue hikes baggage fees for the second time this year
summary: Airlines have raised baggage fees and ticket prices to help offset the surging cost of jet fuel this year.
story: JetBlue on Tuesday said it is raising its checked bag fees for the second time in less than a year as the carrier moves to offset rising jet fuel and operating costs.

As of Tuesday, checking one piece of luggage for domestic, Caribbean and Latin American flights for most economy passengers will cost $50, up from $39 for off-peak periods, according to JetBlue. For peak travel periods, the fee will rise to $55, up from $49.
In March, the airline hiked its checked-bag fees by up to $9, citing "rising operating costs."
The airline told CBS News the baggage fee increase "helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one."
JetBlue also said it encourages customers to add their checked bags to their trips at least 24 hours before departure, enabling them to save up to $15 on the first checked bag.

JetBlue Plus, JetBlue Business and JetBlue Premier cardmembers can check one bag for free for the cardholder and up to three travel companions, according to the airline. TrueBlue Mosaic members may also check at least one bag for free. Mosaic 2, 3 and 4 members each get two free checked bags.

Surging global oil prices this year have sharply pushed up the cost of jet fuel, airlines' second-largest operational cost after labor. The price of jet fuel was $4.41 per gallon on Monday, up from just over $2 per gallon in January, according to Airlines for America's jet fuel price tracker.
Other carriers have also raised their baggage fees this year, including Delta, United and Southwest.
— CBS News' Kathryn Krupnik contributed to this report.

title: How Wall Street analysts think the midterms could affect stocks
summary: Despite the political drama surrounding U.S. elections, stocks have historically risen following midterms, market data shows.
story: The midterm elections could reshape Congress as lawmakers grapple with persistent inflation, high energy prices and rising fiscal debt. For investors, by contrast, the political outcome could deliver a boost.

Data from financial firm Edward Jones shows that the S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970. In the six months following midterm elections, S&P returns averaged 15.5%.

"Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook," Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at the global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email on Tuesday as Americans cast their votes.

With congressional control in the balance, Wall Street analysts are also considering the impact divided government could have on stocks if the Democrats win the House, Senate or both chambers. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to analysts.

"Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, a capital markets firm, said in an email Tuesday. "That tends to be good for earnings."

Less stock market volatility doesn't guarantee investors an easy ride, however. Gridlock in Washington, D.C., could also fuel another partisan standoff on the nation's debt, which recently surpassed $40 trillion, or spur the U.S. government to increase its borrowing to fund its priorities, according to economists.
That could unnerve bond investors, who are worried that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a note to investors.
"Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations," he said.

The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, estimates that the U.S. will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer of 2027. At that point, lawmakers will have to decide whether to raise the debt ceiling, temporarily suspend it or risk another government shutdown.

Volatility could also persist if President Trump continues to rely on his executive authority to accomplish his priorities, Yardeni said. In that case, Democrats would have little power to restrain Mr. Trump even if they controlled Congress, he noted.

"Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings," Yardeni said.

A Democratic sweep could have other implications for the economy beyond financial markets. That could include Democrats blocking Trump-appointed regulators, according to Jaret Seiberg, a financial policy analyst and managing director at investment bank TD Cowen.
"They [could] leverage this power to force the President to fill Democratic seats on independent agencies like the FDIC, SEC and CFTC," he said.

A Democratic majority in the Senate would also elevate Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, to head the Senate Banking Committee, giving her more latitude to pass populist legislation, Seiberg added. Warren would replace South Carolina Republican Sen. Tim Scott, who currently chairs the influential panel.
However, lawmakers would still be restricted in what they can do at a federal level, given the president's ability to veto legislation, UBS analysts said in a research note.

title: New Jersey's governor warns ports against accepting Russian diesel
summary: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said ports and terminal operators receiving shipments of Russian diesel could face criminal penalties.
story: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is warning local port officials and terminal operators against accepting imported Russian diesel, saying that the shipments would break federal law.

In a Nov. 2 letter, Sherrill said that Congress in April 2022 banned energy imports from Russia in response to the country's attack on Ukraine two months earlier. Importing Russian diesel would violate the ban and could lead to civil and criminal charges, she said, pledging to use legal and regulatory measures to ensure that New Jersey's ports and facilities are not used to receive Russian diesel.

In a Truth Social post in October, President Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release millions of tons of diesel over the following three months for use in both the U.S. and global markets. The Treasury Department also announced on Oct. 9 that it would issue a temporary general license "to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
Sherrill, a Democrat, said in the letter that Mr. Trump and Treasury officials do not have blanket authority to waive congressional sanctions on Russia.

"New Jersey will not stand by while Donald Trump supports Vladimir Putin at the expense of Americans. Instead of lowering costs, he is helping finance Putin's war against Ukraine and a global campaign of violence and terror that endangers U.S. service members abroad," Sherrill said in a statement. "As a Navy veteran, I cannot let that stand unchallenged, and New Jersey's ports shouldn't be complicit."
Russia has sent multiple oil tankers carrying diesel to the U.S., including at least one that may be headed for New Jersey, she added.

"Any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties. I urge you to turn away any tanker that seeks to use your facilities in furtherance of such unlawful activity," Sherrill said in the letter, which is directed to port and terminal operators in the state.
A Trump administration official told CBS News that granting the general license allowing Russian diesel to supply global markets complies with all applicable U.S. laws.

"The President secured a deal to supply global markets with diesel, lowering prices for the United States and the world," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement to CBS News. "Lowering prices for America's great farmers, truckers and families remains a top priority as the President simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries that are driving up costs and hurting American consumers. No one has done more than President Trump to bring this brutal war — a war that never would have started if he were President — to an end."

U.S. diesel costs have soared as the ongoing war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries drive up oil prices. As of Tuesday, the national average price for a gallon of diesel was $6.29, according to AAA. Although that is down from a record high of $6.53 in September, prices remain sharply higher than a year ago, when diesel averaged $3.68 a gallon.

title: AI deepfakes pose risks to consumers and voters, experts warn
summary: "When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," said one cybersecurity expert focused on political campaigns.
story: Advances in artificial intelligence are making it a cinch to create so-called deepfake images, videos and audio recordings, raising concerns that bad actors could bombard people with hyper-realistic scams and spread disinformation.

Deepfakes that use the voices and likenesses of public figures, including celebrities or political candidates, can also deceive the public in various ways, security experts told CBS News. By one measure, fewer than 10% of people can recognize an audio deepfake, according to Doppel, a social engineering defense platform for detecting AI-enabled threats.
"In a test, only 8% of people realized an AI agent was calling them, whereas 92% of people thought they were speaking to a human," said Doppel co-founder Kevin Tian.

AI's capacity to churn out deepfakes at scale is a pressing issue in the political arena, according to security experts. AI-generated advertisements featuring deepfakes of politicians have already surfaced across the internet and social media ahead of the midterm elections.

In one such incident in Texas, a phony, AI-manipulated social video targeting Senate candidate James Talarico purported to show a former student accusing the Democrat of sexual misconduct, according to The Poynter Institute's PolitiFact service.

"When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," Michael Kaiser, CEO of Defending Digital Campaigns, a nonpartisan organization that provides free cybersecurity services to political campaigns, told CBS News.

As of mid-October, political campaigns had spent more than $137 million on at least 220 AI-generated ads, some of which feature deepfakes of candidates, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks ads by political candidates.

"AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year. For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle," Erika Franklin Fowler, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, said in a statement this month. She noted that in most cases, the creators of the ads don't disclose that they were made using AI.
Even when someone suspects an ad is AI-generated or features a deepfake, the ad's visuals still can make an impression and shape opinion, the project's co-director, Travis Ridout, told CBS News.
"Even if we know it's not real, that sticks in one's mind," he added.
Prompting for deepfakes

Deepfakes are a kind of synthetic media that replicate a private individual's or public figure's image and likeness. Examples include a voice that sounds like a colleague or relative on the other end of a phone line, or a political figure appealing to voters for support or donations.
Raul Liive, a deepfake expert at Veriff, an AI-powered identity verification company, said the ease and speed with which deepfakes can be made and deployed today pose major risks.

"Every day that goes by, the generation of deepfake data gets easier and easier," he told CBS News. "If you wanted to fake someone's face years ago, you needed to make an effort to create fake data and use Photoshop. But now, to generate a fake face, you can just prompt your AI tool."

Veriff has documented a 300% increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts against businesses this year, compared with 2025. Liive outlined several examples of how bad actors use the tech to target businesses and unsuspecting consumers.
"A purported friend of yours calls and asks for a loan, but you know that person, and they've never made that kind of request before," he said.
Other types of scams center around medical emergencies. A caller could say they have a medical bill they urgently need help paying.

"Ask yourself what is the chance that someone you know would actually ask you something like that?" he said. "You can also hang up the phone and call the contact back on the number you have for them, or use another channel to validate their identity, if the request seems suspicious."

Veriff research on deepfakes found that consumers struggle to spot deepfakes, leaving them vulnerable to manipulation. In one test the firm conducted, 70% of people misidentified a deepfake video of a female character as being real.

The old telltale signs that something was a deepfake, like a human having six fingers or three hands, are also disappearing from AI content. Veriff found that people look for unreliable visual cues, such as unnatural skin or oddities in a subject's hair or teeth, which AI is increasingly eliminating from the content it generates.

Meanwhile, eroding public confidence in what they see could also undermine trust in legitimate content. Kaiser pointed to a photo of Sen. Mitch McConnell posing with his wife from his hospital bed, released amid speculation that the senator had died following a medical emergency earlier this year. Although the photo was authentic, some Internet users suggested it had been manipulated.

"That's an example of people just not trusting what they are seeing," Kaiser said. "People don't know if what they are looking at is legitimate, or if requests for donations are real. They're questioning everything that's going on and that disadvantages and erodes trust in the whole system."

title: Binance customers withdraw $7.42 billion after crypto heist
summary: Binance said the net outflow from the cryptocurrency exchange represents just 3% of its total holdings.
story: Binance customers withdrew $7.4 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.

On Monday, a Binance spokesperson said customers also deposited $2.7 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $4.7 billion in the company's holdings.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 3% of its $157 billion in total assets.

"The net outflow is a relatively limited portion of Binance's overall asset base," the Binance spokesperson said in an email. "Withdrawal levels are stabilizing to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity."
North Korea denies involvement
The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.
North Korea denies involvement in the attack. On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement "a trite provocation" and "an absurd rhetoric."

"This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the 'cyber crime' incidents whenever they occur on an international scale," she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
$3 billion frozen
Roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets were frozen, according to Binance. Freezing crypto funds allows certain issuers to block the transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world.

The hacker group believed to be responsible for the attack, known as "TraderTraitor," was converting most of the stolen assets into Ethereum in a move to hide their tracks, the FBI said Saturday. TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds. By early Sunday morning, it said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount.

title: Snap settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Snap joins Alphabet, Meta and TikTok in resolving allegations that its social media platform was designed to encourage addictive behavior.
story: Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, reached a settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit on Monday, resolving claims before the case was set to go to trial this month, according to lawyers for the plaintiffs.

The teenage plaintiffs, identified in court documents as S.J. and K.D.B., had alleged in the suit that Snapchat was designed to be addictive and that using the platform from a young age contributed to their mental health issues.

"We are glad to reach resolution for our clients," Mark Lanier, founder of The Lanier Law Firm and lead counsel for the plaintiffs, said in a statement to CBS News. "We believe this jury would have found the companies' conduct reprehensible."

Snap was the last social media company named in the lawsuit to settle the case, which was set for opening arguments this week. Meta resolved claims last week, while Alphabet and TikTok, the other defendants, each also resolved the allegations.
Terms of the Snap settlement were undisclosed, according to Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Emily Jeffcott, trial counsel for K.D.B.
In a statement to CBS News, Snap said that "the parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner."
The suit was one of several bellwether cases brought by plaintiffs who have alleged that social media platforms harmed their mental health and were designed to keep young users hooked.
In a landmark decision earlier this year, a jury found Meta and Google-owned YouTube liable and awarded $6 million to the lead plaintiff.

Meta also agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion and add child-safety measures to its social media platforms as part of an August settlement with dozens of U.S. states. The states accused Meta of deliberately designing its platforms to be addictive and of misleading users and the public about the technology's risks.

title: Meta settles social media addiction lawsuit, averting trial
summary: Two plaintiffs alleged that Meta and Snap designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior.
story: Meta has settled a social media addiction lawsuit, resolving claims against the technology giant before the case was set to go to trial next month, according to a lawyer for one of the plaintiffs.

The suit was brought by an 18-year-old woman identified in court documents as K.D.B. who alleged that Meta and Snapchat parent company Snap, which remains a defendant in the case, designed their social media platforms to foster addictive behavior. Another plaintiff in the lawsuit, dubbed S.J., settled with Meta last week.
Terms of Meta's settlement were not disclosed.
S.J. and K.D.B. also originally sued TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube platform, which each separately settled before trial.
The plaintiffs claim that the social media platforms contributed to their mental health struggles.

"We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," Emily Jeffcott, the trial counsel for K.D.B., said in a statement.
Joseph VanZandt, an attorney with the law firm Beasley Allen who is representing S.J., said the plaintiffs will proceed with their complaint against Snap.

"Each plaintiff alleges that Snap designed Snapchat to maximize the time young users spend on the app, using features such as Snapstreaks, Snapscores, push notifications, and filters, and that their compulsive use of Snapchat caused and contributed to severe mental and physical health injuries, including depression, anxiety, an eating disorder, and self-harm," he said in an email.
Snap disputes the allegations and has defended the company's practices.
Jury selection began this week in Los Angeles, with opening statements expected to begin in early November. Lawyers for the plaintiffs have said they expect the trial to last into mid-December.
A spokesperson for Meta, which still faces similar litigation alleging that its social platforms harm users' mental health, said the company will continue to defend itself in court.

"Trials, dismissals and settlements are all common in the bellwether process, and this litigation is no exception," she said in a statement. "We will continue to defend ourselves in court, and we stand by our record. We've spent more than a decade building protections for teens, and our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general goes even further with strict time limits, no access at night, and no notifications during school hours."

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.1 billion to dozens of states that alleged the company used its social platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, to hook young internet users while concealing the risks.

title: Binance resumes withdrawals for some cryptocurrencies after heist
summary: The exchange said it would resume withdrawals in phases, pending security checks.
story: Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X.

As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereum, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."

The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.

The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

title: Marvell to acquire Lumentum in $115 billion AI connectivity deal
summary: Marvell Technology said megadeal for Lumentum will help the merged company serve the growing market for AI data centers.
story: Marvell Technology announced Monday that it would acquire Lumentum Holdings in a deal valued at $115 billion, one of the biggest tech industry deals ever.

Marvell said the purchase of Lumentum, which manufactures lasers, circuit switches and other products used for data centers, would make the enlarged company a "category leader in AI connectivity." Marvell, founded in 1995, makes data infrastructure semiconductor products.

"AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy said in a statement. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come."
Nvidia earlier this year said it was buying a $2 billion stake in Lumentum, according to Bloomberg.

Marvell, despite the aggressive pullback in AI stocks last week, believes the investment is still warranted. Markets appear less certain. Marvell shares slid more than 1% before the opening bell, and Lumentum fell almost 3% after the announcement of the all-stock deal.
Marvell said that the merger will unite the companies' complementary technologies and engineering expertise, allowing it to create an end-to-end system that meets a broader set of customer needs.
The deal, subject to stockholder approval, is expected to close in the first half of 2028. It comes amid a boom in data center construction, which has sparked backlash nationwide.

title: $6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
summary: A cyberattack on Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was likely carried out by North Korea, according to a blockchain intelligence firm.
story: A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.
What is TraderTraitor?

In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
The FBI on Saturday also accused TraderTraitor of being behind the attack, saying the hackers have been converting the stolen funds into Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency.
The hackers are preparing the funds for "further laundering stages," the FBI said in a statement.
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.

Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.
Working "around the clock"

Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: How hard is it to recover the $6 billion stolen from Binance?
summary: Security experts are calling it the "largest bank robbery in human history." Getting all of the stolen crypto funds won't be easy.
story: After hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the cryptocurrency exchange said Friday it is working to recover the assets, a multi-pronged process that experts said involves coordinating with law enforcement and tracking the movement of the stolen funds.

"Binance has begun recovering affected assets for users and continues to work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace, freeze and recover additional funds," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News.

Ari Redbord, a former federal prosecutor and the global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company tracking the stolen funds, called the heist the "largest bank robbery in human history."

TRM and other security firms attributed the attack to an elite hacking unit linked with North Korea known as "TraderTraitor." The funds were siphoned from internet-connected wallets on Binance's trading platform, Redbord said. The entire operation took roughly 20 minutes, according to Binance.

"The way a cryptocurrency exchange works is basically just like a bank. People put their funds in the bank, and those funds go onto wallets that are controlled by the exchange," Redbord told CBS News. "What North Korea was able to do was breach the hot wallets where Binance was keeping all of those funds."
As it works to recover the stolen assets, Binance vowed in a social media post to cover the full losses using company funds.
"We will pursue all available avenues to identify those responsible and hold them accountable," Binance said.
How does the recovery process work?
Redbord called the effort to recover Binance customers' funds the "fastest and largest" he's ever seen.

The first step involved blocking the hackers from transferring the funds. Within an hour after the attack, stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether had frozen $2.4 billion of the stolen assets, he said. Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, also froze assets, according to TRM Labs.

Issuers of stablecoins — a type of cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, such as the U.S. dollar — can block transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world, speeding the recovery effort. A total of $3 billion in crypto assets have been frozen, the Binance spokesperson told CBS News.
However, roughly $2.4 billion in stolen funds consist of bitcoin and ether — those funds are now "beyond any issuer's reach," according to a blog post from TRM Labs.
Bitcoin and ether "move on public blockchains, and they cannot be frozen," Redbord said. "That is a very, very specific capability that [only certain] stablecoin issuers have."
The best shot at recovering those funds is if the thieves try to convert the crypto to regular currencies, including cash, he added.
In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."
The cyberattackers are now likely laundering the stolen funds to evade detection by law enforcement, according to Redbord.
How long could it take to recoup the funds?
To actually recover the frozen funds, stablecoin issuers will start by moving the assets into a wallet that North Korea cannot access, he said.

"Law enforcement will follow up with what they call a 'seizure warrant,' which basically says we need you to actually physically transfer these funds to a U.S. government account," Redbord told CBS News.
After the funds are seized, government officials will have to pursue a civil forfeiture proceeding in court to recover the crypto assets.

"The government must show that the funds were associated with the activity at issue," Redbord said. "It is the final step before the funds can be taken permanently from the bad actor and given to the government or victims."

Any of the Binance funds that aren't recovered could be used by North Korea to carry out illicit transactions with countries like Russia, Roman Bieda, chief intelligence officer at Recoveris, a Swiss blockchain intelligence company, told CBS News.

"Freezing assets and recovering them are two very different things," he said. "North Korea has a history of using stolen cryptocurrency to circumvent international sanctions and finance its activities."
In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.

Given the scale of the Binance theft, it's unclear how long it could take for the crypto exchange to recoup the stolen assets. In one case, Bieda said his team worked for a Swiss client in which it took 14 months to recover $10.5 million in stolen crypto.

"The process remains unpredictable," he said in an email, emphasizing the close coordination required between law enforcement, crypto issuers and other stakeholders to track down the funds. Figuring out where the money went is only half the battle, he said.
"Knowing whom to contact and reaching them before the assets move again can make all the difference, and this is really challenging," Bieda said.

title: Nasdaq sheds more than 700 points as tech stocks slump
summary: Disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears on Friday that the AI trade could unravel.
story: The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled more than 700 points on Friday, a rocky close to October trading amid growing investor concerns about the health of the critical technology sector.

The rout followed a series of earnings reports from major tech companies that fell short of Wall Street's expectations. Intel's stock tumbled nearly 29% on the day, the chipmaker's biggest single-day drop since 1974. Shares of Google's parent, Alphabet, also continued to struggle following a 12% slide on Thursday that erased roughly $500 billion in market value.
Shares of Nvidia, the maker of advanced chips used to power AI models and a bellwether for the sector, fell 4.2%.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

"The slump in tech stocks (and the attendant deterioration in tech sentiment) isn't simply a financial phenomenon and could undermine industry fundamentals by making it more difficult for companies to raise incremental debt and equity," he added in a separate report.
The negative sentiment around tech spread to other major stock indices on Friday. The S&P 500 sank 140 points, or 1.8%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 572 points, or 1.1%.
Debt reckoning?

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

"Mega-cap stocks have faced increased selling pressure over the past two weeks as elevated AI-related spending and rising financing costs raise concerns over the path to profitability," Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for brokerage firm LPL Financial, said in an email. "Recent earnings reports have added to these concerns, revealing slowing growth in select hyperscalers' core businesses."
Another factor weighing on tech stocks is investor expectations that the Federal Reserve will have to keep raising interest rates to curb economic growth and subdue inflation, which remains elevated.

The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged this week, but many economists think it will hike rates as early as December and into 2027. That would make it more expensive for companies to borrow money to build the data centers required to power AI services, cutting into corporate profits.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."
Still, U.S. stocks remain only 3.4% below their all-time high, boosting the value of workers' 401(k) accounts.

Cryptocurrency prices also slumped after hackers believed to be linked to North Korea stole more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell toward $77,000, from more than $86,000 earlier this month.

title: Medline electric beds pose fire hazard after 2 deaths, FDA warns
summary: The medical equipment supplier's motorized beds can overheat and cause fires, regulators said in an urgent alert to consumers.
story: The Food and Drug Administration is warning that electric hospital beds from medical equipment supplier Medline can pose a fire hazard, after two people died and another 16 users were seriously injured.
Medline, based in Northfield, Illinois, issued an "urgent" safety notice this week instructing customers to discontinue using its beds and other products without first modifying them.

The company's hospital beds use built-in electric motors and remote controls that an operator can use to adjust a patient's position for treatment. Medline said that under certain conditions, including when their motors or other components jam, the beds' electrical components can overheat, leading to smoking, melting, burning and fire.

"Overheating of the bed's electrical components may progress to smoking, sparking, melting, burning, and/or fire," Medline said, according to the FDA alert. "These events may increase the risk of adverse health consequences, including electrical shock and burns."
Medline added that using the beds' accessories can pose a risk of asphyxiation or entrapment, both of which can lead to injury or death.
Medline is advising vendors to halt sales of its branded beds and related equipment, including bed rails, mattresses and bed kits.
The company, which is publicly listed and has a market value of $43 billion, said it is ending production of homecare and long-term care beds and accessories and exiting the market.
In an Oct. 24 press release, the company recommended modifications for customers still using the beds.

A Medline spokesperson told CBS News that customers can continue to use its products in accordance with the company's instructions. Medline will also provide users with additional information about any affected products in the future, the spokesperson said.
For more information, Medline customers can contact the company at 800-950-0128 (option 7).

title: Millions of French press coffee makers recalled due to burn risk
summary: Product safety regulators said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, leading to burn injuries.
story: Coffee appliance company Bodum USA is recalling 5.9 million French press makers, warning that the glass carafe can break and cause burn injuries.

Bodum USA is the American subsidiary of a Danish-Swiss company that specializes in coffee hardware. So far, the company has received 70 reports of glass carafes breaking, 48 of which resulted in burns, according to a notice posted by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission.
The French press coffee makers were sold on Amazon.com, in retailers including Target and Walmart, and other stores between 1974 and October 2026.
The agency said the glass carafes can unexpectedly break if they are damaged or cracked, which can happen when customers use metal spoons to stir coffee.

"While the rate of reported incidents involving carafe breakage during use is extremely low, especially considering that Bodum has sold millions of these products in the U.S. for decades, this recall will further encourage the safe use of our French Press Coffee Makers," Bodum USA said in a statement.
A Bodum USA customer service representative told CBS News that the company was not offering refunds to customers.

The recall involves a variety of Bodum USA models, including 8-cup French presses and 12-cup Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper and Kenya models, according to CPSA. The recall number is 27-055.

Safety regulators said customers who purchased one of the recalled French press makers should not use metal utensils to stir the coffee and should avoid using the carafes if they are cracked or damaged. Customers can contact Bodum to receive a plastic stirring spoon.

For more information, consumers can contact the company toll-free at 888-879-8213 Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET; email at Bodum3302@sedgwick.com; or online at www.bodumfrenchpressrecall.expertinquiry.com or www.bodum.com (click on "Recall Information").

title: Midterm elections put Social Security funding gaps on the ballot
summary: With Social Security's main trust fund on course to be depleted in 2032, Congress will face mounting pressure to find remedies and avert benefit cuts.
story: Next week's midterm elections could prove momentous for Social Security, with time running out to put the program on solid financial ground. Social Security trustees' most recent report projects that the program's main trust fund is on course to be depleted by late 2032, after which Social Security recipients would face a more than 20% cut in benefits.

In effect, that means the burden of repairing Social Security will fall on both sitting and newly elected lawmakers. If Congress wants to avert what would amount to a devastating financial blow for millions of Americans, it will need to solve an issue that previous generations of legislators have punted on for decades.

"The pressure on Congress is going to just be tremendous going forward," said Martha Shedden, president of the National Association of Registered Social Security Analysts, an organization that trains Social Security advisers. "Every time that the annual trustees report comes out, there's more and more consternation about what lawmakers are doing."

Social Security's funding is running low largely due to demographic factors, as the U.S. population ages. More baby boomers are claiming benefits while comparatively fewer workers are paying into the program, forcing the agency to draw down its trust funds.

Concerns over the future of Social Security — a key issue for older Americans, a powerful political constituency — have surfaced in multiple electoral races across the country, including in key battleground states.

In the Michigan Senate race, for example, Republican candidate Mike Rogers highlighted the importance of eliminating fraud when asked to outline possible fixes to the program during an Oct. 25 debate. Rogers' opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, expressed support for removing the cap on income subject to employee payroll taxes "so that the rich pay their fair share."
The current payroll tax income limit is $184,500, with any earnings above that amount exempt from payroll taxes. The tax is 12.4%, with employers and workers each contributing 6.2%.

Other candidates around the country have also endorsed scrapping the cap, which would require high-income workers to pay the Social Security tax on a greater share of their income. In a recent analysis of 20 Senate races by economist Jon Schwabish, around half of the candidates said they would support raising or eliminating the cap.

Others have been more vague about their plans to shore up Social Security, simply committing to ensuring that Americans collect their full benefits rather than offering detailed policy proposals. Previous proposals have floated gradually raising the retirement age or means-testing benefits, according to Boston College's Center for Retirement Research.
Battleground battle

Social Security reform is also a hot-button issue in the battleground state of Maine, which data shows has the oldest population of any U.S. state. Around 390,000 Maine residents were collecting Social Security as of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration, more than a quarter of the state's total population.

In a September AARP poll of nearly 1,000 likely Maine voters aged 50-plus, 81% said Social Security is one of the issues that will factor into their vote. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, and her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, have each proposed possible ways to stabilize Social Security.
Jackson, a logger who previously served in Maine's state senate, has committed to eliminating the payroll tax income cap.

"People who work hard their entire lives should be able to retire with dignity," Jackson said in a statement to CBS News. "While Susan Collins has repeatedly voted to weaken Social Security, I'll work to scrap the cap because billionaires should pay into Social Security at the same rate teachers and loggers do. Social Security is a promise, and I intend to keep it."

Collins has painted herself as a champion for reform, having co-sponsored the Social Security Fairness Act with Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio. The bill, which passed in 2025 under former President Joe Biden, eliminated federal policies that barred employees with a public pension from collecting their full Social Security benefits and that reduced benefits for those workers' surviving spouses and family members.

In a television interview last week with News Center Maine, a local media outlet, Collins suggested creating a bipartisan commission to develop solutions to the projected Social Security shortfall, "such as potentially raising the earnings cap for Social Security taxes." She also vowed not to cut benefits, a proposal that has gained traction among some Republicans.

"As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, the author of the Social Security Fairness Act, and a longtime advocate for Maine's seniors, I remain committed to keeping the Social Security program strong for current and future generations," she said in the interview.
Shedden said Maine's Senate race could signal where the national debate over Social Security is heading after the midterms.

"The question is increasingly shifting from whether higher-income Americans should contribute more to how much more, and whether Congress can turn that emerging agreement into bipartisan legislation before the trust fund deadline forces the issue," she told CBS News.

title: DoorDash gobbles up Instacart in $17 billion deal
summary: DoorDash's purchase of Instacart for $65 per share will unite two of the country's largest grocery and food-delivery companies.
story: DoorDash said Thursday that it will buy Instacart for $17 billion, uniting one of the nation's top grocery delivery services with a major food delivery company.
DoorDash, which will pay $65 per share for Instacart, said the acquisition will benefit communities by enabling more supermarkets to use Instacart's platform to run their websites.

"Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash, said in a statement. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
Consumers will benefit by having more stores to choose from, speedier delivery options and access to savings when they shop locally, DoorDash also said in announcing the acquisition.
"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," DoorDash said.
Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada.

DoorDash was founded a year later in San Francisco as a restaurant-delivery business and expanded into grocery delivery in 2020 amid a pandemic-induced surge in demand. The San Francisco-based company later teamed with the supermarket chain Kroger in 2022 and with Costco last month.
The deal will beef up DoorDash's grocery delivery services, making it a more potent competitor to Amazon and Walmart.

DoorDash's most recent earnings report, released on Wednesday, shows its revenue grew 34% from a year ago. Its total number of orders rose 28%, a sign the company is continuing to grow in the highly competitive delivery business. By the end of 2024, DoorDash held nearly 61% of the food delivery market share, topping Uber Eats and Grubhub, which held around 26% and 6%, respectively, according to Consumer Edge.
Survival of the biggest

The acquisition is the latest sign of consolidation in the delivery services industry, which is increasingly dominated by larger players. As competition intensifies, companies like Instacart have struggled to maintain their market share. Instacart now commands 18% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms, down from 26% five years ago, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company.

DoorDash's acquisition of Instacart  also comes as more people migrate from in-person stores toward apps to order their weekly groceries. Nearly 150 million Americans grocery shopped online as of 2025, according to Capital One.
As online shopping becomes more prevalent, some companies are experimenting with personalized pricing, which involves using AI and consumer data to charge shoppers different prices for the same item.

The advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative has slammed the practice as unfair and predatory. In a months-long investigation last year, the group found that identical grocery items on Instacart could differ in price by as much as 23% from one customer to the next.

Federal regulators are now scrutinizing such practices. The Federal Trade Commission on Thursday said it has opened a probe into DoorDash and Instacart, along with seven other companies across retail and transportation, to examine how they set prices.

DoorDash, which has a market value of $73 billion, said the companies will operate as separate entities until the merger is finalized, which is expected in late 2027 or early 2028. After the deal closes, DoorDash said it plans to maintain Instacart's brand, technology and app.
