title: Fed holds interest rates steady even as inflation remains high
summary: The U.S. central bank left borrowing costs unchanged this month after hiking rates in September for the first time in three years.
story: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday after hiking borrowing costs in September to clamp down on inflation.
The central bank left the federal funds rate at a target range of 3.75% to 4%, keeping it unchanged after raising rates last month for the first time in three years.
In a statement, the Fed said economic activity is growing at a "strong pace" while acknowledging that inflation remains elevated.
"The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2% goal," Fed officials said.
Wall Street had forecast that the Fed would stand pat on rates. Investor reaction was muted, with the three major indexes remaining essentially flat after the Fed's announcement.

The Fed's benchmark rate is its main weapon for stabilizing consumer prices, which have crept up in recent months. The latest rate decision comes less than a week before Americans head to the polls for the midterm elections, where affordability issues will be top of mind for voters. President Trump has long urged the Fed to ease borrowing costs.
Stubborn inflation

During a press conference after the rate decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said economic indicators are moving in the right direction, citing robust consumer spending, a low unemployment rate and healthy overall economic growth.

He also said credit conditions — the terms lenders set for borrowing — have tightened for businesses and households since the Fed's September rate hike, a sign the economy is heading toward a "more durable period" of growth and price stability.
At the same time, he said inflation remains "too high" and acknowledged that the Fed hasn't yet succeeded in bringing inflation under control.

"On the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive, and yet Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the committee's objective for close to six years," he told reporters. "It's our responsibility to get inflation down."
Two dissents

Ten members of the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rates, voted to hold the benchmark rate steady. Two FOMC members — Fed Board Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank President Beth Hammack — voted to raise it by 0.25 percentage points.
"We just came out of a heck of a family fight, a serious, sober discussion," Warsh said Wednesday. "I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment."

Investors and Wall Street analysts widely expected the Fed to remain on hold in October, but many economists think policymakers will raise rates at their last meeting of the year in December and again in 2027.

"The two hawkish dissents, the wording of the policy statement, and prior comments from officials all suggest the central bank will hike rates in December," Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist for forecasting firm Oxford Economics, said in an email following the Fed's decision.

Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at investment advisory firm Pantheon Macroeconomics, said financial markets are pricing in an additional 0.75 percentage points of tightening over the next year as the Fed tries to douse inflation.
Warsh stays tight-lipped
Warsh demurred when asked if Fed officials would raise rates at their Dec. 8-9 meeting, citing his stated reluctance to telegraph his policy views.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now," he told a reporter.

The Iran war has kept global energy costs elevated, making it harder to bring down prices in the U.S. Last month, the closely watched Consumer Price Index rose at a 3.7% annual rate; core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.6% from a year ago. Both measures were above economists' expectations.
Solid economic growth and steady consumer spending are also exerting upward pressure on prices, complicating the task of taming inflation, according to economists.
What does this mean for your money?

The federal funds rate — what banks charge each other for overnight loans — influences the cost of borrowing across the U.S. economy. A rate hike can spur higher borrowing costs for bank loans, credit cards and auto loans, while boosting returns for savings accounts.

The Fed's pause in rate hikes could provide borrowers with some breathing room, Bankrate home lending expert Linda Bell said, citing potential relief for home equity rates. Still, consumers may be in for higher borrowing costs down the road. Matt Schulz, a chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree, said it's possible some loan rates could continue to climb heading into the holiday shopping season.

"Even though the Fed is leaving rates alone this month, it might raise rates again at its last meeting of the year in December," Schulz said in an email ahead of the Fed's decision. "That is far from guaranteed, but it is something that Americans should be aware of. It means that the debt they run up during the holidays could get a little more expensive to pay off before the year ends, through no fault of their own."
A surprise change
While the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged was widely expected, Warsh elicited surprise by announcing changes to the central bank's meeting schedule.

Policymakers will continue to meet eight times throughout the year. But starting in 2027, one of those meetings will be reserved for discussion and strategizing on monetary policy, Warsh said. At that meeting, the Fed will not vote on interest rates or issue a policy statement.
By 2028, Warsh said he expects two meetings to be dedicated to policy discussion and six to issuing rate decisions.

The change aligns with Warsh's broader vision for the Fed. He has been vocal in arguing for more limited communication from Fed officials, known as forward guidance, to preserve their flexibility in setting policy.

"Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals," he said. "But it's equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point."

title: See CBS News exit poll results for the 2026 midterm elections
summary: Here's a national look at what's on voters' minds in the 2026 midterm elections as they cast their ballots.
story: Note: Results will continue to update throughout the night; please check the CBS News desktop election app for the latest.
South Carolina Senate: Toss-up

CBS News rates the race between GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews a toss-up. Most voters don't think Darline Graham has the right experience to be a U.S. senator. But it's not a dealbreaker for all voters — about a quarter who hold this view are still voting for Graham, who was named to fill the seat held by her late brother, Lindsey Graham.
At the same time, about half of voters say of Andrews that her views are too extreme. And most of those voters are voting against Andrews.
Georgia Senate: Lean Democratic

Democrat Jon Ossoff is performing very well with Black voters as he defends his seat against GOP Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is on pace to win roughly the same share as when he won his runoff election in 2021. CBS News rates this race as lean Democratic.
He is also making some inroads with White voters, early exit polls show.
Most White voters are backing Collins, but this would be a really good performance by a Democrat in Georgia among White voters if this holds.
Also, on balance, more voters view Colllins' views as extreme than Ossoff's views.
Overview of CBS News 2026 exit polls for the midterm elections

President Trump is on track for the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election, according to early exit polls. Currently at 38%, it's lower than it was during Mr. Trump's first term, and lower than it was for George W. Bush in 2006 when his party lost both houses of Congress.
Midterm elections have often been a referendum on the sitting president, and this one is no exception. Roughly six in 10 say Mr. Trump is a factor in their vote for the House.
This is being driven largely by voters backing Democrats, who are overwhelmingly motivated by opposition to Mr. Trump.
But for those backing Republicans, it's less about the president. Back in 2018, most Republican voters said their vote was to support Mr. Trump. That figure is lower today.

The president has often told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, and for many in the MAGA base, they may be doing just that. Most MAGA Republicans say their vote is to support Mr. Trump, but most non-MAGA Reps say he is not a factor.
The mood of the electorate is a sour one
Voters are just plain not happy.

Current exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More are angry now about how things are going than they were in 2024, as economic anxiety persists. Those voting for Democrats are particularly likely to be angry.
The issue of the economy and trust in Mr. Trump to fix it helped propel him to victory in 2024, but voters feel no better about the condition of the economy today.

In fact, more voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago, and views of the economy are more in line with what we saw in the 2022 midterms, when the party in power lost seats.
Cost of living: Voters are feeling the pinch
Voters are feeling it in their pocketbooks. They are more than twice as likely to say their finances are worse rather than better, based on early exit polls.
Voters across parties express concern about affording everything from gas to groceries to utilities.
For two consecutive elections, most voters have said inflation caused hardship for their family,  including about one in five who describe that hardship as severe.

All this adds up to the cost of living being a major factor for voters across parties, but it's more crucial for those backing Democrats. Immigration enforcement is more crucial for those backing Republicans.

When voters are asked to pick their most important issue from a list, the economy comes out on top, followed by the state of democracy. Those voting for Democrats prioritize the state of democracy — an issue that has long concerned them.
For those backing Republicans, the economy is their most important issue, followed by immigration.
Voters who pick the state of democracy as their top issue are particularly likely to say government corruption is a crucial factor in their vote.
Government corruption: It's a major factor for voters across party lines
Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally say government corruption is a major factor in their vote — about the same as cost of living — and it's crucial to those voting for Democrats.
About six in 10 voters think President Trump puts his own personal interests over the country.
The Iran War

While the war with Iran is less of a factor for voters than the cost of living, the conflict is not popular. Most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.
Those most concerned about affording gas are the most likely to disagree with the decision to attack Iran.
Does all this dissatisfaction translate to satisfaction with the party out of power?
Neither political party is viewed favorably by a majority of voters.
About one in five backing Democrats for the House have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Most Democrats are motivated by their opposition to Mr. Trump.
And the Democratic Party isn't overwhelmingly seen as the party better able to handle key issues.
Emerging issues
Data centers arose as an issue in this campaign. In all the Senate battlegrounds, majorities oppose the construction of a data center in their community.
More voters see artificial intelligence as doing more to harm society than to help it.
Voter confidence

Large majorities of voters are at least somewhat confident that their votes will be counted accurately both nationwide and in their own states, and that eligible voters will be allowed to vote. But while they are confident in their votes being counted, those voting Republican are far less confident that people who are not eligible to vote will be prevented from voting.
This national exit poll measures the general preference for voters nationwide in their choice for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives, of course, is elected seat by seat.
A quick note on the states
Mr. Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including in states that he won by double digits in 2024.
In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.

And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.

title: Midterm results coming in as polls close in key states — live updates
summary: Polls are now closed in nine states and the results of the 2026 midterm elections are beginning to come in. Follow live updates here.
story: Election Day 2026 midterm voting live results:

title: Trump says he could use "tremendous powers" if Democrats win
summary: President Trump remained optimistic about GOP chances ahead of polls closing: "We have a good chance. But we're not going to be embarrassed."
story: "I have the ultimate power — it's called 'veto,'" President Trump told CBS News in an exclusive phone interview before polls closed across the country in this year's midterm elections, when asked about the prospect of a Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Mr. Trump says he is prepared to veto Democratic legislation if necessary, and he welcomes the moniker "Mr. Veto," in terms of describing his approach to Democrats, should they win a majority in the House or Senate.
Pollsters have been predicting some GOP losses and in late October, CBS News' polling suggested Republicans could be on track to lose control of the House.

Still, Mr. Trump remained optimistic on Tuesday when asked about the Republican Party's chances during the phone interview. And he said that regardless of the results and the makeup of Congress next year, he feels confident about his ability to pursue his agenda in the coming two years. He remarked that recent Supreme Court decisions have empowered him and his administration to wield expansive executive powers inside the federal government even if Congress tries to block him.

In the interview, Mr. Trump cited Trump v. Slaughter, a Supreme Court decision from earlier this year that allowed him to fire Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, and said that 6-to-3 decision enables him to exert sweeping control over many federal agencies, boards and commissions, regardless of who holds majorities in the House and Senate.
"We won the Slaughter case and the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before," Mr. Trump said.
The president said that he plans to move forward his agenda next year in numerous federal areas with this ruling as part of the foundation for his coming executive actions.
"The presidency, our presidency, is considered a strong presidency. You can do a lot," Mr. Trump said.
Mr. Trump also believes his veto power could eventually force Democrats to cut bipartisan deals with him, should they make gains.
"Historically, you veto for a couple of months and then they come and say, 'We've got to make a deal,'" Mr. Trump said.

Mr. Trump's comments signal that there will likely be a dramatic showdown between the executive branch and Congress next year, should Democrats win majorities in each respective chamber, and he asserted that he could ramp up his use of executive power if Democrats try to constrain him on Capitol Hill.

Two people close to Mr. Trump, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations, said discussions over executive actions have taken place at the White House in recent weeks, with deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought central figures in those talks. The range of issues being considered for further executive action includes immigration and trade, the people said.

One person close to the president said that "while Democrats may win power," Mr. Trump will "keep the power to do almost everything he wants" next year on trade, the border, managing the federal government and handling U.S. foreign policy and national security.

Regarding the midterm elections, Mr. Trump said he believes he did everything he could to help Republicans across the country in recent weeks, and said his efforts helped to recast the elections as a possible blue wave into something more competitive.

"If you remember, about 30, 40 days ago, people were saying it's going to be a big loss, and now people are talking about, like we could even win it," Mr. Trump said. "I think the tour made a big difference. I did 29 days, 33 of these things, and they were all massive rallies, they were big rallies. No one has ever done anything like it. And I think we got the word out. I think we got the enthusiasm out, too."

When asked about his motivation for his extensive tour of campaign stops, Mr. Trump said, "I just think that we're doing so well that I didn't want to see anything get in the way of what we've done," and he argued that the passage of last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and his efforts on trade are driving growth in different economic sectors.
The president did not make any firm predictions about Tuesday's outcome.
"We'll have to see," Mr. Trump said, noting that most Election Days come with surprises and unforeseen developments. "Will we win? We have a good chance. But we're not going to be embarrassed."

Mr. Trump spent part of Monday delivering a speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., where he talked at length about his push to renovate, clean or rebuild key structures at the White House and around the capital.
In the Tuesday interview, Mr. Trump said his speech was part of his desire to show the American people that he is using skills as a lifelong developer to redevelop Washington for their use.

"Obama criticized me," Mr. Trump said, referring to former President Barack Obama's criticism of Mr. Trump's activity. "But we had broken windows by the front door" at the White House, he said, and "it was such a sad thing to look at."
"It's the White House," Mr. Trump said. "You can't have an area where the stone is cracked and half-falling off the side of the wall. And I fixed it. You know, I'm very good at that."

"I actually enjoy doing it," Mr. Trump said. "A lot of people, that doesn't relax them, it makes them crazy, but with me, it relaxes me because I really do it well, and the White House is now pristine."

When asked about what his focus is for 2027, in terms of renovations in and around Washington, the president said he expects to finish the new ballroom at the White House and to begin work on his proposed 250-foot arch, which has faced legal challenges.
"I'll be finishing that," Mr. Trump said of the ballroom. "It's a ballroom and military complex." As for the arch, "We hopefully will be starting that."
"It's a celebration of success," Mr. Trump said of the planned arch.
"I do that stuff, it's fun for me, but it's important," Mr. Trump said of his many building initiatives, and he framed his projects as a larger attempt to spruce up the country.
"We had 97 places where we had 'S-G,' which means 'serious graffiti,'" Mr. Trump said of his administration's cleanup of Washington, D.C. "Ninety-seven places, like at the base of the Supreme Court."

As for his own political future, Mr. Trump said he is not yet talking with his advisers about pursuing a potential 2028 campaign, which would face steep constitutional and legal hurdles, and, for now, said the GOP has a "very good bench" of possible candidates.

title: Oklahoma man charged with mailing hundreds of white-powder letters
summary: An Oklahoma man faces federal charges after allegedly sending hundreds of letters containing white powder to public officials and media outlets ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections.
story: Washington — An Oklahoma man faces federal charges after allegedly sending hundreds of letters containing white powder to public officials and media outlets ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections.

According to charging documents unsealed on Tuesday, Robin Patrick Martin allegedly sent more than 700 envelopes to public officials of both parties across the country. Authorities said the powder contained in the envelopes was nontoxic and said the envelopes had messages written in UV-reactive ink, not easily seen by the naked eye.

Martin is charged with one count of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and another count of mailing threatening communications. Court records show Martin, 67, was arrested on Monday and was ordered detained pending a preliminary hearing on Nov. 9.

According to an FBI affidavit, Martin "described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election."

Some of the messages were marked with return addresses related to previous headquarters for the Green Party of the United States and Democratic Socialists of America. The DSA has cooperated with the FBI in its investigation, the affidavit said.

In one envelope addressed to the Oklahoma State Election Board ahead of the 2024 election, Martin allegedly wrote "stay on the right side of history your life might depend on it!" Federal prosecutors allege that the handwriting in that message was matched with the new batch of letters through a handwriting analysis.

According to the affidavit, the content of the letters sent in 2026 "all pertained to the upcoming 2026 national elections" and Martin allegedly referenced an organization known as the United States Traitor Elimination Army in his writings, threatening the recipients with being arrested for treason "OR WORSE!!"
Federal investigators also intercepted a message allegedly from Martin to FBI Director Kash Patel.

Surveillance footage allegedly showed Martin dropping off the envelopes at a USPS facility in both 2024 and 2026, and records analyzed by federal law enforcement allegedly show Martin purchased items used for the mailing in August of this year, as well as the ingredients for the "invisible ink" that was used to write on the envelopes.

In October, Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, confirmed that "suspicious mailings" were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including secretary of state offices and related election offices.

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. Dozens of members of Congress and election officials across the country reported being targeted by the mailings.
CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

title: U.S. launches strikes on Iranian targets in Strait of Hormuz
summary: The U.S. launched limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft, a senior U.S. official told CBS News.
story: The U.S. military launched limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News.

The strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island, a senior U.S. official said. It came after two incidents on Monday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired at an American fighter jet, leading it to return fire, according to two U.S. military officials. Later Monday, Iran fired a missile from Qeshm Island that threatened shipping, the officials said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes, which came on the eve of Election Day in the U.S. President Trump has been floating the idea of restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms, at the same time as U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a possible U.S.-Iran deal.
Qeshm Island, in the northern Strait of Hormuz, is crucial to the Iranian regime's efforts to monitor and exert control over commercial traffic through the waterway.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday that Tehran retained "the right to legitimate self-defense" after the new U.S. strikes, and would do so "until the military aggression has been completely and permanently brought to an end."

Iran has retaliated for attacks on its territory throughout the war sparked by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28 by targeting commercial shipping traffic in the strait and U.S. allies and interests across the Persian Gulf region.

As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between suggesting he could strike a deal to end the war with Iran, to warning that he could resume major attacks against the country.
In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible."

Later Monday night, however, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with" the Israeli leader, but he did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.

The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
In Israel, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.
As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47.1 billion in military expenditure alone, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

CENTCOM said the cost of replacing spent munitions alone was about $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. Another $6.1 billion was needed to replace lost equipment, and there has been around $11.9 billion spent on incremental costs including support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which have been targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.

title: Here's what Americans are voting on in today's elections
summary: Control of the House and Senate are at stake as Republicans and Democrats focus on battleground races in key states.
story: Voters throughout the country headed to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3, for the midterm elections, with control of Congress, dozens of governorships, and major policy proposals all on the line. More than 60 million others voted early, either in person or by mail.
What's on the ballot today?

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 seats in the Senate are up for grabs. Beyond Washington, 36 states will choose their next governor, while voters also decide on ballot measures on issues ranging from redistricting to abortion rights to a proposed billionaire tax in California.
What is a midterm election?

Midterm elections get their name because they happen in the middle of a presidential term. Although the president isn't on the ballot, the midterm elections often turn into referendums on the president and the party in power.
Key races that are high-stakes today:
House of Representatives

Republicans hold a narrow, three-seat majority in the U.S. House as voters head to the polls on Tuesday. Historically speaking, that could be a tall task for the GOP, as the party controlling the White House hasn't picked up seats in the House during the midterms since 2002.

The road to a majority for both parties runs through several key districts, the most prominent of which may lie in Pennsylvania. A cluster of four suburban Philadelphia, Lehigh Valley and central Pennsylvania districts are all held by Republicans in competitive territory. With control of the House being decided by such narrow margins, Democrats can put themselves within striking distance of a majority if they're able to flip all four seats, potentially making Pennsylvania an early bellwether for how the night will go.

Just to the north, in New York's 17th Congressional District in the Hudson Valley,  incumbent two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democratic challenger Cait Conley in a race that has focused a lot of time on foreign policy, immigration and data centers. Lawler has won this seat by less than 30,000 votes in the last two cycles and the district voted for Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but faces a much tougher hill to climb, with the national environment blowing strongly in the face of House Republicans.

Further to the west in Iowa, Republicans control all four House seats and have tight races expected in three of them.  In the 1st District in the southeastern part of the state, incumbent Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks will seek to defend herself in a seat that is no stranger to tight races, including in 2020 where Miller-Meeks won by just six votes. Another potentially vulnerable Republican incumbent lies in the 3rd District, where Rep. Zach Nunn seeks a third term in what has traditionally been Iowa's "bluest" district. The northeastern 2nd District, currently held by now-Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, is a slightly taller task for Democrats, and features two young candidates: 29-year-old GOP nominee Joe Mitchell, and 42-year-old Democrat Lindsay James.

Arizona, long a bastion of tight elections, is set to feature two more in the 1st and 6th congressional districts. In the state's 1st District, which includes parts of Phoenix, Scottsdale and other suburbs, GOP nominee Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, will face Democrat Amish Shah, a physician. Shah, who worked on the medical team for the New York Jets at the same time Feely played there, narrowly lost in 2024 to current Rep. David Schweikert. In the 6th district near the border, incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani is seeking a third term in a seat that he has held on to by less than 3 points in each of the last two cycles.

In Colorado, two House races could potentially make headlines for very different reasons on Election Night. In the deep-blue 1st Congressional District in Denver, 29-year-old Melat Kiros is a heavy favorite to become the first member of "Gen Z" to be elected to Congress, after she defeated longtime incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the primary. In the western part of the state, Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert faces an unexpectedly tight battle for reelection in the 4th District. This is a district with a strong Republican lean, as Mr.  Trump won it by more than 17 points just two years ago, but recent polling shows Boebert in a close  race with Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.

California is also set to potentially play a major role in determining who may control the House, as Democrats try to capitalize on a set of newly redrawn districts. The new map, designed to help Democrats pick up five seats currently held by Republicans, is intended to offset gains made by the GOP redistricted states. Among them is the hotly contested Central Valley 22nd congressional district, where incumbent Rep. David Valadao faces Democrat Randy Villegas. In southern California, Republicans look to hold onto the seat in the 48th district, which is being vacated by retiring Rep. Darrell Issa.

But the most intriguing races may be in South Texas, where Republicans hope to hold on to their gains among Latino voters in 2024. In the Corpus Christi border 15th District, Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz faces Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning music artist. President Trump has made gains among Latino voters in South Texas, but after the GOP-led push to redraw districts, most of the voters are unfamiliar with De La Cruz. A bit further north, in the newly-redrawn open 35th District near San Antonio, Johnny Garcia, a longtime county sheriff's deputy, will seek to flip the seat away from Republican candidate Carlos De La Cruz, Monica's brother. There are two other border districts that Democrats are hoping to hold onto that were drawn to be more friendly to Republicans: longtime Rep. Henry Cuellar's Laredo-area 28th District and Rep. Vicente Gonzalez's 34th District.
Senate
The GOP is also looking to protect a 53-47 majority in the Senate. While a total of 35 seats are on the ballot, the race is likely to come down to 11 battleground races.

Democrats look set to retain their seat in Georgia, as incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff appears to have a lead on his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins, according to polling. North Carolina, a longtime Democratic target, seems poised to turn blue, as popular former two-term Democratic governor Roy Cooper has been leading polls to take the seat currently held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.

In Maine, longtime Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is facing one of the toughest reelection battles of her 29-year Senate career. Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, is seeking a sixth term in a state Kamala Harris won by three points in 2024. She faces former state Senate President Troy Jackson, who was chosen at the state party convention to replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner on the ballot.

In Alaska, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola faces not one but two Dan Sullivans, one of whom is the Republican incumbent. The other, a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan, has drawn criticism from Republicans who argue his presence on the ballot could siphon votes away from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign has recently come under fire following reports that operatives linked to her campaign recruited the "other Dan Sullivan" in an alleged attempt to confuse voters. Peltola's campaign has denied those claims.

Ohio, meanwhile, is a chance for Democrats to reclaim a Senate seat in a state that has moved sharply toward the GOP in recent cycles. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his reelection bid in 2024, faces incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a race to finish the final two years of now-Vice President JD Vance's term. Mr. Trump won the state by more than 11 points in 2024, but recent polling shows Brown with a narrow  lead heading into Election Day.

Texas, Iowa and Kansas are all states where Mr. Trump won in 2024 by more than 13 points, but are squarely in play. In Texas, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a race that Democrats hope will deliver their first statewide election win in more than 30 years. Although Iowa has moved to the right over the last decade, Democrats also have their eyes on the Senate seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Joni Ernst. Rep. Ashley Hinson has been locked in a tight contest with Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for months. Kansas, on the other hand, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 1932, has also emerged as a battleground state. In a state Mr.  Trump won by more than 16 points, recent polling by The Washington Post shows Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton leading incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall by as much  as 9 points.

Michigan could be an opportunity for Republicans to flip a seat currently held by Democrats. Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers is making his second consecutive bid for the Senate two years after losing a tight race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. He now faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive who would be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate, in the race to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters.  If Rogers is able to win, it would mark the first Republican Senate victory in the state since 1994, although Mr. Trump has won the state twice. El-Sayed narrowly won the August primary against Democrat Haley Stevens, who then reversed course over the weekend and backed Rogers.
Governors' races
Voters in 36 states will be electing governors on Tuesday, with several contests taking place in states that could also play important roles in the 2028 presidential election.

In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in a race to replace term-limited GOP Gov. Brian Kemp. The contest has featured heavy spending, particularly on Jackson's side, while polls have Democrats within striking distance of winning the governor's mansion for the first time since 1998. If Bottoms wins, she would also become the first Black woman elected governor in American history.

Iowa presents what may be Democrats' best opportunity to flip a governor's mansion blue. State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Democrat currently holding statewide elected office in Iowa, faces Republican farmer Zach Lahn in a contest to replace retiring GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds. Sand has emphasized his bipartisan credentials throughout the campaign, and has held a consistent lead in the polls since the summer, giving his party a shot to win the governor's mansion for the first time since 2006.

Elsewhere in the Midwest, two other races in traditional battleground states have drawn national attention. Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is taking on  Republican Rep. John James in the race to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany are competing to replace retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Both states voted for Mr. Trump in 2024 and Biden in 2020, and both have outgoing Democratic governors.

The race in Ohio, which has trended red in recent years, may have attracted the most controversy, as Republican entrepreneur and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, the state's former health director. The race grabbed headlines in recent weeks when Ramaswamy's campaign released an ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, who accused her daughter of lying about her childhood. Acton has been estranged from her mother for nearly 50 years after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Although the ad recently drew bipartisan backlash, Ramaswamy — and then Mr. Trump — defended the ad but eventually stopped airing it just days before Election Day.
Ballot measures

Beyond the race for elected office, voters will also have their say on statewide and local ballot measures. The proposals cover a broad range of issues, including abortion rights, voting requirements, redistricting, taxes and government powers.

In California, one of the most closely watched proposals is Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state. The measure, which supporters claim would raise tens of billions of dollars, would direct the funds toward healthcare, food assistance programs and education. It's caused an intra-party fight among Democrats, with Sen. Bernie Sanders, who supports the proposal, repeatedly sparring with outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom, who opposes it.

Redistricting will also be on the ballot across the country, as states continue to fight over changes to their congressional maps mid-decade. Voters in Maryland and Missouri will consider proposals that would entail major changes to how congressional maps are drawn in their respective states. The passage of either could have significant implications for the balance of power in Washington, particularly in an era when House majorities are especially narrow.

Changes to the electoral process go beyond redistricting, as election rules are also on voters' minds in several states. Voters in California, Arizona, Colorado and Nevada will consider proposals that would create more stringent voter identification requirements. In Alaska, the ballot will feature a proposal that would repeal the state's controversial ranked-choice voting system.

Abortion will also take center stage in several states once again, more than four years after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Missouri voters will decide whether to repeal a state constitutional amendment protecting reproductive freedoms passed just two years ago. Idaho will consider a measure that would protect abortion until fetal viability, while Virginia voters will consider a similar measure to protect reproductive rights that would allow some restrictions later in pregnancy.

An emerging local ballot issue is the rapid expansion of data centers. More than 40 local ballot measures across over a dozen states will address key issues relating to data centers, including construction, zoning and approval requirements. Voters throughout Ohio will decide on more than 20 such measures, while communities in parts of Maine, Florida and Kansas will do the same.

title: Attorney and Trump foe targeted in Alaska ballot probe, sources say
summary: Marc Elias, a longtime Democratic attorney and vocal opponent of the Trump administration, received one of about 20 target letters sent by the DOJ in its Alaska ballot investigation.
story: Marc Elias, a longtime Democratic attorney and vocal opponent of the Trump administration, is a target in the Justice Department's criminal investigation into whether Democrats sought to confuse voters in Alaska by recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan, according to a law enforcement official and a second source familiar with the matter.

Elias is just one of a number of individuals who received either target letters, preservation letters or grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department in connection with the investigation, which is being led by the U.S. Attorney's Office in Alaska and also involves prosecutors from the Civil Rights Division's criminal section, multiple sources said.

Approximately 20 target and preservation letters have been issued to date in the probe. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, meanwhile, has separately received a grand jury subpoena, a law enforcement source told CBS News.
CBS News has reached out to the DSCC for comment.
President Trump in recent days has made public statements denouncing Elias on social media and calling for his prosecution.
"No one should be surprised that President Trump's Department is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day," Elias said in a statement to CBS News.
"This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets."

He added that his firm, Elias Law Group, "proudly" counts itself among Mr. Trump's political enemies and said they are "proud" to represent Democratic campaigns and progressive groups that fight back against his administration.

"We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation," he said. "We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box."
Federal prosecutors have not articulated what crimes they are investigating.

Last week, Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff for policy, suggested during an appearance on Fox News that they could investigate violations of 18 USC 241 — a civil rights statute that makes it unlawful for two or more people to conspire to threaten or intimidate anyone freely exercising their constitutional or federal rights.

The timing of the letters and subpoenas, which were sent out in recent days, appear to run afoul of the Justice Department's own internal guidelines and historic norms limiting investigative steps ahead of a national election.

Brandon Wrobleski, the acting chief of the criminal section at the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, has personally sought to recruit assistant U.S. attorneys in Alaska to assist with the probe, but some have declined or expressed discomfort about getting involved, several sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

Michael Heyman, the court-appointed U.S. Attorney in Alaska, took the unusual step last week of holding a press conference along with the FBI's special agent in charge in Anchorage in which he publicly disclosed the existence of a criminal investigation into whether operatives for Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola helped recruit independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan in a bid to confuse Republican voters.

The investigation picked up steam shortly after The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign's lawyers, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, were involved in the recruitment effort.

Such ballot-stacking tactics have been used in the past by members of both political parties and, while controversial, are generally not considered illegal. Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied any connection to the effort to put Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.

"This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska, and I have assigned several attorneys in my office to assist in the matter as well," Heyman said on Friday, adding: "As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters."

Heyman denied that the Justice Department was escalating its investigation or attempting to time its actions around the election, and cited the public reporting by the New York Times as the basis for the increased activity.
"We're not escalating anything except to the extent that a new article came out," he told reporters on Friday.

"This has been going on, you know, sort of quietly for several months, with the intent not to escalate anything. But to the extent that there are allegations that are made on the eve of the investigation that can go to the heart of the induction integrity, we are going to take it seriously — even if it is a few days before the election."

Elias and his team of lawyers have been involved in over 90 voting and election lawsuits, including dozens of challenges to the Justice Department's efforts to access unredacted voter rolls so they could be screened for possible non-citizens.

He is also involved in the civil litigation in Alaska, in which the Justice Department sought to block certification of the state's Senate election results in the midterm elections if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.
A U.S. district judge dismissed the Justice Department's lawsuit on Sunday, finding it lacked standing to bring the case.
Over the weekend, Mr. Trump called the efforts to get the second Sullivan onto the ballot a "fraud" and a "Democrat con job" that was perpetrated by Senator Charles Schumer and Elias.
"It was done by Schumer. I mean, that really started with Schumer and the lawyer, Marc Elias. And I think they should be held criminally responsible for it," Trump said.
Elias is one of several of Mr. Trump's political adversaries who have been targeted in recent DOJ criminal investigations.
Recently, prosecutors also obtained a search warrant for Minnesota Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, as part of an investigation into possible immigration fraud.

They also sought to charge two former senior FBI officials for lying to Congress about their roles in the bureau's Hunter Biden investigation and they tried to secure an indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who gave damaging testimony about President Donald Trump's actions during the attack on the U.S. Capitol to a House committee probing the event.

The grand jury declined to indict Hutchinson, and a federal magistrate judge dismissed the complaint against the former FBI officials, saying it lacked probable cause and appeared to be a politically-motivated prosecution that was intentionally timed with the midterm elections.

title: Supreme Court seems likely to favor Catholic schools in pre-K fight
summary: The Supreme Court is weighing a case involving Catholic preschools' efforts to participate in Colorado's universal preschool program.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared likely to side with Catholic preschools challenging Colorado's refusal to exempt them from a nondiscrimination requirement and let them participate in its universal preschool program.

The nondiscrimination mandate at the center of the dispute, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, requires participating schools to provide children with an "equal opportunity" to enroll regardless of their race, religion, sexual orientation and gender identity, among other characteristics.

When Colorado was preparing to implement the program, the Archdiocese of Denver, which oversees 34 Catholic preschools, sought an exemption from the nondiscrimination rule, since they only enroll families that align with the Catholic Church's teachings, including on marriage, family and sexual identity.
The state, however, denied the request for an accommodation and said the Catholic schools could not "discriminate against children or families in violation of state statute."

The Archdiocese, two of its parishes and a family then sued the state, arguing that their exclusion from the universal preschool program violated the Constitution's Free Exercise Clause. Lower courts sided with the state and said the sexual orientation and gender identity provisions of the nondiscrimination rule are neutral and apply generally to providers participating in the universal preschool program.

But in arguments that spanned two hours on Tuesday, the court's conservative majority appeared likely to rule in favor of the Catholic preschools. Such a decision would join a line of recent rulings in which the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has sided with religious institutions challenging their exclusion from state benefits programs, opening the door for more public dollars to flow to religious schools.
Oral arguments
Several of the conservative justices repeatedly raised concerns that the nondiscrimination rule was effectively a back-door way to keep religious entities out of the universal preschool program.

"You agree, don't you, that Colorado could not say that Catholic schools or evangelical schools or Orthodox Jewish schools were excluded from participation in the UPK program?" Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Helen Norton, Colorado's deputy solicitor general. "Then explain what the difference is between that and choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools would be unable to agree to."
Barrett suggested the effect of the nondiscrimination requirement is to "push out" those with traditional beliefs.

"Why not seek the win-win?" Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Norton about the state's refusal to exempt Catholic preschools. He noted that there are more than 2,000 preschools that participate in Colorado's universal preschool program, and only 34 are overseen by the Archdiocese of Denver.

"There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools an appropriate fit for their children," he said.
Justice Samuel Alito raised Colorado's recent record of losses at the Supreme Court in religious liberty cases, in which the high court sided with a Christian baker, website designer and counselor.
"We have the state's record" in other First Amendment cases, Alito told Norton. "What should we make of this?"
But Norton, the Colorado deputy solicitor general, said Colorado "welcomes" religious preschools to its program.

"The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike," she said, adding that religious preschools can teach their beliefs on sex, gender or marriage and are "free to teach them while receiving public funding."

Nicholas Reaves, a lawyer with the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty who argued on behalf of the Archdiocese, said Colorado is denying Catholic preschools the ability to receive public benefits because of their religious exercise.

The three liberal justices each raised concerns that the Catholic schools were asking for a "special" accommodation from the state that would allow them to discriminate against families based on protected characteristics.
Justice Elena Kagan said that the principle the Supreme Court upheld in a 2022 case involving a Maine tuition-assistance program was that the state cannot treat religious institutions differently.
"That's not the principle that's at issue here," she said. "The principle at issue here is, do you have to treat them better?"

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said the Archdiocese and its preschools are asking for a "special rule" that would allow them to turn away students based on their or their parents' sexual orientation or gender identity.

Colorado's universal preschool program launched after voters in the state approved a ballot measure in 2020 to provide state funding for a new program that intended to make preschool "widely available for free" to all 4-year-olds in the state.

Families are reimbursed for the cost of 15 hours of preschool per week, which amounts to more than $6,000 per year. The state uses a mixed-delivery system, meaning public, private, faith-based and secular preschools can participate. Those that do must sign a contract and meet state quality standards.
The statute that created the universal preschool program also imposed a nondiscrimination rule.

Colorado estimates there are roughly 40,000 children who are eligible for universal preschool across nearly 2,000 providers. The Archdiocese's 34 Catholic preschools do not participate in the program.

title: How Alaska's ranked choice voting system works
summary: Voters in Alaska are going to the polls to cast their ballots in key races, and the state's unique ranked choice voting system is back in the spotlight.
story: Voters in Alaska are going to the polls to cast their ballots in key races Tuesday, including a Senate election that has garnered widespread attention amid scrutiny over the presence of a candidate bearing nearly the same name as the sitting senator, Dan Sullivan.
Alaska's election system itself has also been in the spotlight in recent years, since the state instituted a top-four nonpartisan primary and ranked choice voting in the general election.
Here's what to know about Alaska's voting system:
What is ranked choice voting?

Ranked choice voting allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference, rather than selecting a single candidate on the ballot. First implemented in 2022, the unique system aims to stymie polarization by moving the state away from party primaries. Instead, the top four candidates in the nonpartisan primary move on to the general election.

On Tuesday, if any candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, they win. But if nobody wins an outright majority, the count goes to a second round. The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their supporters' votes are redistributed to their second choice. That process continues until one candidate wins a majority.

For example, say 100 people voted in the Alaska Senate race. Fifty of those voters ranked Candidate A as their top choice, 40 picked Candidate B, seven picked Candidate C and three picked Candidate D. Since no candidate reached 51 votes in the first round, Candidate D — the one with the fewest votes — would be eliminated in the second round of counting. The voters who ranked Candidate D first would then have their second-choice candidates tabulated. If one of those three votes went to Candidate A, Candidate A would have 51 votes and win. If not, the process would repeat.

In 2022, a special election was held to fill a vacancy in the House, and three candidates faced off under the new system. No candidate won more than 50% of first-choice votes, and the contest went to the ranked choice tabulation. Democrat Mary Peltola secured a majority in results that came 15 days after Election Day. Later that year, as she sought election to a full term, Peltola also won on the second round, with 55% of the voters after an initial 48.8%.
Who are the Alaska Senate candidates?

Alaska's Senate race could be key to determining control of the upper chamber. Voters will be presented with four choices: Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent; Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate with nearly the same name; Gerald Heikes, another Republican; and Peltola.

Sen. Sullivan is a second-term senator and a Marine veteran who worked at the State Department during the George W. Bush administration. His main opponent is Peltola, who became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022. But Daniel J. Sullivan has added a wrinkle to the race.
The second Sullivan is a former teacher who announced he was challenging the sitting senator in June, prompting an unsuccessful push to remove him from the ballot.
Two Dan Sullivans on the ballot

Daniel J. Sullivan's decision to run sparked a legal fight over his eligibility to appear on the primary ballot that played out in state court over the summer. The state supreme court eventually allowed Daniel J. Sullivan to remain on the ballot and directed Alaska's Division of Elections to determine how he should be listed.
During Alaska's open Senate primary in August, Peltola garnered 49.5% of the vote, followed by Dan Sullivan, the senator, at 41.4%. The retired teacher, Daniel J. Sullivan, won just 2.5%.
A sample ballot for the general election shows the senator listed as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent." Daniel J. Sullivan has no identifiers beyond his name.
Still, the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan raised concerns that it could lead to voter confusion and drew a late-breaking effort by the Justice Department to intervene.

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit late last month that sought to block Alaska election officials from certifying the results of the Senate election if Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, loses to Peltola. But on Sunday, a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, finding that the federal government did not have the legal right to sue.
The Justice Department has said it will appeal.

Amid the litigation, the New York Times reported last week that there was a secret effort by political operatives aligned with Peltola's campaign to help recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to peel voters away from the senator. Peltola has denied any involvement in the alleged plan.

President Trump has denounced Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy, calling him a "FAKE" candidate in a Truth Social post shortly after 1 a.m. Tuesday. The president claimed that the retired teacher is "MISSING IN ACTION" and has "TOTALLY DISAPPEARED."
"MAYBE HE HAS BEEN 'KIDNAPPED' BY THE CORRUPT DUMOCRAT LAWYERS??? THEY ARE SCARED STIFF OF BEING PROSECUTED FOR ELECTION FRAUD!!!" Mr. Trump wrote in an all-caps post.
How long could counting votes in Alaska's ranked choice voting system take?

Conducting the election in Alaska is expected to take some time, experts have warned, emphasizing the need for patience as the Senate race holds the potential to play a key role in the balance of power in Washington.

Part of the lengthy process could come from Alaska's sprawling geography, remote locations and mail ballots, since Alaska counts mail ballots received 10 days after Election Day, or 15 days in some cases.

Tabulation rounds in Alaska's ranked choice voting system also begin after the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot, the process could drag on for weeks.
Alaska election officials are targeting Nov. 25 as the day to certify the election results. In 2022, Peltola secured a full, two-year term on Nov. 30.
