title: Why some key races won't be decided on election night
summary: Experts expect some politicians on Tuesday night to claim the 2026 elections are rigged, but here's why that's not the case — and why it may be a while before some races are called.
story: Washington — Control of the House and Senate may not be immediately clear on election night, and some of the 2026 midterm election calls will take longer than others. But that's not unusual or an indication of fraud, as some candidates may claim.

As the nation watches to see how the elections unfold on Tuesday night, election experts advise voters against listening to politicians who cry foul without offering evidence of fraud as ballots are being cast or counted. Many key races will be close. And when they're close, the results are likely to come later.

David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research and a CBS News contributor, says he has some doubts about whether Americans will even know who controls the House or Senate on election night.
"If we do, then there's a very big wave going on," Becker said.
Candidates "who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it"
Becker says there is a type of candidate who's likely to complain early and often about the integrity of the election.

"It's almost certain that the candidates who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it, trying to fill that vacuum," Becker said, adding that he believes President Trump "will probably spread lies and disinformation about the election on election night because he did it in 2020."
When the president was asked last week if he would accept the results of the midterms, whatever the outcome, he responded, "I will if they're honest elections."

Lawrence Norden, vice president of the Elections and Government Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, is concerned about the spread of misinformation on election night and afterward. He says it "flourishes in that period of time between voting and getting the results" and suggests that "period of time" will be longer when the race is close.
"When it's super close, it's not going to matter how fast you are counting the ballots," Norden said.
"Our perception of counting speed is not related to actual counting speed"

Becker points out that "our perception of counting speed is not related to actual counting speed." Election officials "are racing to unofficially count as many ballots as possible and report them out," he said, "but our perception is largely driven by when the media calls elections."

News outlets, including CBS News, project election winners based on their analysis of the ballots that have been counted, and this is partly driven by the margin of victory. The bigger the margin of victory, the more quickly a winner can usually be projected, though this also depends on the determination by news outlets of the amount of the vote that remains outstanding and the character of those votes.

California, the nation's largest state, is likely to have both races that are called very quickly and others that could take days or even weeks to call. William Gates, executive director of the Arizona State University's Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory, noted that for some California contests, "they call the race at 8:01 (p.m.) because we all know the Democrat's going to win." Those races don't attract much notice.

But he added that "we had some primaries that people were paying a lot of attention to — mayor of Los Angeles, the California governor's race." It took several days to finalize who would move on to the general elections in both those races.

Part of the reason it took so long to determine the outcome of those closely watched primaries is that mail ballots — which can be received until a week after Election Day if they are postmarked that day — took longer to be counted. All registered voters in California may vote by mail and are sent ballots.

Mail ballots must undergo signature verification, and those received before Election Day can be processed beforehand, but they are not counted until after polls close. Mail ballots received on Election Day or later end up being counted more slowly since they must undergo the signature verification process before they can be counted.

Gates, a former member of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, knows what it's like to live under a microscope. Arizona's Maricopa County endured intense scrutiny over the 2020 presidential election when Joe Biden won the Republican-leaning state, the first Democrat to do so since Bill Clinton in 1996. Though Fox News called Arizona for Biden on election night, CBS News and other networks did not project him as the winner for nine more days, until Nov. 12, 2020. Gates said his family received threats over that election.
"The reality is that Arizona doesn't really take any longer to count the votes than other states," Gates said.

"But the reason that they can attack us while they, you know, don't receive any comments is because we have very close elections," Gates said. "We are one of the few swing states left, and Maricopa is sort of the quintessential swing county."
Becker said all the ballots simply can't be counted on election night.

"Election officials have never completed counting on election night," he said. "It can't be done. Our ballots are way too complex. So it's going to take some time, and every state takes weeks to certify the election."
Mail voting and counting the ballots

Still, some states do take longer than others to count votes, especially states with high numbers of mail-in ballots. In Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, the counting is also slowed by the fact that state law prevents election officials from even processing mail ballots until the morning of Election Day.
In addition to California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Vermont, Utah, Washington and the District of Columbia automatically send mail ballots to all active registered voters.

And the voter composition for mail-in votes, early-in-person votes, and Election Day votes can look different, meaning numbers can appear to shift suddenly throughout the night and days after, as ballots are processed and counted.
"The votes are already in," Norden said. "They just all aren't counted at the same time."

He used a basketball game to illustrate the counting process: "It's like you are watching a recording of a game that already happened, right? So the game is over. But we don't know what's in those ballots, and we find out over election night, but it's already done."

"The fact that you know the Knicks come back against the Lakers at the end of a game when you're watching on the videotape of the game doesn't mean that the Knicks got to add points after the game was over," Norden said.

Mr. Trump has called mail-in voting "mail-in cheating" and knocked it as a fraud carried out by Democrats. But mail-in voting didn't skew Democratic until 2020, Becker said, when Mr. Trump railed against mail voting that increased during the pandemic.

"Since mail ballots, especially those that are delivered late, are among the last reported, you do see this 'red mirage,' 'blue wave' effect in some places," Becker said. "It's moderated, I think, since the 2020 election, but you do see (it) because those mail ballots are being reported out late." The "red mirage" effect describes how early results of in-person voting may show a Republican leading, but batches of mail-in votes that are processed and counted later in the evening could swing the election to the Democrat in the race.

For example, Becker pointed to Pennsylvania in 2020, where mail ballots weren't reported publicly for days because unlike California, election officials couldn't begin processing them until Election Day.

"So the Election Day votes came out first," Becker said. "Those skewed Republican." Then, the mail votes were processed. "And those were overwhelmingly Democratic, but the batches of those were getting reported out much later, because that's what was required under Pennsylvania law."

Becker offered one more thing to remember Tuesday night: "If you hear candidates complaining about the process, I don't know whether they won or lost, but I can tell you that they think they lost, because the winners do not complain about the process," Becker said. "The winners let the process play out."

title: "Your vote is your voice": A look at why voting matters
summary: Why is it important to vote even if the president isn't on the ballot? House and Senate control, governor's mansions, ballot questions and more that will be determined by the 2026 midterm elections.
story: Millions of Americans are voting Tuesday, and more than 57 million Americans voted early, according to the University of Florida Voting Lab. All 435 seats in the House are on the ballot, and voters in 35 states will elect senators, 36 states will vote in governor's races and there are more than 150 ballot measures across 40 states. The people and policies elected will shape the future of the Iran War, AI regulation and so much more.
Brody Saner, a college student in Kansas says he believes it's his duty to vote."If there's something you're not happy with, go out and vote. Do your part to change it."

However, midterm elections tend to draw millions fewer voters than presidential, despite being "arguably more opportune moments for voters to get what they want," according to Professor Donald Green, a Columbia University political scientist who has spent three decades studying voting, "because relatively small shifts in the overall vote can lead to dramatic shifts in policy."
Here's what's at stake and why the experts say showing up matters:
Why is voting important in general?
"Your vote is your voice," said Kansas voter Tracy Preisser when asked why she thinks it's important to vote. And it's true. Voting decides who writes the rules communities live under.

At the national level, which party controls the House and the Senate is at stake. And whether the Democrats or the Republicans win will determine whether Congress acts as a check or an enabler on presidential power for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Locally, candidates down the ballot vote play a part in deciding taxes, the price of a doctor's visit, school funding, or who sits on the bench in a local court.

But a CBS News/YouGov poll conducted found that most voters don't believe that either party has a plan to make people better off. The majority of voters believed that they wouldn't be better off financially regardless of which party wins the electorate.

This sentiment is leading some voters to consider sitting this election out. "I just don't trust anybody at this point enough to vote for them, Republican [or] Democrat," says Kansas farmer Mandy Sieren. "I think they're all crooked."

To that, Green would argue that "although they might be dissatisfied with both parties, typically it comes down to the candidates themselves, and [voters] have to make an informed choice one way or the other," he said.
Why does your vote in midterm elections matter?

By some metrics, midterm elections are when a person's vote can matter the most, because less people participate in them. In the 2022 midterms, 46% of eligible voters cast ballots, compared to 65% in the 2024 presidential elections. The smaller the electorate, the more weight each ballot carries.

And the margins can be razor-thin. In  Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert race in the 2022 midterm election, she held onto her Colorado seat by 546 votes. In 2024, Democrat Adam Gray won California's 13th Congressional District by just 187 votes. And in  2020, Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks won her Iowa House race by just six votes. This round of elections is expected to have some equally contentious races.
But Green says voting isn't only about an individual's ballot. What matters, he said, is who shows up as a group.

"It may be surprising to them how attentive politicians are… to which groups vote at high rates and which groups don't," says Green. He says that this is the reason that candidates tend to pay more attention to older voters, who are most likely to vote, and issues important to young and poor people, who vote less frequently, "are often devalued."
How could votes in the 2026 midterm elections impact our country?

Midterm elections are when voters most often change the course in Washington, and are a check on the president's power halfway through a term. The president's party has lost seats in 37 of the past 41 midterm elections
And this time around, control of both chambers of Congress is in play, and the margins couldn't be slimmer.

In the house, Republicans currently hold a narrow majority. Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to win control. In the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the chamber. Whoever controls Congress will decide whether more funding for the Iran War is approved or if AI regulation is proposed, amongst countless other pieces of potential legislation.

Meanwhile, more than 30 states are electing governors, with competitive races from Georgia to Ohio. Governors have immense power over the fate of the data center buildout, because of their power to approve moratoriums, decide on tax breaks, and appoint utility commissioners. And there are 41 ballot initiatives on data centers across 13 states.
In New York City, voting is personal for poll worker Sandra Strother. She says her uncle was killed trying to vote in Alabama in the 1950s because he was an African American.
"That's my great motivator" she says for why she makes time not just to vote herself, but to ensure others can too.

title: Josh Turek pitches "generational change" in tight Iowa Senate race
summary: In Iowa's crucial Senate race, Democrat Josh Turek pitched his campaign as an opportunity for a "generational change."
story: Sioux City, Iowa — Democratic Senate hopeful Josh Turek was with former Sen. Tom Harkin in a driveway in a small Western Iowa town when the former senator pulled out his phone to show the candidate something.
"Oh my God," Turek said as he leaned over to glance at Harkin's phone, which appeared to show the prediction market Kalshi's odds for the Senate race.

The odds had Turek up over GOP candidate Ashley Hinson, 52% to 48%. But Turek knows the race against Hinson is making out to be one of the most competitive Senate contests in the country. He said as much there in the final hours of the campaign.
"This may very well be the closest election on the entire U.S. Senate map," Turek said, surrounded by a small crowd of supporters at the canvass launch in Le Mars, Iowa.

He's pitching the race in Iowa as an opportunity for a "generational change." After moving right in recent years, a departure from its former status as a battleground, the state could send a Democrat to the governor's office this year and flip a handful of House seats — along with a closely watched Senate seat left open by GOP Sen. Joni Ernst's retirement.

A state lawmaker, Turek likens himself to Harkin, whom he calls a "common-sense prairie populist." And Turek doesn't eschew things that others in his party might consider a bridge too far, like working with President Trump.

"How will I work with him? In the exact same way that I've done in the Iowa legislature," Turek told CBS News at the campaign stop Monday. "I don't believe that any party has a monopoly on good ideas. And I've said openly that I agree with President Trump that we should have no tax on tips, overtime, Social Security, and driving private equity out of housing, for example."
Turek said "on a lot of these issues," he sees an opportunity to find agreement.

Asked about the president's visit to Iowa for a rally on Sunday, which marked his second in the Hawkeye State in a matter of weeks, Turek said, "I thought it was good for him to come out here" because "I don't think he understands" the challenges Iowans face.

"I think it was good to see what healthcare cuts are doing to a state with a healthcare and a cancer crisis," he said. "That it is good for him to see what has happened with the tariffs and with the war in Iran, because both have hurt Iowa more than any other state."
Some of Turek's supporters say they like his willingness to work with the president. At another campaign stop in Onawa, Iowa, earlier Monday, Doug Zima lauded the openness.
"I'm 76 years old, I have never seen the United States so divisive," Zima said. "I've never seen families not get along because of this silly Republican-Democrat division, and it needs to stop."

On the airwaves, Turek's closing message to Iowans has centered on high gas and diesel prices, which he has tied to his opponent, whom he argues hasn't done enough to fight the president on tariffs and the Iran war. He also highlights the state's high cancer rates.
And on what will be among his final stops on the campaign trail, the Iowa Democrat invoked a Republican former president in his closing pitch.

"My message is a similar message to what Ronald Reagan said when he first ran for office in 1980, and that is, 'Are you better off than you were four years ago?' Are you better off? Are Iowans better off than they were two years ago, four years or six years ago when Ashley Hinson first ran?" Turek said.

For her part, Hinson has pitched herself to Iowa as a fighter for the state, often speaking of being a minivan-driving mom who is ready to get things done for Iowa. And while she pledged to be the president's "top ally" early on in the campaign and has campaigned with Mr. Trump, she's tweaked that message in recent weeks, promising to push back on Mr. Trump when needed.

More broadly, Hinson argues that Turek is too liberal for Iowa, and pledged to work with members of both parties to get results. She has called in recent weeks for the Iran war to come to an "immediate and successful end" in order to bring down energy prices, breaking with the president.
In a recent interview with CBS News, Hinson called herself an "Iowa common-sense conservative" who is "pro-Iowa ... no matter who's the president."

On the campaign trail Monday, Turek said Iowans "are hurting more than almost any other state." He rattled off a laundry list of troubles facing the Hawkeye State, pointing to a contracting economy, as well as healthcare, cancer and water quality crises. He cited the public education system, farmers who are going into foreclosure, unpopular tariffs, the war in Iran and high energy prices.
"Every single way it's going in the wrong direction," he said. "And there's a better way to do this."

Turek, a former Paralympic wheelchair basketball player who grew up with spina bifida that he attributes to his father's exposure to Agent Orange in Vietnam, said he's pushing to be a fighter for Iowans like him, who have experienced economic and health-related struggles.

"There's a lot of people in D.C. that come from wealth and privilege. I don't think there's that lot of places like where I come from, Council Bluffs, Iowa," Turek said. "I think when you've experienced that yourself firsthand, you'll have a different level of understanding, a different level of compassion, a different level of empathy, and a different level of fight."
The sentiment resonated with one voter, Dan Hicks, who said he's an independent. But he said he supports Turek because he "actually talks more like me than a politician."

Speaking alongside Harkin, the last Democrat to be elected to the Senate in Iowa, Turek argued that Iowans want a senator like they had in the Iowa Democrat. Harkin, who represented the state for three decades and has appeared with Turek on campaign stops throughout the state, spoke of returning to "some better representation in the United States Senate."

It's a possibility that seemed unthinkable at the start of the cycle. But like a number of states that supported Mr. Trump by double digits in 2024, it now appears on the table for Democrats heading into Election Day.
As he rallied volunteers to knock on doors, Turek said, "We just got today and tomorrow."
"But if we do this, if we win this election here in Iowa, we will not only make a generational change to the state of Iowa," he said, "we will change this country."

title: ICE planning to deport Afghans through Pakistan, official says
summary: The plan has triggered alarm among advocates for Afghans, who warn that the proposal could lead to the deportation of Afghans who could be persecuted by the Taliban.
story: The Trump administration has made plans to deport nearly 200 Afghan nationals by first sending them to Pakistan, where officials would then return the deportees to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, a U.S. official told CBS News.
The official cautioned the plans are still in flux, and that it's unclear when such deportations could take place.
The Afghans in question are in ICE custody, accused of violating U.S. immigration law.

The plan has triggered alarm among advocates for Afghans, who warn that the proposal could lead to the deportation of Afghans who could be persecuted by the Taliban because of the connections they or their relatives had to the U.S. war effort in Afghanistan.

The U.S. suspended operations at its Kabul embassy in 2021 and does not have official diplomatic relations with the current Taliban government, which would complicate any efforts to deport people directly to Afghanistan.

A U.S. immigration enforcement official confirmed in a sworn court declaration that a planned deportation flight originally scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3, would land in Pakistan before an Afghan national would be transported onward to Afghanistan via land.

Sergio Aguilar, a supervisory detention and deportation officer at U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, said he initially understood that the charter would land in Afghanistan but subsequently learned that Pakistan would be its destination.

"The plane's final destination would be Pakistan with further transport onward to Afghanistan," Aguilar wrote in the Oct. 30 declaration, adding, "The alien's intended removal destination was Afghanistan, as reflected in his removal order."

The declaration was filed in Sadat v. Mullin, a federal case involving Said Mansor Sadat, a 30-year-old Afghan national assigned to a special charter flight scheduled to depart from Alexandria, Louisiana, after U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff ordered federal officials to explain whether the planned charter would fly directly to Afghanistan or stop in Pakistan.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney representing Sadat and another Afghan national facing deportation, said both clients were told independently they would be flown to Pakistan on Tuesday before being transported overland to the Afghan border.
"They were not told who would be taking them overland and in what manner," Sandoval-Moshenberg said in an email to CBS News on Monday.

Sadat has since been removed from the flight list and released from ICE custody, according to his attorney, after a judge ruled his continued detention violated his due process rights. His second client, however, was awaiting a decision on an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order as of Monday night.
The disclosures raise significant questions about whether Pakistani authorities have agreed to receive the deportees and which government would ultimately oversee their transportation to Afghanistan.

Most Afghans who arrived in the U.S. in recent years came after the 2021 fall of Kabul, either through a Biden administration-era resettlement effort or through their own means, with some even first traveling to Latin America and crossing via the U.S.-Mexico border.

The Department of Homeland Security declined to address the planned removal flights, citing operational security concerns in a statement to CBS News, but defended its broader third-country removal practices.

"Illegal aliens being sent to a third country receive notice and assurances prior to their removal," a DHS spokesperson said, adding that ICE receives diplomatic assurances from destination countries that deportees will be safe.

The department did not specify whether Pakistan had provided such assurances for this operation or whether any guarantees would extend to the deportees' onward transportation and treatment in Afghanistan.
"When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them," the spokesperson said.
The Pakistani embassy did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

DHS referred questions about third-country agreements to the State Department. However, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pressed about the planned Afghan deportations during an Oct. 31 news conference, he directed the question back to DHS.
CBS News has reached out to the State Department, but did not receive a response.

Afghanistan's Taliban-led Foreign Ministry aired its own concern Monday over reports that the United States intended to transfer Afghan nationals to Pakistan, calling for coordination and urging that the rights and dignity of Afghan citizens be respected.

"Third countries should not bargain over the transfer of another country's nationals in pursuit of short-term, limited concessions or other considerations, nor should their decisions and actions undermine human dignity, rights, or established ethical and humanitarian standards," a spokesperson for Afghanistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.

Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president and founder of #AfghanEvac, a nonprofit focused on supporting Afghan allies who resettled in the U.S. following the U.S. military's withdrawal from the country, said in a statement, "When even the Taliban are voicing 'serious concern' about this plan, the administration should stop and ask what it is doing."

"Handing the families of our allies to Pakistan, a government that has no plan for them and every reason to send them to the Taliban, is not immigration enforcement," he said. "It is abandonment with a boarding pass."
As of Monday, 66 members of Congress in a letter called on Rubio and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to cancel deportation flights of Afghans and Iranians.
The planned removals of Afghans through Pakistan have also surfaced in separate federal court proceedings in Texas and Louisiana.

In an Oct. 15 order, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone said ICE had acknowledged that Basir Ahmad Ahmadi, an Afghan detainee in El Paso, had been "nominated for an Afghanistan removal mission tentatively scheduled for early November."

Ahmadi then sought emergency relief, arguing that Pakistan could arrest him and turn him over to Taliban authorities. Cardone denied his request on Oct. 29, ruling that the district court lacked jurisdiction to halt his removal.

In Louisiana, another Afghan national, Khaled Khaleeq, sought emergency intervention after learning through news reports and conversations with other detainees that he might be deported to Pakistan or Afghanistan. A federal judge denied his request on Oct. 30, though subsequent reconsideration notices have been filed.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request in California mail ballots dispute
summary: Earlier Monday, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to order California election officials to set aside mail ballots from 20,000 people it alleges are noncitizens.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday turned down a last-ditch effort from the Trump administration to require California to separate mail ballots received from thousands of people that it claims are not U.S. citizens.

The court said in a one-line, unsigned order that it was denying the Justice Department's request for an injunction requiring election officials from California to set aside the ballots from 20,000 alleged noncitizens. There were no noted dissents.
The Supreme Court acted only on the Trump administration's request for emergency relief and did not ask the California election officials to respond before ruling.

The Justice Department sought the Supreme Court's intervention earlier in the day after a divided federal appeals court refused to order California election workers to set aside mail ballots cast by people on a government list of "likely" noncitizens.

A U.S. district judge, David Carter, last week rebuffed the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order that would've required ballots received from those on the list to be segregated and said the Trump administration's process for identifying the alleged noncitizens was "rife with uncertainty and errors."

The dispute over the ballots in California has played out in the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign season as Republicans have been fighting to maintain their control of the House and Senate. Voting in the state has been underway since early October, and more than 6 million mail ballots have been returned to election offices across California.

President Trump has repeatedly claimed that there are significant numbers of noncitizens voting in U.S. elections, though confirmed instances of noncitizen voting are rare. It is a violation of federal law for people who are not citizens to vote in U.S. elections. The Justice Department has brought criminal charges against more than 200 individuals who prosecutors have alleged illegally voted in past elections.

The Trump administration told officials with the state and Los Angeles County last month that there were more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens on its voter rolls and ordered ballots received from those people to be set aside and not tabulated until their citizenship could be confirmed. It has since sent letters to officials in all of California's 58 counties with lists of alleged noncitizens on their voter registration lists and demanded ballots from them be put to the side. There are more than 23 million registered voters in California.

But the state and local election officials raised concerns with the accuracy of the list and the potential that U.S. citizens could be disenfranchised if they complied with the federal government's demand.

The Justice Department went on to file a lawsuit against California officials and Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, and sought a court order requiring the ballots to be segregated.
Neither the district court nor the 9th Circuit, however, agreed to the Justice Department's request.

As Tuesday's midterms have approached, the Trump administration has taken steps to intervene in the elections. Federal prosecutors sent a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs and demanded he set aside mail ballots from more than 400 people they claimed are not U.S. citizens. But Hobbs said the government's list of alleged noncitizens contained "many" people who actually are U.S. citizens.

The Justice Department also filed a lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from certifying the results of its Senate election if incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, loses to Democrat Mary Peltola. But a judge tossed out the suit Sunday.

Supreme Court of the United States
California

title: Dingell: Stevens' GOP endorsement is "galvanizing" voters behind El-Sayed
summary: "It's galvanizing many communities," the Michigan Democrat told CBS News on Monday.
story: Washington — Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan said Rep. Haley Stevens' stunning endorsement of GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is having the opposite effect of what she intended.
"You're seeing a backlash," Dingell said in an interview on "The Takeout with Major Garrett" on Monday. "It's galvanizing many communities."
El-Sayed's campaign says it raised more than $2.4 million on Sunday, the same day that Stevens — his former Democratic primary rival — came out in support of Rogers.
"I've had Black pastors talk to me and say, 'Who said she represented us?' There's a lot of anger in how she did what she did yesterday," Dingell said.
The endorsement came after days of hostility between El-Sayed and Stevens, who were expected to appear together on Sunday before tensions boiled over.

El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens offered starkly differing visions for the future of the party during the primary, and although Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after he won the nomination, the two largely haven't campaigned alongside each other.

The attempt at Democratic unity fell flat after Stevens demanded Friday that El-Sayed — a vehement critic of U.S. aid to Israel — apologize for his past remarks about Israel and condemn an ad from an outside PAC that she said was antisemitic. (El-Sayed's campaign said last week it was not affiliated "in any way" with the ad.)

After Stevens' criticism on Friday, El-Sayed said in his own statement that she "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." He later asked Stevens not to attend the Sunday campaign event.

Dingell, an influential member of Michigan's congressional delegation, has suggested she also encouraged Stevens not to attend the unity event, telling NPR she told Stevens "this has become a distraction."

On Sunday morning, Stevens instead appeared at church alongside Rogers before offering her endorsement, which drew outrage from Democrats. She told reporters that she initially "stood with my party" but was "booed off the stage."
Dingell told CBS News she's "tired of the drama" and she's "worried" about Stevens.
"As this day has gone on, I'm probably getting angrier," she said. "I can't believe we are where we are. But I'm not going to let that emotion win."
But when asked whether there will be repercussions against Stevens within the House Democratic Caucus, Dingell said she's told everyone to "please don't make more drama, give it more attention."
"We need to focus on winning tomorrow, and that's where our focus needs to be," she said.

title: A bitter sheriff's primary, a write-in campaign and a county divided
summary: An unusual sheriff election in Lee County, Alabama, highlights how elected law enforcement often shapes issues of public safety, immigration and gun control.
story: It began with a phone call. A grassroots write-in campaign had been launched weeks before Tuesday's midterm election in an effort to keep longtime Alabama Sheriff Jay Jones in office. Jones was ousted in May by about 300 votes in a bitterly fought Republican primary in Lee County by a former sheriff's deputy, Cameron Hunt.
"Somebody has started this write-in campaign," Lee County resident Jack Carter said, recalling his recent phone conversation, in an interview with CBS News. "And I said, really?"

Carter said he had spoken with others about trying to write in their votes for Jones after the primary, but nothing ever materialized — until he got that phone call. He said he didn't know who was behind the campaign, and it's challenging to find out.
A Facebook page dedicated to the "write-in campaign" lists a Proton email address, which is an encrypted account. A query to the email address from a CBS News reporter went unanswered.

Carter, a former sheriff's deputy — who said Jones was a mentor — and now a local furniture maker, said he was directed to a woman with access to campaign signs reading, "On Election Day write in Sheriff Jay Jones." Soon, the signs began popping up across yards, pickup trucks and local businesses.
He placed one in the back of his black Ram pickup truck and posted a picture online. Then, things began to "blow up," he said.

Supporters of Hunt accused Jones' camp of being sore losers, while Jones' supporters insisted voters have every right to write in any candidate they choose. Social media posts captured signs being stolen from yards, accompanied by mounting accusations and online bickering.
"This has not gone the way that this needs to go," Carter said, adding, "It's chaotic."

Sheriff Jones said he was "humbled" by the grassroots campaign in an interview with CBS News, saying, "I was not involved and nor have I solicited anyone for votes." Jones wanted to make clear he isn't involved, as he claims the Alabama Republican Party threatened to remove him from the party because of the growing write-in campaign.
Sheriff elections and quality-of-life issues

While congressional and marquee statewide races dominate midterm headlines, down-ballot contests often play a far more direct role in shaping people's daily life. A sheriff sets local public safety priorities and typically oversees jail operations, budget allocation, response to crime and bail management.

Nationally, sheriffs are overwhelmingly White and male, according to a 2020 report released by a progressive group, Women's Donor Action, examining sheriff demographics. There are 3,801 sheriffs in the country. In several states, the office is established by the state constitution, often allowing for broad authority — and for many counties the sheriff might be the most visible and powerful position around.

There are about 1,400 sheriffs up for election in 2026. In 20 states, including Colorado, Alabama, Maryland, Utah and Wisconsin, most of the elected sheriffs are up for the vote, according to Yesim Karaman, a spokesperson at the National Sheriffs' Association, a national organization supporting training, education and advocacy.

"They're policing, they're making sure that they have the good community relationships, they have the leadership in their counties, and they're responding to the citizens that they serve and who they're elected by," said Karaman.

Sheriffs can also help shape regional policies such as immigration enforcement and gun control. Several 2026 midterm contests feature debates over partnerships with federal immigration authorities, known as 287(g) agreements. In Wisconsin, voters across two counties are weighing in directly on their local sheriffs' cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Jones and Hunt differed over various policy issues in their campaign, including immigration, guns and Flock intelligence. Jones said his office has often cooperated with ICE, but doesn't have a signed Memorandum of Understanding. He said there is misinformation around what this means for the county.

"We have cooperated with any request we received from ICE, from the local agencies here and federal agency offices in the state of Alabama, to actually, and this is on record, in the last two years, we've actually transferred over 450 individuals to ICE custody from the Lee County Jail," he said.
However, Karaman cautioned that sheriffs' immigration abilities are often based on state law.
"Whether a sheriff signs a 287(g) agreement and has the ability to cooperate extensively with ICE is a matter of state law and local politics," she said.

Jones also said he supports the continuation of concealed carry permits, which are issued by the sheriff's office, because it helps keep guns out of the hands of criminals. (Alabama law changed in 2023 to no longer require a permit to carry a concealed handgun in much of the state.) He said he's in "full support of the Second Amendment."

Hunt said he plans to sign a 287(g) agreement, supports open carry laws saying a permit isn't needed, and said publicly that he plans to end the county's Flock contract. He wrote in an email, "I strongly support the Second Amendment, believe immigration laws should be enforced, and recognize the importance of providing law enforcement with the tools necessary to protect our communities."

Notwithstanding the issues, many sheriffs are still running in nationwide races uncontested. A 2024 data analysis found that over a two-year period from 2022 to 2024, about 62% of sheriff elections were uncontested.
In Lee County, which holds a population of 190,118 people, Jones has been in office for more than 27 years — and he's rarely had an opponent.
A "simple" grassroots effort grows after an escalating feud
That changed late last October when Hunt, a deputy sheriff at the time, requested a private meeting with Jones to announce his plan to challenge him in the Republican primary.

"Within approximately ten minutes, I was terminated," Hunt wrote in an email to CBS News, attaching a copy of his termination letter. "There was no legal requirement for Sheriff Jones to terminate me at that point, yet his termination letter specifically cited my intention to run against him as the reason for terminating me."
Jones said he gave Hunt several chances to resign from his deputy position. Local media reported on the firing and subsequent feud.

"It simply would've been an untenable situation" to keep him, Jones said. Several courts have upheld the firing of deputy sheriffs for political reasons. A federal appellate court found in 2021 — when Missouri deputies sued after they were fired for political reasons — the position of deputy sheriff requires political loyalty. The sheriff can fire deputies because they hold policymaking positions for which political loyalty is necessary for effective job performance, the court said. In 2016, North Carolina's Supreme Court upheld the firing of sheriff's deputies who declined to donate to the sheriff's political campaign.

A month after the May primary — where results showed Hunt defeating Jones by 9,301 to 8,994 votes — Hunt said he filed a formal complaint with the Alabama Ethics Commission. He alleges the sheriff used a departmental GPS tracking system to set up a geofence around Hunt's private residence to monitor any deputies visiting his home. The Alabama Ethics Commission said it couldn't confirm or deny that the complaint exists.
Jones said if there is to be an investigation, he stands ready to "cooperate fully." Hunt said he is also going to call for an independent investigation.

Jones touted his length of service, which he says has provided stability for the county and allowed him to grow the sheriff's office, which has a budget of $25 million, from 80 people in 1999 to 230 people today.
He said he wanted to make clear he respected the outcome in May, but what was happening now was "a simple, basic grassroots effort by the members of the community who want a choice in this effort."

Still, the race in Lee County is rare, said Mirya R. Holman, a public policy professor at the University of Houston, and co-author of the book "The Power of the Badge: Sheriffs and Inequality in the United States."

"It is very unusual for longtime incumbents in any office (including sheriff) to lose primaries," she wrote in an email. "Write-in campaigns are a big unknown — they are very rarely successful for any office, including sheriffs."

But she said she doesn't know of any data tracking write-in campaigns. (In Oswego, New York, a candidate is running a write-in campaign for sheriff, but never served in the position. In Washington, a successful write-in campaign propelled a candidate onto the sheriff ballot.)

Some voters supporting the write-in campaign for Jones pointed to the differing policies between the two candidates. Debra Beil, a self-proclaimed "liberal" who has lived in conservative Lee County for 35 years, said she was organizing for and supporting Jones because of his experience level.

She cited his educational programs on gun safety and his stance regarding gun permits among her primary reasons for supporting him. Supporter Chad Lanier added that while Jones' experience was his primary consideration, he also preferred to avoid a heightened presence of federal agents in the county.
Hunt said he's not particularly worried about the write-in campaign and instead remains focused on the commitments he's made to the people of Lee County when he prepares to take office in January.

"I'm the only candidate for sheriff whose name will appear on the November 3 ballot, and I respect everyone's right to participate in the democratic process, including their right to cast a write-in vote," Hunt said.
In that area, the two agree. Jones said this vote is all about what the will of the people is.
"After all, that's who's being served here," he said. "And their choice should be what matters."

title: Supreme Court to hear religious liberty case over Colorado preschools
summary: The Archdiocese of Denver and Catholic preschools said they were unlawfully excluded from Colorado's universal preschool program over their refusal to admit students from LGBTQ families.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday is set to hear a dispute over religious rights when it weighs whether Colorado can exclude Catholic schools from its universal preschool program over their refusal to enroll students from families that don't adhere to the church's teachings on marriage and sex.
The case, known as St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, is the latest clash over religious liberty and efforts to protect gay and transgender people from discrimination.

If the Catholic plaintiffs prevail, the decision would join a line of recent rulings in which the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has sided with religious institutions challenging their exclusion from state programs, opening the door for more public dollars to flow to religious schools.

"This is a program that was sold to them in Colorado as being universal, every child in the state would benefit," Amanda Dixon, a lawyer with the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, which is representing the Catholic preschools and families in the case, said of her clients. "Yet they've had multiple children now go through preschool who haven't been able to benefit because they feel religiously obligated to send their kids to Catholic schools. They can't get the same benefit that everyone in the state is getting."
Colorado's universal preschool program
Colorado voters approved a ballot measure in 2020 to provide state funding for a new program that intended to make preschool "widely available for free" to all 4-year-olds in the state.

Families are reimbursed for the cost of 15 hours of preschool per week, which amounts to more than $6,000 per year. The state uses a mixed-delivery system, meaning public, private, faith-based and secular preschools can participate. Those that do must sign a contract and meet state quality standards.

The statute that created the universal preschool program also imposed a nondiscrimination rule. It requires participating preschools to provide eligible children with an "equal opportunity to enroll," regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, income level or disability.
Colorado estimates there are roughly 40,000 children who are eligible for universal preschool across nearly 2,000 providers.

When the program was being implemented, the Archdiocese of Denver, which oversees 34 Catholic preschools, raised concerns about the nondiscrimination requirement and its ability to comply without compromising its religious beliefs, particularly on sexual orientation and gender identity.
The Catholic providers sought a religious exemption to the mandate, since they only admit families that align with the Catholic Church's teachings, including on sexual identity, marriage and family.

But the state denied the request and told the Archdiocese at the time that while it can give enrollment preference to its members, it cannot "discriminate against children or families in violation of state statute." The preschool program's regulations, however, no longer allow faith-based providers to limit enrollment to their congregants.
As a result, none of the preschools that the Archdiocese oversees participate in the universal preschool program.

In August 2023, the Archdiocese, two Catholic parishes with preschools and parents of preschool-age children filed a lawsuit, arguing that their exclusion violated the Constitution's Free Exercise Clause.

The Catholic schools said that the mandate violated a 2022 Supreme Court decision in a case involving a tuition-assistance program in Maine. In that decision, the high court ruled that the state's exclusion of religious schools from the program violated the First Amendment.

The plaintiffs also said that the state treated them differently when refusing to grant them exemptions to the nondiscrimination rule, since Colorado had granted exceptions for secular conduct by allowing preschool providers to prioritize enrollment for students from low-income families and with disabilities, but not religious conduct.

A federal district court ruled in favor of the state, finding that the sexual orientation and gender identity provisions of the nondiscrimination rule are neutral and apply generally to providers participating in the universal preschool program. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the lower court's decision.
The fight before the Supreme Court

In papers with the Supreme Court, lawyers for the Archdiocese and Catholic parishes argue that they are being unfairly excluded from the universal preschool program because of their religious exercise.
"This case is about whether states can do things like promise a universal program and then leave religious folks out," Dixon said.
Catholic families, she said, "don't want to be excluded from the ability to participate in this universal program just because they've chosen a Catholic program."

The plaintiffs argued that the state has allowed more than 1,000 other preschools to serve 4-year-olds in specific communities by creating exceptions from the very provision it is saying the Catholic schools must follow.

The state allows preschools to prioritize enrollment for children with certain disabilities or who are living in poverty, conflicting with the requirement that eligible children have equal access to preschool services regardless of income level or disability, the Archdiocese argued.
Lawyers also said certain preschools can give enrollment preference to children of color or who are from families in the LGBTQ community.

"It was billed as universal, and instead we're the ones that are being discriminated [against] because we've chosen our Catholic faith and a Catholic education for our children," said Lisa Sheley, who, with her husband Daniel, is a plaintiff in the case.

The couple's children attend school in St. Mary's Catholic Parish, and they estimated that they have lost out on roughly $24,000 in reimbursements from the universal preschool program. Erika Nagle, who is preparing to send her third child to St. Mary Catholic Parish's preschool, said the program would've saved her family around $18,000.

"We're being forced to pay the price because of our Catholic beliefs," Nagle said. "And it's just such a tough pill to swallow — it's a double standard because you see other schools that have been granted exemptions for communities that they serve. But here come the Catholic schools wanting an exemption for the communities that they serve, and they're being denied."

The Catholic parishes said that because Colorado excluded them from the universal preschool program because of their religious exercise, its actions should be evaluated under the most stringent form of judicial scrutiny. The state, they said, has failed to show it has a compelling interest in excluding religious schools from the program.

"The inevitable result of Colorado's thumb on the scale is that more Colorado children will be funneled toward preschools that share Colorado's perspective on matters of sex and marriage," they said in a filing.
The Trump administration is backing the Catholic plaintiffs in the case.

But Colorado officials defending the program said religious preschools that participate can teach and develop curricula according to their faith. They just have to comply with the same "equal opportunity" mandate that applies to the other providers, which "requires all preschools — secular and religious alike — to deliver publicly-funded services without excluding families based on protected-class status," they said.

The Catholic preschools want to receive public funding without following the nondiscrimination requirement, which would allow them to turn away students based on their or their parents' sexual orientation or gender identity, the state said.

"When the state is putting its stamp on something and then the entity is able to say, 'You don't belong,' that communicates something," said Scott Skinner-Thompson, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School. "Even if there is a second-best option, it still deeply negatively impacts the people who are turned away and have to go look for that second-best option."
Skinner-Thompson said nothing in Colorado's law requires the schools participating in the universal preschool program to change what they teach.

"Colorado isn't telling any of those schools what to believe or what not to believe, what to practice or what not to practice," he said. "All they're saying is, if you want to have a preschool and get this subsidy, please accept LGBTQ kids and families."

Colorado officials argued in a filing with the Supreme Court that the Archdiocese and Catholic preschools are asking it to allow them to receive public dollars on terms that are different from the ones applied to every other participating preschool. Under those terms, they would be allowed to exclude families based on protected-class status.
"The Constitution," the state said, "does not support that result."

title: Trump asks Supreme Court to intervene in California ballot case
summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its effort to force California to set aside mail ballots from thousands of people it claims are not U.S. citizens.
story: Update: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request Monday evening. Read the latest here. Our earlier coverage is below.

Washington — The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to intervene in its effort to force California election workers to set aside mail ballots from thousands of people it claims are not U.S. citizens.

The Justice Department's request for emergency relief came after a federal appeals court on Friday declined to order California officials to segregate the ballots cast by more than 20,000 people included on a government list of suspected noncitizens.

More than 6 million mail ballots have been returned statewide as of Sunday, according to the California secretary of state's office. Voting has been underway in California since early October. There are more than 23 million registered voters in the state.

The emergency appeal to the high court came in the fast-moving legal battle unfolding in the run-up to Tuesday's elections. The Trump administration so far has not been successful in convincing lower courts to require the ballots at issue to be put aside.

But in the request to the Supreme Court, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the government is seeking a "modest remedy" that will ensure any ballots cast by people who are not American citizens do not "debase or dilute valid votes."

"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," he wrote in a filing. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now."

The dispute arose after the Justice Department sent letters to California's secretary of state and the top elections official in Los Angeles County with a list of 20,000 people it claimed were registered to vote but not U.S. citizens, and demanded any ballots returned by them be set aside and not tabulated until their citizenship could be verified.
But the officials have expressed concerns about the accuracy of the list and the potential for eligible voters to be disenfranchised.
The Justice Department sued California and Dean Logan, the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and county clerk, and sought a court order requiring the ballots to be segregated.

But on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge David Carter rejected the Trump administration's request for a temporary restraining order blocking election workers from counting ballots from the alleged noncitizens.

"Constitutional rights and our democracy are at stake. The public interest favors their protection," Carter, appointed by President Bill Clinton, said. "Individuals who have met the requirements of California's voter registration laws must not be deprived of a core right merely because of unfounded allegations stemming from a procedure rife with uncertainty and errors."
A three-judge panel on the 9th Circuit divided 2-1 on Friday in denying a Justice Department request to require the ballots to be separated and not counted pending citizenship verification.

title: Judge tosses lawsuit seeking to delay certification of Alaska Senate race
summary: The Justice Department argued that Daniel J. Sullivan's name on the ballot potentially diverted voters, and the Democrat running in the race would benefit as a result.
story: A federal judge in Alaska has thrown out the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the state's Senate election results in this week's midterm elections if the Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses.

U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason wrote in a 20-page order Sunday that the Justice Department did not have proper legal standing to bring the suit last week. The suit asked Gleason to block the state's election results from being certified because a teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan is also on the state's ballot, alleging that his candidacy deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name and party affiliation as the state's incumbent senator.
The Justice Department argued that Daniel J. Sullivan's name on the ballot potentially diverted voters, and the Democrat running in the race, Mary Peltola, would benefit as a result.

The Justice Department "provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote, adding that the it "failed to satisfy its burden to show that its alleged injury is redressable by a court order."
The Justice Department filed a notice of appeal on Sunday.

Earlier, a DOJ spokesperson told CBS News that the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds "but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.
"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," the spokesperson said.

The suit, which argues Sullivan's candidacy violates the National Voter Registration Act, was amended on Thursday to include recent reporting by The New York Times on alleged efforts by people associated with Peltola's campaign to find candidates who could draw votes away from the Republican senator. It included a second claim for relief, arguing the court needs to intervene under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause in order to allow the government to enforce the law and prevent a "conspiracy."
Peltola's campaign responded to the Times story by saying the campaign "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
"I am not interested in tricking voters," Peltola said during a recent campaign event.

Sen. Sullivan on Sunday told CNN's "State of the Union" that he thought the presence of a second Sullivan on the ballot would impact the election, saying: "I'm sure I'm going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery."
He also said he doubted Peltola's claims that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
"There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," Sullivan said. "She got caught lying, and she's still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us."

In addition to the civil lawsuit, the Justice Department is also criminally investigating an alleged plot to add Daniel J. Sullivan to the state's ballot and has issued subpoenas targeting several Democratic officials believed to be tied to the effort to recruit him to appear on Alaska's ballot. Nobody in the race has been charged with a crime.

title: NASA telescope is plunging back to Earth after 22 years in orbit
summary: The Swift Observatory is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
story: An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower. The space agency said Monday it predicts the Swift Observatory will likely come crashing down on Wednesday.

Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

"As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours," NASA said on Monday.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.
In a statement on Monday, NASA said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely" — roughly 1 in 2,100.
"NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions," the agency said.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning, yet full of gratitude, for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma-ray bursts and supernovas.

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 7 miles to 9 miles to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.
Shawn Domagal-Goldman, Astrophysics Division director at NASA, told "CBS Mornings" in June that nothing pinpoints gamma-ray bursts like the Swift Observatory.
"A nuclear weapon going off doesn't even compare to the magnitude of energy that comes out of these things and it's literally the biggest explosions in the universe," Domagal-Goldman said.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

title: Is the truth really out there? Studying UAP sightings
summary: Seven decades after the first reported sightings of Unidentified Flying Objects, a scientific council is investigating records and video released by the government of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), to possibly answer the question: Are we alone?
story: On a May evening back in 1950, Evelyn Trent had just finished feeding her rabbits when, she claims, she looked up and saw a slow-moving, metallic disk-shaped object hovering above her farm. Though some dismissed it as a hoax, her account was added to a growing list of unexplained events that sparked America's first UFO craze.

At the annual McMenamins UFO Festival in McMinnville, Ore., just a few miles from Evelyn Trent's farm, there are costumes, a parade, and some theories that might be generously described as fringe: "Well, based on what I've read, it could be us from the future visiting us from, you know, the past," said one attendee, "and then it could also be trans-dimensional or inter-dimensional beings."

Fringe, but definitely something Americans seem interested in. According to a CBS News Poll, nearly one in five Americans (17%) has seen a UFO, which has led to an explosion in podcasts and documentaries on the topic.

Matthew Szydagis, one of the UFO festival's invited speakers, teaches physics at the State University of New York at Albany. He spoke to us about Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (or UAPs), or what we used to call UFOs back in the old days: "I think the possibility that at least some small fraction of UFOs or UAPs represent a non-human intelligence," Szydagis said. "That will be the greatest discovery in human history. So, of course that's going to fire people up and get their imaginations going."

Szydagis would like to believe in aliens, but he also knows that extraordinary claims demand extraordinary evidence, especially in the world of "UFOlogy," where the more extreme the claims, the more attention they get.

"We still don't have definitive evidence," Szydagis said. "We haven't been provided with a dead alien body, for instance, although claims of the existence have been made. But I think we have enough indirect evidence to say that the existence of non-human intelligence is no longer laughable, that it's not irrational."

Szydagis is part of a new Scientific Advisory Council, established by the Trump Administration, to study UAPs. The person in charge of that council is none other than respected Harvard professor Avi Loeb, former chair of the university's astronomy department.

"Now, there are some objects the U.S. government cannot figure out," Loeb said. "I would like to figure them out. Because at the very least, as an American citizen, I will be helping the Pentagon and the intelligence community fulfill their mission of, if these are human-made technologies, if they come from adversarial nations, then I can help them identify what they are and where they came from."

The things Loeb and the other council members are trying to identify are the many sightings over the years of lights and objects and movements in the sky that defy simple explanation. Someone who's experienced it firsthand? Former U.S. Navy pilot Ryan Graves, whose testimony in front of Congress got the nation's attention back in 2023, when he recounted an experience during a training mission ten miles off the coast of Virginia Beach: "Two F-18 Super Hornets were split by a UAP," Graves said. "The object, described as a dark grey or a black cube inside of a clear sphere, came within 50 feet of the lead aircraft."

For many people, seeing no-nonsense U.S. military personnel calmly describing things they'd seen and couldn't explain, along with actual images, made the whole thing seem a lot less crazy. Graves told us, "We were seeing these things, we were nearly hitting them, and yet we're still unwilling to talk about them in our safety briefs and incorporate them into the conversation."

Graves was also recently added to the Advisory Council, tasked with getting to the bottom of things, and there are a lot of things that have been released in the last eight months: seven tranches of first-person accounts, photographs, and lots of grainy video, more than 155,000 pages of files overall.

But not enough of the good stuff, says Graves: "What's being released is not satisfactory to me. What you are seeing are very short clips from infrared sensors aboard different platforms. And ultimately, these are not the high-end sophisticated tools that are used by pilots in order to make critical decisions about whether [an] object in the air is hostile, whether it's a decoy, whether it is a threat or not. And so, I think we're left with more ambiguity."

Loeb said, "The mistake that is often made about science is the belief that, 'Oh, the data will come and guide us.' But the problem is that to collect the data, you need to put in effort. And it's often a heroic effort to get the high-quality data."

Questions linger about what exactly the government knows about UFOs, after former Air Force intelligence officer David Grusch testified to Congress that he was told of the existence of recovered UFOs.

When Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) asked whether possession of a crashed craft also meant possession of the bodies of the craft's pilot(s), Grusch replied, "As I have stated publicly already in my News Nation interview, biologics came with some of these recoveries, yeah."
Of course, evidence for all of this is "classified," leading some ufologists to call Grusch and others making claims about government conspiracies "Trust Me Bros."

Loeb, who's floated a number of controversial theories on possible alien life, says the Advisory Council is working to get access to as much information as possible, starting with what's been publicly released. "My role is really simple, because it's like a detective," he said. "And the worst that can happen to a detective is that the detective is starved of data. So, if I don't have data, the quality of my deliberations [is] poor. I mean, only in politics, with very little data, you can make a huge story!"

For his part, Ryan Graves started an organization called Americans for Safe Aerospace, which encourages everyone (but especially pilots) to share their stories of UAPs. And of course, he's got a podcast.

"Recently I've been astounded, in fact, that almost everyone is willing to talk about this," said Graves. "It is fighter pilots. It is commercial aviators. And I think that really speaks to how this conversation has changed over the past few years."

Asked whether he believes he'll get answers within his lifetime, Graves replied, "My lifetime, yes. We are moving towards a point in time where we're perhaps not going to get every answer we want, but we're going to potentially have the confirmation that something truly strange is happening."
Until that conformation, the truth will have to remain (as they say) out there.

title: Meteorite found in the Sahara Desert turns out to be piece of Mars
summary: A meteorite found in the Sahara Desert has been determined to be 4.1 billion years old and from Mars.
story: A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara Desert in 2022 has been identified as a 4.1-billion-year-old chunk of the Red Planet, a NASA study determined.
The nearly two-pound meteorite was found in Mali. It was named Teghaza 001, after the salt plain where it was discovered, NASA said in a news release.

Study of the meteorite allowed NASA scientists to determine it was one of roughly 435 from Mars. Meteorites can be verified as having been part of Mars by comparing their chemical and mineral makeup to samples and data collected by NASA's Martian missions.

Age-dating of the meteorite led researchers to conclude it was about 4.1 billion years old, making it one of the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth, NASA said. That provides "a rare snapshot" of the planet's crust and formation, the agency said.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the lead author of a paper detailing the age-dating process and related discoveries. Liu is part of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Previous ancient Martian meteorites provided narrower glimpses into the planet's history. But Teghaza 001 shows how Mars' crust formed from cooling magma and was then changed by water on the planet's surface.

The meteorite is made of a unique mix of volcanic minerals, including zircon crystals, NASA said, matching samples observed by the agency's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's southern highlands. Francis Tissot, a geochemistry professor at Caltech, helped the researchers use a pioneering age-dating method that studied a piece of meteorite smaller than a fingernail. The precise method allowed scientists to analyze single grains of minerals.

That analysis showed the rock had been altered by Martian water about 4.1 billion years ago. The rock itself may have been formed even earlier, NASA said. The data also showed that early Mars may have had a more dynamic water cycle than scientists previously believed.

Paper author Lee Saper said that the meteorite "records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." Another study of the meteorite, published in June, focused on the rock's water content and considered how water might have shaped the early topography of Mars.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," Lee, a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center, added.
Liu said that further research on the meteorite is likely.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.

"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the lead author of a paper detailing the age-dating process and related discoveries. Liu is part of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."

Previous ancient Martian meteorites provided narrower glimpses into the planet's history. But Teghaza 001 shows how Mars' crust formed from cooling magma and was then changed by water on the planet's surface.

The meteorite is made of a unique mix of volcanic minerals, including zircon crystals, NASA said, matching samples observed by the agency's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's southern highlands. Francis Tissot, a geochemistry professor at Caltech, helped the researchers use a pioneering age-dating method that studied a piece of meteorite smaller than a fingernail. The precise method allowed scientists to analyze single grains of minerals.

That analysis showed the rock had been altered by Martian water about 4.1 billion years ago. The rock itself may have been formed even earlier, NASA said. The data also showed that early Mars may have had a more dynamic water cycle than scientists previously believed.

Paper author Lee Saper said that the meteorite "records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water." Another study of the meteorite, published in June, focused on the rock's water content and considered how water might have shaped the early topography of Mars.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," Lee, a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center, added.
Liu said that further research on the meteorite is likely.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.
