title: Co-pilot's friend describes hearing audio of her last moments
summary: The co-pilot, 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, can be heard saying in the audio recordings that the jet was rapidly descending.
story: A longtime friend of the co-pilot who died in a Florida plane crash on Sunday said air traffic control audio revealing her final moments "was definitely, probably the worst thing I've ever heard."
The co-pilot, 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, can be heard saying in the audio recordings that the jet she was flying alongside 55-year-old captain Jeffrey Gregory was rapidly descending.
"722 Bravo Delta, we're descending 8000 Mayday, Mayday, we're descending 10,000 ft per minute," Filgueiras said.
The messages grew increasingly alarming before the Learjet 60, which was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, ultimately crashed in Palm Beach County, killing all nine people on board.
"Declare an emergency 722 Bravo Delta, we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," Filgueiras said.
Mikaela Schluth, who knew Filgueiras since middle school, said she is proud of how her friend handled it, "and how she was able to stay calm and give information, up until the last minute."

The passengers who died in the crash have been identified as Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, a couple from Austin, and their two young children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2; Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.

In a joint statement, their families wrote that "Adam and Helen were devoted parents," and "Charmi and [Rachel] were full of joy and adventure." And Anita Maria "showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."

Among the big questions now facing investigators is whether the pilots had a clear understanding of a storm they were approaching, and whether the plane's horizontal stabilizer broke off, which would make the plane virtually uncontrollable. Weather data shows the aircraft entered a rapidly intensifying thunderstorm cell shortly before the pilots reported icing and significant turbulence.

"The two scenarios in my mind, they're both atmospherically related," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "One is icing, the other is thunderstorms and turbulence associated with the thunderstorm."
Typically, the Learjet 60 would have weather radar, as do airliners. Pilots also generally try to avoid thunderstorms and the turbulence associated with them.
A priority for NTSB investigators is recovering the plane's cockpit voice recorder, hoping its contents will help them better understand what occurred leading up to the crash.
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," Timothy Monville, the NTSB investigator in charge, said about the crash site.
Sumwalt said he is very confident investigators will determine what caused the crash and come up with recommendations to prevent something like this from happening in the future.

title: AI deepfakes pose risks to consumers and voters, experts warn
summary: "When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," said one cybersecurity expert focused on political campaigns.
story: Advances in artificial intelligence are making it a cinch to create so-called deepfake images, videos and audio recordings, raising concerns that bad actors could bombard people with hyper-realistic scams and spread disinformation.

Deepfakes that use the voices and likenesses of public figures, including celebrities or political candidates, can also deceive the public in various ways, security experts told CBS News. By one measure, fewer than 10% of people can recognize an audio deepfake, according to Doppel, a social engineering defense platform for detecting AI-enabled threats.
"In a test, only 8% of people realized an AI agent was calling them, whereas 92% of people thought they were speaking to a human," said Doppel co-founder Kevin Tian.

AI's capacity to churn out deepfakes at scale is a pressing issue in the political arena, according to security experts. AI-generated advertisements featuring deepfakes of politicians have already surfaced across the internet and social media ahead of the midterm elections.

In one such incident in Texas, a phony, AI-manipulated social video targeting Senate candidate James Talarico purported to show a former student accusing the Democrat of sexual misconduct, according to The Poynter Institute's PolitiFact service.

"When you can't tell what's legitimate, you question everything," Michael Kaiser, CEO of Defending Digital Campaigns, a nonpartisan organization that provides free cybersecurity services to political campaigns, told CBS News.

As of mid-October, political campaigns had spent more than $137 million on at least 220 AI-generated ads, some of which feature deepfakes of candidates, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks ads by political candidates.

"AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year. For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle," Erika Franklin Fowler, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, said in a statement this month. She noted that in most cases, the creators of the ads don't disclose that they were made using AI.
Even when someone suspects an ad is AI-generated or features a deepfake, the ad's visuals still can make an impression and shape opinion, the project's co-director, Travis Ridout, told CBS News.
"Even if we know it's not real, that sticks in one's mind," he added.
Prompting for deepfakes

Deepfakes are a kind of synthetic media that replicate a private individual's or public figure's image and likeness. Examples include a voice that sounds like a colleague or relative on the other end of a phone line, or a political figure appealing to voters for support or donations.
Raul Liive, a deepfake expert at Veriff, an AI-powered identity verification company, said the ease and speed with which deepfakes can be made and deployed today pose major risks.

"Every day that goes by, the generation of deepfake data gets easier and easier," he told CBS News. "If you wanted to fake someone's face years ago, you needed to make an effort to create fake data and use Photoshop. But now, to generate a fake face, you can just prompt your AI tool."

Veriff has documented a 300% increase in deepfake-related fraud attempts against businesses this year, compared with 2025. Liive outlined several examples of how bad actors use the tech to target businesses and unsuspecting consumers.
"A purported friend of yours calls and asks for a loan, but you know that person, and they've never made that kind of request before," he said.
Other types of scams center around medical emergencies. A caller could say they have a medical bill they urgently need help paying.

"Ask yourself what is the chance that someone you know would actually ask you something like that?" he said. "You can also hang up the phone and call the contact back on the number you have for them, or use another channel to validate their identity, if the request seems suspicious."

Veriff research on deepfakes found that consumers struggle to spot deepfakes, leaving them vulnerable to manipulation. In one test the firm conducted, 70% of people misidentified a deepfake video of a female character as being real.

The old telltale signs that something was a deepfake, like a human having six fingers or three hands, are also disappearing from AI content. Veriff found that people look for unreliable visual cues, such as unnatural skin or oddities in a subject's hair or teeth, which AI is increasingly eliminating from the content it generates.

Meanwhile, eroding public confidence in what they see could also undermine trust in legitimate content. Kaiser pointed to a photo of Sen. Mitch McConnell posing with his wife from his hospital bed, released amid speculation that the senator had died following a medical emergency earlier this year. Although the photo was authentic, some Internet users suggested it had been manipulated.

"That's an example of people just not trusting what they are seeing," Kaiser said. "People don't know if what they are looking at is legitimate, or if requests for donations are real. They're questioning everything that's going on and that disadvantages and erodes trust in the whole system."

title: Binance customers withdraw $7.42 billion after crypto heist
summary: Binance said the net outflow from the cryptocurrency exchange represents just 3% of its total holdings.
story: Binance customers withdrew $7.4 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.

On Monday, a Binance spokesperson said customers also deposited $2.7 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $4.7 billion in the company's holdings.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 3% of its $157 billion in total assets.

"The net outflow is a relatively limited portion of Binance's overall asset base," the Binance spokesperson said in an email. "Withdrawal levels are stabilizing to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity."
North Korea denies involvement
The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.
North Korea denies involvement in the attack. On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement "a trite provocation" and "an absurd rhetoric."

"This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the 'cyber crime' incidents whenever they occur on an international scale," she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
$3 billion frozen
Roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets were frozen, according to Binance. Freezing crypto funds allows certain issuers to block the transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world.

The hacker group believed to be responsible for the attack, known as "TraderTraitor," was converting most of the stolen assets into Ethereum in a move to hide their tracks, the FBI said Saturday. TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds. By early Sunday morning, it said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount.

title: How Alaska's ranked choice voting system works
summary: Voters in Alaska are going to the polls to cast their ballots in key races, and the state's unique ranked choice voting system is back in the spotlight.
story: Voters in Alaska are going to the polls to cast their ballots in key races Tuesday, including a Senate election that has garnered widespread attention amid scrutiny over the presence of a candidate bearing nearly the same name as the sitting senator, Dan Sullivan.
Alaska's election system itself has also been in the spotlight in recent years, since the state instituted a top-four nonpartisan primary and ranked choice voting in the general election.
Here's what to know about Alaska's voting system:
What is ranked choice voting?

Ranked choice voting allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference, rather than selecting a single candidate on the ballot. First implemented in 2022, the unique system aims to stymie polarization by moving the state away from party primaries. Instead, the top four candidates in the nonpartisan primary move on to the general election.

On Tuesday, if any candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, they win. But if nobody wins an outright majority, the count goes to a second round. The candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their supporters' votes are redistributed to their second choice. That process continues until one candidate wins a majority.

For example, say 100 people voted in the Alaska Senate race. Fifty of those voters ranked Candidate A as their top choice, 40 picked Candidate B, seven picked Candidate C and three picked Candidate D. Since no candidate reached 51 votes in the first round, Candidate D — the one with the fewest votes — would be eliminated in the second round of counting. The voters who ranked Candidate D first would then have their second-choice candidates tabulated. If one of those three votes went to Candidate A, Candidate A would have 51 votes and win. If not, the process would repeat.

In 2022, a special election was held to fill a vacancy in the House, and three candidates faced off under the new system. No candidate won more than 50% of first-choice votes, and the contest went to the ranked choice tabulation. Democrat Mary Peltola secured a majority in results that came 15 days after Election Day. Later that year, as she sought election to a full term, Peltola also won on the second round, with 55% of the voters after an initial 48.8%.
Who are the Alaska Senate candidates?

Alaska's Senate race could be key to determining control of the upper chamber. Voters will be presented with four choices: Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent; Daniel J. Sullivan, a candidate with nearly the same name; Gerald Heikes, another Republican; and Peltola.

Sen. Sullivan is a second-term senator and a Marine veteran who worked at the State Department during the George W. Bush administration. His main opponent is Peltola, who became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022. But Daniel J. Sullivan has added a wrinkle to the race.
The second Sullivan is a former teacher who announced he was challenging the sitting senator in June, prompting an unsuccessful push to remove him from the ballot.
Two Dan Sullivans on the ballot

Daniel J. Sullivan's decision to run sparked a legal fight over his eligibility to appear on the primary ballot that played out in state court over the summer. The state supreme court eventually allowed Daniel J. Sullivan to remain on the ballot and directed Alaska's Division of Elections to determine how he should be listed.
During Alaska's open Senate primary in August, Peltola garnered 49.5% of the vote, followed by Dan Sullivan, the senator, at 41.4%. The retired teacher, Daniel J. Sullivan, won just 2.5%.
A sample ballot for the general election shows the senator listed as "Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent." Daniel J. Sullivan has no identifiers beyond his name.
Still, the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan raised concerns that it could lead to voter confusion and drew a late-breaking effort by the Justice Department to intervene.

The Trump administration filed a lawsuit late last month that sought to block Alaska election officials from certifying the results of the Senate election if Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, loses to Peltola. But on Sunday, a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, finding that the federal government did not have the legal right to sue.
The Justice Department has said it will appeal.

Amid the litigation, the New York Times reported last week that there was a secret effort by political operatives aligned with Peltola's campaign to help recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to peel voters away from the senator. Peltola has denied any involvement in the alleged plan.

President Trump has denounced Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy, calling him a "FAKE" candidate in a Truth Social post shortly after 1 a.m. Tuesday. The president claimed that the retired teacher is "MISSING IN ACTION" and has "TOTALLY DISAPPEARED."
"MAYBE HE HAS BEEN 'KIDNAPPED' BY THE CORRUPT DUMOCRAT LAWYERS??? THEY ARE SCARED STIFF OF BEING PROSECUTED FOR ELECTION FRAUD!!!" Mr. Trump wrote in an all-caps post.
How long could counting votes in Alaska's ranked choice voting system take?

Conducting the election in Alaska is expected to take some time, experts have warned, emphasizing the need for patience as the Senate race holds the potential to play a key role in the balance of power in Washington.

Part of the lengthy process could come from Alaska's sprawling geography, remote locations and mail ballots, since Alaska counts mail ballots received 10 days after Election Day, or 15 days in some cases.

Tabulation rounds in Alaska's ranked choice voting system also begin after the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot, the process could drag on for weeks.
Alaska election officials are targeting Nov. 25 as the day to certify the election results. In 2022, Peltola secured a full, two-year term on Nov. 30.

title: Why some key races won't be decided on election night
summary: Experts expect some politicians on Tuesday night to claim the 2026 elections are rigged, but here's why that's not the case — and why it may be a while before some races are called.
story: Washington — Control of the House and Senate may not be immediately clear on election night, and some of the 2026 midterm election calls will take longer than others. But that's not unusual or an indication of fraud, as some candidates may claim.

As the nation watches to see how the elections unfold on Tuesday night, election experts advise voters against listening to politicians who cry foul without offering evidence of fraud as ballots are being cast or counted. Many key races will be close. And when they're close, the results are likely to come later.

David Becker, executive director and founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research and a CBS News contributor, says he has some doubts about whether Americans will even know who controls the House or Senate on election night.
"If we do, then there's a very big wave going on," Becker said.
Candidates "who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it"
Becker says there is a type of candidate who's likely to complain early and often about the integrity of the election.

"It's almost certain that the candidates who think they're doing poorly are going to be spreading lies and disinformation about it, trying to fill that vacuum," Becker said, adding that he believes President Trump "will probably spread lies and disinformation about the election on election night because he did it in 2020."
When the president was asked last week if he would accept the results of the midterms, whatever the outcome, he responded, "I will if they're honest elections."

Lawrence Norden, vice president of the Elections and Government Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, is concerned about the spread of misinformation on election night and afterward. He says it "flourishes in that period of time between voting and getting the results" and suggests that "period of time" will be longer when the race is close.
"When it's super close, it's not going to matter how fast you are counting the ballots," Norden said.
"Our perception of counting speed is not related to actual counting speed"

Becker points out that "our perception of counting speed is not related to actual counting speed." Election officials "are racing to unofficially count as many ballots as possible and report them out," he said, "but our perception is largely driven by when the media calls elections."

News outlets, including CBS News, project election winners based on their analysis of the ballots that have been counted, and this is partly driven by the margin of victory. The bigger the margin of victory, the more quickly a winner can usually be projected, though this also depends on the determination by news outlets of the amount of the vote that remains outstanding and the character of those votes.

California, the nation's largest state, is likely to have both races that are called very quickly and others that could take days or even weeks to call. William Gates, executive director of the Arizona State University's Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory, noted that for some California contests, "they call the race at 8:01 (p.m.) because we all know the Democrat's going to win." Those races don't attract much notice.

But he added that "we had some primaries that people were paying a lot of attention to — mayor of Los Angeles, the California governor's race." It took several days to finalize who would move on to the general elections in both those races.

Part of the reason it took so long to determine the outcome of those closely watched primaries is that mail ballots — which can be received until a week after Election Day if they are postmarked that day — took longer to be counted. All registered voters in California may vote by mail and are sent ballots.

Mail ballots must undergo signature verification, and those received before Election Day can be processed beforehand, but they are not counted until after polls close. Mail ballots received on Election Day or later end up being counted more slowly since they must undergo the signature verification process before they can be counted.

Gates, a former member of the Maricopa County Board of Supervisors, knows what it's like to live under a microscope. Arizona's Maricopa County endured intense scrutiny over the 2020 presidential election when Joe Biden won the Republican-leaning state, the first Democrat to do so since Bill Clinton in 1996. Though Fox News called Arizona for Biden on election night, CBS News and other networks did not project him as the winner for nine more days, until Nov. 12, 2020. Gates said his family received threats over that election.
"The reality is that Arizona doesn't really take any longer to count the votes than other states," Gates said.

"But the reason that they can attack us while they, you know, don't receive any comments is because we have very close elections," Gates said. "We are one of the few swing states left, and Maricopa is sort of the quintessential swing county."
Becker said all the ballots simply can't be counted on election night.

"Election officials have never completed counting on election night," he said. "It can't be done. Our ballots are way too complex. So it's going to take some time, and every state takes weeks to certify the election."
Mail voting and counting the ballots

Still, some states do take longer than others to count votes, especially states with high numbers of mail-in ballots. In Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, the counting is also slowed by the fact that state law prevents election officials from even processing mail ballots until the morning of Election Day.
In addition to California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Vermont, Utah, Washington and the District of Columbia automatically send mail ballots to all active registered voters.

And the voter composition for mail-in votes, early-in-person votes, and Election Day votes can look different, meaning numbers can appear to shift suddenly throughout the night and days after, as ballots are processed and counted.
"The votes are already in," Norden said. "They just all aren't counted at the same time."

He used a basketball game to illustrate the counting process: "It's like you are watching a recording of a game that already happened, right? So the game is over. But we don't know what's in those ballots, and we find out over election night, but it's already done."

"The fact that you know the Knicks come back against the Lakers at the end of a game when you're watching on the videotape of the game doesn't mean that the Knicks got to add points after the game was over," Norden said.

Mr. Trump has called mail-in voting "mail-in cheating" and knocked it as a fraud carried out by Democrats. But mail-in voting didn't skew Democratic until 2020, Becker said, when Mr. Trump railed against mail voting that increased during the pandemic.

"Since mail ballots, especially those that are delivered late, are among the last reported, you do see this 'red mirage,' 'blue wave' effect in some places," Becker said. "It's moderated, I think, since the 2020 election, but you do see (it) because those mail ballots are being reported out late." The "red mirage" effect describes how early results of in-person voting may show a Republican leading, but batches of mail-in votes that are processed and counted later in the evening could swing the election to the Democrat in the race.

For example, Becker pointed to Pennsylvania in 2020, where mail ballots weren't reported publicly for days because unlike California, election officials couldn't begin processing them until Election Day.

"So the Election Day votes came out first," Becker said. "Those skewed Republican." Then, the mail votes were processed. "And those were overwhelmingly Democratic, but the batches of those were getting reported out much later, because that's what was required under Pennsylvania law."

Becker offered one more thing to remember Tuesday night: "If you hear candidates complaining about the process, I don't know whether they won or lost, but I can tell you that they think they lost, because the winners do not complain about the process," Becker said. "The winners let the process play out."

title: A bitter sheriff's primary, a write-in campaign and a county divided
summary: An unusual sheriff election in Lee County, Alabama, highlights how elected law enforcement often shapes issues of public safety, immigration and gun control.
story: It began with a phone call. A grassroots write-in campaign had been launched weeks before Tuesday's midterm election in an effort to keep longtime Alabama Sheriff Jay Jones in office. Jones was ousted in May by about 300 votes in a bitterly fought Republican primary in Lee County by a former sheriff's deputy, Cameron Hunt.
"Somebody has started this write-in campaign," Lee County resident Jack Carter said, recalling his recent phone conversation, in an interview with CBS News. "And I said, really?"

Carter said he had spoken with others about trying to write in their votes for Jones after the primary, but nothing ever materialized — until he got that phone call. He said he didn't know who was behind the campaign, and it's challenging to find out.
A Facebook page dedicated to the "write-in campaign" lists a Proton email address, which is an encrypted account. A query to the email address from a CBS News reporter went unanswered.

Carter, a former sheriff's deputy — who said Jones was a mentor — and now a local furniture maker, said he was directed to a woman with access to campaign signs reading, "On Election Day write in Sheriff Jay Jones." Soon, the signs began popping up across yards, pickup trucks and local businesses.
He placed one in the back of his black Ram pickup truck and posted a picture online. Then, things began to "blow up," he said.

Supporters of Hunt accused Jones' camp of being sore losers, while Jones' supporters insisted voters have every right to write in any candidate they choose. Social media posts captured signs being stolen from yards, accompanied by mounting accusations and online bickering.
"This has not gone the way that this needs to go," Carter said, adding, "It's chaotic."

Sheriff Jones said he was "humbled" by the grassroots campaign in an interview with CBS News, saying, "I was not involved and nor have I solicited anyone for votes." Jones wanted to make clear he isn't involved, as he claims the Alabama Republican Party threatened to remove him from the party because of the growing write-in campaign.
Sheriff elections and quality-of-life issues

While congressional and marquee statewide races dominate midterm headlines, down-ballot contests often play a far more direct role in shaping people's daily life. A sheriff sets local public safety priorities and typically oversees jail operations, budget allocation, response to crime and bail management.

Nationally, sheriffs are overwhelmingly White and male, according to a 2020 report released by a progressive group, Women's Donor Action, examining sheriff demographics. There are 3,801 sheriffs in the country. In several states, the office is established by the state constitution, often allowing for broad authority — and for many counties the sheriff might be the most visible and powerful position around.

There are about 1,400 sheriffs up for election in 2026. In 20 states, including Colorado, Alabama, Maryland, Utah and Wisconsin, most of the elected sheriffs are up for the vote, according to Yesim Karaman, a spokesperson at the National Sheriffs' Association, a national organization supporting training, education and advocacy.

"They're policing, they're making sure that they have the good community relationships, they have the leadership in their counties, and they're responding to the citizens that they serve and who they're elected by," said Karaman.

Sheriffs can also help shape regional policies such as immigration enforcement and gun control. Several 2026 midterm contests feature debates over partnerships with federal immigration authorities, known as 287(g) agreements. In Wisconsin, voters across two counties are weighing in directly on their local sheriffs' cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Jones and Hunt differed over various policy issues in their campaign, including immigration, guns and Flock intelligence. Jones said his office has often cooperated with ICE, but doesn't have a signed Memorandum of Understanding. He said there is misinformation around what this means for the county.

"We have cooperated with any request we received from ICE, from the local agencies here and federal agency offices in the state of Alabama, to actually, and this is on record, in the last two years, we've actually transferred over 450 individuals to ICE custody from the Lee County Jail," he said.
However, Karaman cautioned that sheriffs' immigration abilities are often based on state law.
"Whether a sheriff signs a 287(g) agreement and has the ability to cooperate extensively with ICE is a matter of state law and local politics," she said.

Jones also said he supports the continuation of concealed carry permits, which are issued by the sheriff's office, because it helps keep guns out of the hands of criminals. (Alabama law changed in 2023 to no longer require a permit to carry a concealed handgun in much of the state.) He said he's in "full support of the Second Amendment."

Hunt said he plans to sign a 287(g) agreement, supports open carry laws saying a permit isn't needed, and said publicly that he plans to end the county's Flock contract. He wrote in an email, "I strongly support the Second Amendment, believe immigration laws should be enforced, and recognize the importance of providing law enforcement with the tools necessary to protect our communities."

Notwithstanding the issues, many sheriffs are still running in nationwide races uncontested. A 2024 data analysis found that over a two-year period from 2022 to 2024, about 62% of sheriff elections were uncontested.
In Lee County, which holds a population of 190,118 people, Jones has been in office for more than 27 years — and he's rarely had an opponent.
A "simple" grassroots effort grows after an escalating feud
That changed late last October when Hunt, a deputy sheriff at the time, requested a private meeting with Jones to announce his plan to challenge him in the Republican primary.

"Within approximately ten minutes, I was terminated," Hunt wrote in an email to CBS News, attaching a copy of his termination letter. "There was no legal requirement for Sheriff Jones to terminate me at that point, yet his termination letter specifically cited my intention to run against him as the reason for terminating me."
Jones said he gave Hunt several chances to resign from his deputy position. Local media reported on the firing and subsequent feud.

"It simply would've been an untenable situation" to keep him, Jones said. Several courts have upheld the firing of deputy sheriffs for political reasons. A federal appellate court found in 2021 — when Missouri deputies sued after they were fired for political reasons — the position of deputy sheriff requires political loyalty. The sheriff can fire deputies because they hold policymaking positions for which political loyalty is necessary for effective job performance, the court said. In 2016, North Carolina's Supreme Court upheld the firing of sheriff's deputies who declined to donate to the sheriff's political campaign.

A month after the May primary — where results showed Hunt defeating Jones by 9,301 to 8,994 votes — Hunt said he filed a formal complaint with the Alabama Ethics Commission. He alleges the sheriff used a departmental GPS tracking system to set up a geofence around Hunt's private residence to monitor any deputies visiting his home. The Alabama Ethics Commission said it couldn't confirm or deny that the complaint exists.
Jones said if there is to be an investigation, he stands ready to "cooperate fully." Hunt said he is also going to call for an independent investigation.

Jones touted his length of service, which he says has provided stability for the county and allowed him to grow the sheriff's office, which has a budget of $25 million, from 80 people in 1999 to 230 people today.
He said he wanted to make clear he respected the outcome in May, but what was happening now was "a simple, basic grassroots effort by the members of the community who want a choice in this effort."

Still, the race in Lee County is rare, said Mirya R. Holman, a public policy professor at the University of Houston, and co-author of the book "The Power of the Badge: Sheriffs and Inequality in the United States."

"It is very unusual for longtime incumbents in any office (including sheriff) to lose primaries," she wrote in an email. "Write-in campaigns are a big unknown — they are very rarely successful for any office, including sheriffs."

But she said she doesn't know of any data tracking write-in campaigns. (In Oswego, New York, a candidate is running a write-in campaign for sheriff, but never served in the position. In Washington, a successful write-in campaign propelled a candidate onto the sheriff ballot.)

Some voters supporting the write-in campaign for Jones pointed to the differing policies between the two candidates. Debra Beil, a self-proclaimed "liberal" who has lived in conservative Lee County for 35 years, said she was organizing for and supporting Jones because of his experience level.

She cited his educational programs on gun safety and his stance regarding gun permits among her primary reasons for supporting him. Supporter Chad Lanier added that while Jones' experience was his primary consideration, he also preferred to avoid a heightened presence of federal agents in the county.
Hunt said he's not particularly worried about the write-in campaign and instead remains focused on the commitments he's made to the people of Lee County when he prepares to take office in January.

"I'm the only candidate for sheriff whose name will appear on the November 3 ballot, and I respect everyone's right to participate in the democratic process, including their right to cast a write-in vote," Hunt said.
In that area, the two agree. Jones said this vote is all about what the will of the people is.
"After all, that's who's being served here," he said. "And their choice should be what matters."
"The sheriff answers to the people," Jones said.

title: NASA telescope is plunging back to Earth after 22 years in orbit
summary: The Swift Observatory is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.
story: An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower. The space agency said Monday it predicts the Swift Observatory will likely come crashing down on Wednesday.

Most of the 1 ½-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive reentry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

"As of Monday, the U.S. Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound spacecraft will re-enter the atmosphere at approximately 3:30 a.m. EST, Nov. 4, with an uncertainty of 11 hours," NASA said on Monday.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the reentry zone. The U.S. Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.
In a statement on Monday, NASA said the "risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely" — roughly 1 in 2,100.
"NASA and Space Force will continue to monitor the re-entry and update predictions," the agency said.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning, yet full of gratitude, for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma-ray bursts and supernovas.

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 7 miles to 9 miles to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.
Shawn Domagal-Goldman, Astrophysics Division director at NASA, told "CBS Mornings" in June that nothing pinpoints gamma-ray bursts like the Swift Observatory.
"A nuclear weapon going off doesn't even compare to the magnitude of energy that comes out of these things and it's literally the biggest explosions in the universe," Domagal-Goldman said.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.
"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

title: Iran dismisses U.S. response to peace proposal
summary: President Trump said on the eve of U.S. elections that a deal with Iran "could happen," but after new U.S. strikes, Tehran called America's response to the latest proposal "not convincing."
story: What to know about the Iran war today:

A senior Iranian figure on Tuesday cast doubt on diplomatic efforts to broker a peace deal with the U.S., calling the Trump administration's response to the latest proposal "not convincing" and insisting that Iran's demands, including for a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, must be met if the Strait of Hormuz is to reopen.American forces launched limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets near the strait on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, in response to an apparent Iranian attack targeting a U.S. aircraft.  President Trump said on the eve of U.S. midterm elections that a deal with Iran to end the eight-month war still "could happen," insisting Tehran "wants a settlement, as soon as possible."

A senior Iranian figure on Tuesday cast doubt on diplomatic efforts to broker a peace deal with the U.S., calling the Trump administration's response to the latest proposal "not convincing" and insisting that Iran's demands, including for a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, must be met if the Strait of Hormuz is to reopen.

title: U.S. launches strikes on Iranian targets in Strait of Hormuz
summary: The U.S. launched limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz after Iran fired at a U.S. aircraft, a senior U.S. official told CBS News.
story: The U.S. military launched limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News.

The strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island, a senior U.S. official said. It came after two incidents on Monday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired at an American fighter jet, leading it to return fire, according to two U.S. military officials. Later Monday, Iran fired a missile from Qeshm Island that threatened shipping, the officials said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes, which came on the eve of Election Day in the U.S. President Trump has been floating the idea of restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms, at the same time as U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a possible U.S.-Iran deal.
Qeshm Island, in the northern Strait of Hormuz, is crucial to the Iranian regime's efforts to monitor and exert control over commercial traffic through the waterway.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday that Tehran retained "the right to legitimate self-defense" after the new U.S. strikes, and would do so "until the military aggression has been completely and permanently brought to an end."

Iran has retaliated for attacks on its territory throughout the war sparked by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28 by targeting commercial shipping traffic in the strait and U.S. allies and interests across the Persian Gulf region.

As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between suggesting he could strike a deal to end the war with Iran, to warning that he could resume major attacks against the country.
In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible."

Later Monday night, however, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with" the Israeli leader, but he did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.

The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
In Israel, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.
As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47.1 billion in military expenditure alone, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

CENTCOM said the cost of replacing spent munitions alone was about $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. Another $6.1 billion was needed to replace lost equipment, and there has been around $11.9 billion spent on incremental costs including support for American service members.
The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which have been targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.

title: Poland launches major security operation along border with Russia
summary: Poland's prime minister says a rapid, major deployment of extra security forces to the border with Russia may have prevented "attempted acts of provocation."
story: Berlin — Poland launched a large-scale security operation this week along its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the country's national police chief said, and the Polish prime minister said the effort may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation targeting the NATO member.

Additional police and counterterrorism units, as well as troops from the elite military special forces unit GROM, have been deployed as part of the operation, which national police chief Marek Boroń said would run from Monday until at least Nov. 8.

Polish and allied intelligence agencies had warned of possible sabotage operations and provocations during the first half of November, particularly along Poland's border with Kaliningrad, and including possible border incursions by armed groups.
Those warnings had already put domestic security agencies on high alert even before the additional security forces were deployed to the northeast regions of Warmia-Masuria and Podlaskie.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Tuesday that suspicious movements were observed overnight near Kaliningrad, including individuals carrying flashlights close to the border area.
He said the quick reaction by Polish security forces may have prevented an unspecified provocation this week.

"We very quickly mobilized the necessary security forces and means on site, and we successfully prevented any attempted acts of provocation, if that was the intention. Of course, we will never be able to completely confirm that," Tusk said Tuesday, adding that intelligence had pointed for weeks to possible "acts of diversion or more serious provocation" against the European Union, including "the intrusion of armed individuals into Polish territory."
A special command center was set up at Polish national police headquarters to coordinate the new security operation.
The goal is to protect the public, detect suspicious activities early, and prevent attacks on critical infrastructure, the police said Tuesday.

Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad, bordered only by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and the Baltic Sea to the west, is of considerable military and strategic significance. It is widely believed that Russian security agencies, including the FSB and GRU intelligence agencies, have a presence in the territory in eastern Europe.

To the immediate east of Kaliningrad is the strategically important Suwałki Corridor — the only land border connecting the Baltic NATO states with the rest of the alliance, where Poland and Lithuania share a short border sandwiched between Russian and Belarusian territory.

Polish authorities had not published any evidence of specific plans for an act of sabotage or an attack originating from Kaliningrad by Tuesday afternoon, but the alert comes after months of sabotage, air incursion and other low-level incidents across Europe blamed largely on Russia.

During a joint news conference with Lithuania's prime minister on Oct. 13, Tusk referred to a conversation he had recently had with NATO Supreme Allied Commander Alexus Grynkewich, and said it had reinforced his own concerns about increasing threats of sabotage, including possible provocations involving aircraft or attacks on border crossings.

At about the same time, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture of the security threats facing the U.K. and Europe, and he said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one."

"The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum warned, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.
"It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia was sticking to "tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."

Among the numerous incidents attributed to Russia across Europe this year alone, there was a fire in August at a Polish factory that produces drones and other military components, and an arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station that Polish officials blamed directly on Russia in September.

Russian drones have also crossed into NATO airspace in Eastern Europe repeatedly during the war in Ukraine, and just this week the U.K. Royal Navy said it had intercepted a Russian spy ship off the far northern coast of Scotland.
The navy said helicopters were dispatched to track the intelligence-gathering ship, which was "closely monitoring" a NATO exercise taking place near Scotland's Outer Hebrides islands.

title: 5 people rescued in South Pacific after months at sea, 4 still missing
summary: The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing in July.
story: Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing.

Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported, after they had drifted an estimated 3,355 miles east from the Federated States of Micronesia.

The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. The group had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo at the time, ABC reported.
A 10-day search covering 33,000 square miles followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said.
"Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care," the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email.
"Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them," the email added.
When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible.
A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island.
Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery.
"They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," she told the ABC.
The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. ABC said the group went missing after their boat was caught in a storm.
The governor of Micronesia's Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.
"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter.
"We continue to pray for their four companions," he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
Other rescues in the Pacific

There have been previous incidents where people have become lost at sea among the tiny island chains that stud the Pacific Ocean. An Australian man survived more than two months lost at sea in 2023 with his dog Bella after rough seas damaged their boat and its electronics system. Tim Shaddock, 51, had been traveling from Mexico to French Polynesia, but found himself drifting in the Pacific Ocean for more than two months. Shaddock and his canine companion survived by drinking rain water and eating raw fish that Shaddock caught, he said. They were spotted by a helicopter and rescued in July 2023.

Two American sailors and their two dogs were rescued after five months at sea in the Pacific in 2017. Jennifer Appel and Tasha Fuiaba were discovered 900 miles southeast of Japan by a Taiwanese fishing ship, the U.S. Navy said at the time. The vessel's engine died during bad weather, and they were unable to get to land using the ship's sails. The women said the boat drifted off course, and no ships were near enough to hear their distress calls. Water purifiers and a year's supply of food aboard the vessel kept them alive, the Navy said.
In 2024, three fishermen were stranded on a remote Micronesian island for more than a week. They were rescued after using palm leaves to spell out "HELP" in large letters on a beach.

title: 1 dead, 2 injured in helicopter crash near Mount Everest base camp
summary: The two helicopters were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season.
story: Two helicopters collided Tuesday while trying to land just below Mount Everest's base camp, killing at least one person and injuring two others, officials said.

The aircraft were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season. Heavy snow had covered the route before the weather improved Sunday and thousands of trekkers were able to move around.
There are no roads on Everest, and helicopters are the only way to bring down trekkers and guides who become sick or exhausted in the cold and high altitude.
The helicopters crashed at Pheriche village, which is at an altitude of 13,780 feet.

A 47-year-old tourist from India was killed in the crash, according to Bhupendra Thapa, a Solukhumbhu district administration officer. Arrangements were being made to airlift the tourist's remains to Kathmandu, the Agence France-Presse reported.
A passenger from New Zealand was injured and was being transported to the capital, Kathmandu, for treatment. A Nepali pilot sustained injuries but was treated locally.
The number of people on the two helicopters wasn't clear.

The Mount Everest base camp trek lasts up to two weeks and goes from the only airstrip in the area at Lukla to base camp located at 17,380 feet. Everest's summit is at an altitude of over 29,000 feet. The trek is popular during the fall season, right after the rainy season and before the harsh winter months.

The helicopter collision is the second incident along the route to Everest Base Camp this week. On Friday, Octo. 30, a fire broke out at a hotel in Dingboche, which is known as a stop for trekkers to pause while they acclimate to Everest's high altitude.

The fire may have been sparked by a cooking gas cylinder explosion, local media reported. Guests and hotel staff were safely evacuated. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Video obtained by CBS News shows the building in flames.
Dingboche is about 2 miles from Pheriche. The two destinations are about a 40-minute hike from each other, according to trail guides.

title: Soccer player dies following on-field collision in Spain
summary: Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision in a match.
story: A Spanish soccer player's death is now under investigation as possible involuntary manslaughter, after he suffered a fatal injury in an on-field collision during a match.
The country's National Police said Tuesday that proceedings were opened and prosecutors will also be involved.
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest from the on-field collision in a Spanish second-division match, his club said. He was 30 years old.
De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by the onrushing Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during added time.
Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

Tenerife said in a statement to Spanish media late Monday that De Miguel suffered cardiac arrest but that his pulse was restored in the ambulance to the hospital. However, it later said his condition had "worsened neurologically" and subsequently announced that De Miguel had died at 8 a.m.
The club, located on Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken."

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness," the club wrote, in part, in a statement announcing the death on social media. "The family of Jesús de Miguel thanks each and every one of the expressions of support received, and likewise requests, from the heart, the utmost respect for their privacy in these terrible moments."
De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."
The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina match to be held later on Tuesday.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun was playing for CSKA Moscow when he died from head injuries received in a collision during a match.

title: Stolen watch worth $290,000 returned to store with apology note
summary: The case of the stolen Audemars Piguet timepiece took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a note saying sorry.
story: A Swiss luxury watch worth about $290,000 that was stolen from a Tokyo store last week has been returned with an apology note, according to local media.
The theft occurred when a man posing as a customer tried on the Audemars Piguet timepiece and then fled the shop in the Japanese capital while it was still on his wrist.

But the case took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a handwritten note saying sorry, the Asahi Shimbun newspaper and other media reported on Monday, citing unnamed investigative sources.
The watch's serial number reportedly identified it as the stolen item.
A name and address were also written on the package, but police believe the information is fake, the Japan Times reported.
The shop declined to comment when contacted by AFP.
Tokyo police are still searching for the man on suspicion of theft, according to the Asahi Shumbun.

In August, four luxury watches worth 200 million yen ($1.3 million) were stolen from another store in the same shopping complex. Two Chilean nationals were arrested on suspicion of theft in connection with the incident and subsequently indicted, the Japan Times reported.

After that robbery, police conducted a crime prevention session for watch store owners, advising that they only display replicas, the Asahi Simbun reported. They were also taught how to use a special lining on display cases to make them difficult to break.

title: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
summary: The envoy will also meet with European and NATO allies to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine.
story: The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.

Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory seized over the course of the grueling war.

Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's land grab would set a dangerous precedent.

Witkoff's latest announcement of planned talks at the working level — which generally means discussions among technocrats, not at the senior diplomatic or national leadership level — comes after a rare, localized cease-fire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson ended on Sunday.
The brief truce allowed humanitarian supplies into the small Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and the evacuation of an undisclosed number of residents.

The cease-fire, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, has raised some hope for more diplomatic progress toward ending the war sparked by Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
Russia has continued pummeling the rest of Ukraine during and after the local ceasefire, however, with more strikes coming overnight into Tuesday across the country.
At least 29 people were killed in a village in the southeast Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia, authorities said Tuesday.
In the northeast city of Kharkiv, the regional administration said a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people and forcing the evacuation of around 200 patients.
Russia's defense ministry said Tuesday that it had carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine, and port infrastructure in the Odesa region.
Moscow's mayor said, meanwhile, that 500 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital were destroyed overnight.

title: More European grocery stores hit by apparent fridge-freezer hacks
summary: Grocery chains in European nations say temperatures in some stores' fridges and freezers soared over 100 degrees just weeks after a similar incident in France.
story: Grocery store chains in at least three European countries reported unexpected temperature spikes Monday in refrigerators and freezers that ruined food — the second time in less than a month that similar incidents have raised concerns about cyberattacks on increasingly interlinked infrastructure.

Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium both said an IT incident overnight had sent temperatures inside fridges and freezers in dozens of their stores in Belgium and Luxembourg soaring, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar spikes, with one outlet explicitly blaming a cyberattack, according to the Reuters news agency.

The incidents come less than three weeks after several French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that sent refrigerator temperatures surging as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit in hundreds of outlets.
French chains E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U told the AFP news agency last month that they had suffered a cyberattack.

On Monday, Reuters said Ahold, the Dutch grocery store chain, had reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands in October after detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure. The chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems on Monday, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester told Reuters.

The CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates the systems used by Delhaize and other chains, told Belgium's national Belga news agency a cyberattack was to blame after fridge and freezer units' evaporators were switched into defrost mode.

"We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans told Belga. "We've been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network."

"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," he told the news agency, but he added that many units would require physical modifications, and "that requires investment."

A handful of Swedish supermarkets also saw refrigerator and freezer temperatures soar early Monday, two chains said, forcing them to throw away spoiled food. ICA and Coop both told AFP they had no immediate information about their systems being subjected to a cyberattack.

ICA told AFP "a limited number" of its stores were affected, but it did not provide a number. One of its stores, in Sjobo in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had "been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees" Celsius (about 122 degrees Fahrenheit).
"We are looking into what has happened and the scale of it," spokesperson Helena Johansson told AFP, adding that the company was focusing on how to help affected stores.

The Coop chain said six of its around 800 stores in Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers and had to throw out food, with company spokesman Carlos Cancino telling AFP that the units "either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired."
"I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack," he said.

On Oct. 12, major French retailers said hundreds of stores were hit by a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems, which forced them to throw out food and raised concerns about food security. In that incident, refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
There has been no claim of responsibility for any hack targeting grocery retailers in Europe to date.

Speaking after the French stores were forced to discard thousands of pounds of wasted food last month due to the still-unattributed hack, European Union food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said in a post on X that "food security requires more attention at all levels," calling the "exploitation" of vulnerabilities in such essential, networked systems a new "reality."

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X last month.
Prosecutors in Paris confirmed a cyberattack and said it also hit other major chains and sparked fires as some equipment overheated.

title: Hacked alert apps send Ukrainians, Russians fake attack warnings
summary: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps were hacked just hours apart, sending civilians false warnings of chemical and nuclear attacks.
story: Kyiv — Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps used to warn civilians of incoming missiles, drones and other military attacks were hacked hours apart on Sunday night, sending out false messages about radiation, chemical attacks and nuclear strikes.

At 10:47 p.m. local time (3 p.m. Eastern), Air Alert, a Ukrainian app developed by Ajax Systems and Stfalcon with support from Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation, started sending out false warnings of radiation, chemical threats, a nuclear attack and even street fighting in Kyiv.

Some Ukrainians rely on the app to decide whether or not to take shelter ahead of incoming Russian missile and drone strikes. Many also rely on the social media platform Telegram, however, where the country's Air Force and security analysts share more specific information about incoming strikes.

The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed just 10 minutes later, at 11:02 p.m. local time, on multiple platforms, that the notifications were false. "The Air Alert app appears to have been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat!" the Air Force said in a message shared on Telegram, urging Ukrainians to remain calm and follow official updates.
Some Kyiv residents told CBS News they immediately knew the notifications were fake after checking Telegram channels.

A couple of hours later, at 2:45 a.m. in Moscow (6:45 p.m. Eastern), Russia's Emergencies Ministry app was also hacked. False alerts were sent to users in 33 regions, according to Russia's tightly controlled media, which said the messages warned of "nuclear warheads" being launched across the country and instructed residents to stock up on food for three weeks and shelter in basements.
The Russian ministry said attackers had exploited a vulnerability in its app's administrative panel, prompting officials to disconnect and isolate affected services.
Developers of the Air Alert app in Ukraine said "unauthorized interference" had occurred and temporarily disabled push notifications and the app itself.

Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said the hack had no impact on Ukraine's security operations and that the Air Alert app is not affiliated with the country's military command systems.
The hacks came as a temporary ceasefire expired at 10:59 p.m. Ukraine time on Sunday in and around Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian city that has been occupied by Russia since 2022.

The truce, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, began on Oct. 27. It allowed humanitarian aid into the city and some civilians to evacuate. Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said both sides had observed the agreement and were discussing further humanitarian measures.

title: U.K. man returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
summary: Karl Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998.
story: Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.

His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.

It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.

"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.

"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. We've had to create two world records just to get back here. And I couldn't have done it on my own. So it was a world, global effort."

Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998. He made his way north through Central America, the United States and Canada, then crossed the Bering Sea to Russia in the world's first recorded attempt. He then carried on through Central Asia and swam for 31 days across the Caspian Sea in another reported first, in order to circumvent the war in Ukraine.

Over the past few years, he crossed Europe, and just last month, he swam from France across the English Channel, setting foot on the country of his birth where British immigration officers had set up to check his passport.

"It's almost like arriving in a foreign country," Bushby told CBS News over the weekend as he neared home. "I've worked with dollars for 28 years. I don't know the brands in the stores. So I'm going around wondering what I'm going to be buying. A couple of times I got caught out crossing the road because I'm looking in the other direction because these people drive on the wrong side of the road."
His home stretch Monday, quite literally, was a roughly 3-mile brisk walk from near Hull's town center to a quiet, sprawling neighborhood to the north of two-story, red-brick terrace homes.
Children lined the turn to his mother's home and cheered while an honor guard led the way.
Bushby pushed the cart that had been with him for about 25 years the last few steps.
He then embraced his waiting mother on the street outside her home. The cheers quieted, and the two shared a moment in this homecoming.
Bushby said he feels like a man wondering what home truly means after spending a generation around the world.

"I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long. And it's an odd feeling. And I almost feel guilt," he said. "Like there are other parts of the world now that feel more like home to me. And now I'm going to be faced with this weird static thing."
Now, after more than 10,000 days away, Bushby faces a different task: processing it all.
Confronted with the question of whether the world had gotten better or worse, he acknowledged the troubles but did not give up on his optimism.

"The world's in a little bit messier time; there are more wars, you know," he told CBS News. "But it's all good. At the end of the day, we've been through worse. So we all need to breathe a little bit, get through the tough times; we're going to be just fine. My bet is on us, no matter what. My bet is on humanity."
His final advice for anyone wondering if they could also accomplish something extraordinary: dream bigger.
"Yeah, you can, because I'm nothing special. Maybe we need the art of dreaming big again. People seem to dream outside of a very confined space mentally at the world that they live in," he said.

"You've got to have that little confidence. You got to realize that you're more capable than you think you are. People constantly underestimate themselves. So that's the first step, I think. Dream big. Realize you're probably capable more than you'd think. If you take nothing else from this … take that!"

title: Record bounty offered for fugitive drug kingpin "Chubby Jos"
summary: Jos Leijdekkers is one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.
story: Dutch authorities are offering a record reward of 2 million euros ($2.2 million) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.

The arrest of Leijdekkers, also known as "Bolle Jos" ("Chubby Jos"), is "the highest priority for the Public Prosecution Service and the police," said Dutch prosecutors in a statement, multiplying by 10 their previous reward.
Leijdekkers is considered to be one of the key players in the international cocaine trade.
A court in Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in 2024 to 24 years in prison for drug shipments totaling nearly 7,000 kilos of cocaine, an armed robbery, and ordering a "liquidation."
He has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch police have tracked the 35-year-old to Sierra Leone. Any information shared with prosecutors will be kept secret, the Dutch authorities said in a statement.

Justice Minister David van Weel said the increase in the reward was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order."
"The Netherlands, in cooperation with the international community, is doing everything in its power to secure the arrest of Leijdekkers," the minister said in a letter to parliament.
Links to Sierra Leone

In January 2025, Dutch authorities said they were "absolutely certain" he was hiding out in Sierra Leone. The BBC reported that Dutch prosecutor Wim de Bruin said the fugitive's return to the Netherlands was of "the highest priority."

Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of officials as high as President Julius Maada Bio have sparked speculation that the cocaine baron has cozied up to Sierra Leone's political class — including the president's daughter.

Suspicions that he was in Sierra Leone arose after the country's first lady, Fatima Bio, posted pictures and a video on social media that showed a man strongly resembling Leijdekkers at a religious service, also attended by President Bio.

Leijdekkers is also believed to be involved in the disappearance and death of Naima Jillal, a woman who went missing in 2019 after she got into a car in Amsterdam, according to Europol. Intercepted messages allegedly showed that Leijdekkers "played an important role in Jillal's disappearance," the agency said.

"For a long time, there was no trace of Naima Jillal, until photos of a woman believed to be her were found on a phone seized in the Marengo investigation," Europol said. "The photos show that she was most likely tortured and is probably no longer alive."
