title: Ex-Rep Justin Amash says Mike Rogers 'would be more dangerous in the US Senate' than Abdul El-Sayed
summary: Former Rep. Justin Amash suggested that former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers "would be more dangerous in the U.S. Senate" than Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
story: Observers wonder whether Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens' surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers will cost Abdul-El-Sayed the Senate seat in the hotly-contested Michigan race.

Former Rep. Justin Amash — who announced on Monday that he did not vote for Abdul El-Sayed or former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's U.S. Senate race — said he thinks El-Sayed would "be far less dangerous in practice than Rogers."
Rogers, a Republican candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump, is facing Democratic candidate El-Sayed in the widely-watched Senate contest.

"It goes without saying that I have major disagreements with both Mike Rogers and Abdul El-Sayed, and neither one particularly likes me," Amash wrote in a thread on X. "I also don’t vote for 'the lesser of two evils.' I believe you should support a candidate only if you truly want the person to hold that office. I’ve already voted, and consistent with the above principle, I didn’t vote for Rogers or El-Sayed. But I do know which one would be more dangerous in the U.S. Senate — and it’s not even close."
ELECTION DAY 2026: VOTERS CAST BALLOTS WITH CONTROL OF CONGRESS ON THE LINE
Former Rep. Justin Amash is seen on the House floor on Jan. 4, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Amash pointed to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as a political figure who resembles El-Sayed. Sanders has supported El-Sayed in the Senate race.

"To assess who is the greater threat to American freedom, let’s take a look at my time in Congress with Rogers and Bernie Sanders, who shares many of El-Sayed’s views and can serve as his stand-in," Amash wrote. "Several of Sanders’s key proposals, in my opinion, would be exceptionally bad for our country. But given the structure of our government, he’s in no position to get those ideas enacted and enforced.

"In contrast, Rogers is extraordinarily bad on all the issues on which an individual member of Congress may be the deciding vote. Again, these are issues like war powers, surveillance, privacy, the freedom of speech, criminal justice, and government oversight and accountability," he asserted. "In this world — the real world, not the imaginary one that partisan pundits on the right and left live in — Rogers poses a far greater threat to individual liberty and the Constitution than Sanders. Moreover, it’s not just that Rogers is awful here; it’s that Sanders is actually much better on these issues than the median member of Congress."
MICHIGAN VOTERS MAKE SURPRISING CROSS-PARTY CHOICES AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED RACE REACHES FINAL HOURS
Former Rep. Mike Rogers, left, the Republican U.S. Senate candidate, and his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Katie McTiernan/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Amash asserted that between Rogers and El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate would be "less dangerous."

"I think it’s fair to view El-Sayed as someone who mostly will follow in Sanders’s footsteps on policy and therefore will be far less dangerous in practice than Rogers," Amash wrote, adding in parentheses, "(Again, El-Sayed as a senator will do many things that are bad. The question addressed at length is not whether he’s good but simply whether he’s better on the whole than Rogers.)"
The Rogers and the El-Sayed campaigns did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment on Tuesday.
MICHIGAN VOTERS WEIGH IN AFTER DEM REP HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP CANDIDATE
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Amash, who served in the U.S. House of Representatives from early 2011 until early 2021, voted to impeach President Donald Trump in late 2019. While he served most of his congressional tenure as a Republican, Amash switched to Independent in 2019 and then to Libertarian in 2020.
He lost the 2024 GOP Michigan U.S. Senate primary to Rogers.
Rogers went on to lose the general election that year to Democrat Elissa Slotkin, who was a House lawmaker at the time.
Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who lost the Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed this year, shook up the 2026 general election when she endorsed Rogers on Sunday.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Susan Collins' Maine Senate office vandalized with 'disturbing' graffiti on night before Election Day
summary: Susan Collins' Biddeford, Maine, office was hit with red paint and the message "BLOOD on her HANDS," marking the second vandalism incident in a month.
story: Protesters swarmed Senator Susan Collins’ office and entered through the front doors, chanting "vote her out,
The Biddeford, Maine, office of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, was vandalized Monday night for the second time in a month, Collins' chief of staff told Fox News.

After vandals previously spray-painted the building's door in September, saboteurs on Monday dumped a bucket of red paint in front of the location while writing in crimson — "BLOOD on her HANDS" — on the sidewalk in front of the building.

"This is another incident in a series and the second attempt at our Biddeford office to intimidate the Senator and her staff. These tactics are disturbing, but not effective. Our staff is undeterred and on the job," Collins' chief of staff Katie Brown told Fox News' Alexis McAdams.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES
Photo of graffiti outside of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Biddeford, Maine, offices. (Fox News)

The Biddeford office is near the scene of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer-involved shooting in which a law enforcement officer shot and killed 26-year-old Colombian national Johan Sebastián Guerrero in July.
Days after the shooting, protesters barged into the Biddeford office's front door, chanting "vote her out."
PERSONAL JABS, BILLIONAIRE DONORS AND PARTY LOYALTY FUEL HEATED MAINE SENATE DEBATE
In September, the "Trump whore" epithet was spray-painted in red on her office door.
Photo of graffiti outside of Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Biddeford, Maine, offices. (Fox News)

TRUMP REAFFIRMS ICE ARREST POLICY AFTER CONFUSING GUIDANCE SPARKS ALARM AMONG AGENTS

"There’s no place for this in Maine. Vandalism and intimidation are wrong, full stop. Senator Collins and her staff should be able to do their jobs without anyone defacing their office, and I condemn whoever did this," Jackson said.
Jackson had also condemned the September incident in another statement to Fox News Digital.
COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME'
"Senator Collins and her staff should be able to do their jobs without anyone defacing their office, and I condemn whoever did this," Jackson said.
Sen. Susan Collins directs a question to Troy Jackson during a debate at Husson University in Bangor on Thursday. (Gregory Rec/Portland Press Herald)
Biddeford police are investigating the incident, according to Collins' campaign.

title: Paper ballots in NY county unable to be accepted by voting machines, will still be counted
summary: Westchester County Board of Elections confirms voting machines are rejecting paper ballots countywide as officials scramble to resolve the issue.
story: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., pushes back on Fox News Power Rankings favoring his Democratic opponent, defending his record on taxes and immigration.

Voting machines in Westchester County, New York, the state's seventh most populous county, are not accepting paper ballots at polling locations throughout the county, the Westchester County Board of Elections said in a statement Tuesday morning.

"The Westchester County Board of Elections (BOE) is aware of an issue involving the paper ballots that is preventing some voting machines from accepting ballots at polling locations throughout the County," the statement read.
The board, in a separate statement issued later in the day, said the issue stemmed from an update to the county's election programming that occurred after initial testing of equipment.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES

"A change affecting a contest in one municipality required updated election programming, which was subsequently tested and deployed for early voting and for Election Day machines in that municipality," the statement read.

"However, Election Day machines elsewhere in the county continued to use the original programming and therefore could not recognize and accept the ballots being used for Election Day," the statement continued.
WATCHDOG, GOP LAWMAKER WARN NY VOTER REGISTRATION SYSTEMS LACKS KEY SAFEGUARDS
A voter casts their ballots at a polling location inside the Lincoln Depot Museum, in Peekskill, New York, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Rep. Mike Lawler, R,-N.Y., whose district contains a large swath of Westchester County, said the specific issue was that the paper ballots are too thick for the machines to read.
"There was an issue with the thickness of the ballot and the formatting of the machines. And so none of the machines were accepting the ballot across the entire county," Lawler told CNN.
Lawler first alerted voters to the apparent ballot scanner problem in the county in a Tuesday morning post on X.
OUTGOING HOUSE DEMOCRAT BACKS INCUMBENT REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER FOR RE-ELECTION

"There is a problem with every ballot scanner in Westchester County. We do not yet know the exact cause of the issue, whether it is the ballot or the machine. The Board of Elections is working with their vendors to resolve it," Lawler wrote.
"However, every ballot will be counted. Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting," Lawler's post concluded.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last vote of the week on January 9, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Multiple voters in Westchester County told Fox News Digital that their paper ballots were taken and placed into red or orange bags. Lawler confirmed the procedure of using the bags to store ballots.

"As is often the case, when there's an emergency, they take the ballot, and they put it in an emergency voting bag. Every ballot will be counted. And everybody should be rest assured that their vote will count. They should wait on line. I know the lines may be impacted a little bit. With some delays, but do not leave the line. Make sure you vote. Your vote will be counted. The machines are being fixed," he said.
The county's board of elections reiterated Lawler's insistence that all ballots will be counted.

"Voters should continue to complete their paper ballots as instructed by poll workers. Ballots that cannot be processed by voting machines will be placed in designated orange emergency ballot bags, which will remain secure and monitored. These ballots will subsequently be counted," the BOE said.

In a statement, Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins said, "My office is fully aware of the ongoing problems with ballots and voting scanners across Westchester County, and I want to be absolutely clear: this situation is unacceptable.

"Voters should remain in line and exercise their right to vote. Every eligible voter will have the opportunity to cast their ballot, and every vote must be counted. I have directed County officials, including representatives from our Law Department, to monitor the voting process and ensure that voters can cast their ballots without interference and that every vote is properly and accurately counted.

"Once these issues are resolved, I will convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again.

"Westchester County voters deserve a fair, secure and seamless election process. Today, we have fallen short of that standard. The voters deserve better, and I intend to make sure they get it," Jenkins said.
The board also apologized to voters and to poll workers for the inconvenience.

"Let us be absolutely clear: Every eligible vote will be counted. No voter should be discouraged from participating in this election because of this issue. Your voice matters. Your vote matters. Please stay in line and vote," the board's statement said.
Voter Patrick Reagan, who has been voting in Westchester County for the last 40 years, spoke to Fox News outside a polling place in Yonkers.

"I hope all the votes are going to be corrected properly and accounted for. And, you know, it's a big year for everybody just voting. You know, we need to keep the country safe and good. And I hope, it's going to turn out the way I wanted to," Reagan said.
Voter Linda Giaimo, a woman who took her friend to vote, said she would be calling the Board of Elections about what was happening on Election Day.

"It's all through Westchester County, that all these machines are down. So now we've got to put our vote in a bag and believe that that bag is going to be delivered. I got a problem with this," Giaimo said.
INSIDE HOUSE GOP'S UNPRECEDENTED PUSH TO MONITOR MIDTERM ELECTIONS AND PREPARE FOR LEGAL FIGHTS
New York's Democratic Attorney General Letitia James also weighed in.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University in New York City on October 2, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution. Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count," she wrote in a Tuesday morning post on X.
James also reminded state residents that New York has a dedicated Election Protection Hotline — (866) 390-2992 — to assist New Yorkers experiencing issues at the polls.

"Today is your opportunity to make your voice heard, and every eligible New Yorker deserves to cast their ballot without fear or intimidation," James said in a statement. "My office is here to help New Yorkers navigate any problems they encounter at the polls and ensure their voices are heard. If you experience an issue while voting today, call our Election Protection Hotline. We are ready to help," she continued.
New York's polls opened at 6 a.m. and will close at 9 p.m.
Fox News Digital contacted Rep. Mike Lawler for further comment.

title: Michigan voters make surprising cross-party choices as Rogers, El-Sayed race reaches final hours
summary: A former Democrat backs Mike Rogers while a lifelong Republican holds his nose to vote for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan's pivotal Senate race.
story: The afternoon before Election Day, three voters on the streets of Rochester told Fox News Digital why they are backing former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers or his Democratic Senate opponent, Abdul El-Sayed.

Michigan voters showed the swinginess of their state in conversations with Fox News the day before the midterm elections, with one former Democrat firmly backing GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers and a lifelong Republican holding his nose to vote for Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat.
After casting a ballot for Rogers, voter Marjorie Mehney said she was a Democrat "years ago" and would be "embarrassed to be one today" with candidates like El-Sayed representing the party.
However, she pointed out that El-Sayed has won over many voters in her hometown of Petoskey, located in Emmet County, where President Donald Trump took more than 55% of the vote in 2024.

"The majority are Republican. However, there's a great deal of signage for Abdul. So it's very mixed. We've never seen anything like the support that's going on with signs in front yards," Mehney told Fox News in downtown Rochester.
Signs supporting Abdul El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates are seen in a resident's front yard in Petoskey, Michigan, on Sept. 9, 2026. (cbarnesphotography)
ROGERS WARNS MICHIGAN VOTERS AGAINST EL-SAYED’S ‘EXTREME’ AGENDA AHEAD OF ELECTION
When asked if she knew why there had been a shift toward El-Sayed, she said she had "no idea" and called the momentum he is experiencing in her community "a bit shocking."
"They are people I've known and never knew that they felt this way that Abdul does," she said. "It's a little concerning."
Mehney predicted that El-Sayed will prevail over Rogers on Tuesday, but warned that Michigan voters will come to regret sending him to the Senate.

Marjorie Mehney, a Michigan voter, said she voted for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. She described herself as a former Democrat and predicted that Rogers' Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, will win the race. (Fox News)
I'M DR ABDUL EL-SAYED. THIS IS WHY I WANT MICHIGAN'S VOTE FOR SENATE
Another voter, Tom Wright, told Fox News that he voted for El-Sayed despite disagreeing with him on "60% to 70% of his policy positions."
"I cannot bring myself to vote for a Trump minion under any circumstances," Wright said, referring to Rogers.

Rogers left Congress before Trump launched his first presidential campaign, representing Michigan's 8th District from 2001 to 2015, meaning he has no congressional voting record on Trump's legislative agenda across either of his two terms.

Rogers has made his position clear on a series of Trump policies. For instance, he backed the Iran war in its early stages and has supported giving presidents broad authority to impose reciprocal tariffs, as Trump did.
Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed speaks to his supporters at his last rally at The Majestic Theater on Nov. 2, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Salwan Georges/Getty Images)
TRUMP DOMINATES EL-SAYED'S ATTACKS AGAINST ROGERS, BUT GOP RIVAL OFFERS UNEXPECTED POLICY SPLIT

However, as the Senate campaign entered its final stretch, Rogers has distanced himself with Trump on both issues. In late September, he released an ad calling for a quick end to the Iran war, and in early October, another ad of his demanded an end to the "tariff war" with Canada.
Wright, who described himself as "a lifelong Republican," said Rogers' shifts on those issues were not enough to win his support.
Wright argued that the GOP is "too far toward Trump" and that "Mike Rogers won't stop it."
"The litmus test is, are people willing to hold their nose and vote for Abdul because they are so appalled by Trump? Not that they like Abdul or are a progressive," Wright said.
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers greets people at an election eve event on Nov. 2, 2026, in Rochester Hills, Michigan. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya)
EL-SAYED, ROGERS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD, TRUMP AND GUNS: 5 FIERY DEBATE MOMENTS
When asked about his reservations about El-Sayed, Wright said he doesn't like his stance on Israel and Palestinians.

"I don't think he has sufficiently disavowed elements that I consider divisive. A man is judged by the company he keeps and he keeps some pretty bad company," Wright said. "Nonetheless, he is one senator out of 100. I don't care what he says he's going to do. He can't do a damn thing. And if some sanity returns to the Republican Party in six years, I can vote for the opposition."

Tom Wright, a Michigan voter, described himself as a "lifelong Republican" but snubbed Mike Rogers and cast a ballot for Abdul-El Sayed. He told Fox News he views Rogers as a "Trump minion." (Fox News)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A third Michigan voter, Gerald, said he was planning to split his ticket, telling Fox News he would vote for Rogers for Senate and Democrat Jocelyn Benson for governor.
Gerald wasn't comfortable voting for El-Sayed because he heard he is a "communist."

As in past midterm elections, Michigan could play a pivotal role in determining control of Congress. Polls are open across the state Tuesday from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., with voters still able to cast a ballot as long as they are in line by the time polls close.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: FBI nabs suspect accused of sending hundreds of white powder letters to public officials: source
summary: Federal investigators linked more than 700 suspicious mailings to the same sender, with fingerprints and surveillance footage allegedly tying the Oklahoma City suspect to the letters.
story: The FBI arrested an Oklahoma City man suspected of sending hundreds of suspicious white powder letters to election offices and public officials nationwide.

FIRST ON FOX: The FBI arrested an Oklahoma City man early Monday suspected of sending hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder to public officials across the country during the 2024 and 2026 election cycles, a federal law enforcement source told Fox News Digital.

Robin Patrick Martin, 67, is charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications, according to a federal criminal complaint filed in the Western District of Oklahoma.

Federal investigators linked more than 700 suspicious mailings sent in 2026 to the same sender, according to the complaint. The letters were addressed to state election boards, Republican, Democratic and independent members of Congress, pollsters, media organizations and the FBI.
Postal inspectors and their law enforcement partners recovered the majority of the mailings before they reached their intended recipients, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ).
FBI PROBES SUSPICIOUS WHITE POWDER LETTERS SENT TO SCHUMER, DEM SENATORS AS THREAT SPREADS NATIONWIDE

The FBI arrested an Oklahoma City man early Monday suspected of sending hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder to public officials across the country during the 2024 and 2026 election cycles. (REUTERS/Joshua Roberts)

"The alleged subject had avoided authorities until now — as the Biden administration failed to catch him — but this FBI got it done," FBI Director Kash Patel in a statement. "Every American citizen deserves a free and fair election — and anyone who attempts to undermine that process by breaking our laws and threatening public officials will be brought to justice."

The FBI's Oklahoma City field office, FBI Criminal Division, U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), U.S. Capitol Police and Oklahoma City Police Department participated in the investigation, the federal law enforcement source said.
The complaint alleges the mailings date back to September 2024, when state election officials began reporting letters containing a white powdery substance.
Investigators identified similar mailings addressed to election officials in all 50 states, 49 of which were either recovered from recipients or intercepted in the mail stream.

The initial 2024 mailings contained white powder and a three-page letter titled "DECLARATION OF WAR." The writer threatened that if certain demands were not met, another mailing would be sent to "1000's of destinations" and "it won't be flour next time," according to the complaint.

"The writer of the letter described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election," the complaint states.
Testing found the powders examined so far were nonhazardous substances, including yeast or flour, though not every letter has been fully tested, according to the FBI.
Investigators said some letters contained hidden messages visible under ultraviolet light. One warned recipients to remain on the "right side of history" and suggested their lives could depend on it.
Some mailings listed "U.S.T.E.A.," described as the "United States Traitor Elimination Army," as the sender and gave a return address in Takoma Park, Maryland, according to the complaint.
The FBI said surveillance footage showed a vehicle associated with Martin stopping at Postal Service mailboxes in Oklahoma City, Dallas and San Antonio in October.
Investigators also said Martin's fingerprints were found on a letter sent to FBI Director Kash Patel.
Authorities further linked Martin to Walmart purchases of turmeric and vinegar, items investigators said could be used to create writing visible under ultraviolet light.
The arrest follows a nationwide investigation into suspicious mail sent to congressional and election offices ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
JUDGE TOSSES CASE AGAINST EX-FBI OFFICIALS ACCUSED OF LYING TO CONGRESS ABOUT HUNTER BIDEN INVESTIGATION

The FBI said last month it was working with USPIS to investigate "a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices." (Brendan Smialowski/AFP, File )

The FBI said last month it was working with USPIS to investigate "a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices," The Associated Press reported last month.
Authorities warned recipients to treat the mailings as "potentially hazardous" while investigators worked to intercept additional letters before they reached their destinations.
The FBI said in an Oct. 23 advisory that no hazardous material had been identified in the suspicious substances tested at that point, though laboratory testing remained ongoing.
Several Senate offices reported receiving or being sent suspicious mail.
Martin on Tuesday appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin for his initial appearance in Oklahoma City.

title: Talarico warms to Trump, says he wants to help fulfill some MAGA promises
summary: James Talarico told the "Diary of a CEO" podcast he'd work with Trump on healthcare, housing and childcare despite months of attacks from the president.
story: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, said he would work with President Donald Trump on a number of MAGA priorities if he is elected to the Senate. (Credit: The Diary Of A CEO Nov 2, 2026)

James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, appeared to extend an olive branch to President Donald Trump in a podcast released Monday, expressing a willingness to work with Trump on a wide range of issues.

"I would love, as the next U.S. senator from Texas, to work with Donald Trump to actually fulfill some of the promise of his political project," Talarico told Steve Bartlett, the host of "The Diary of a CEO" podcast.

"The promise of MAGA was that we were going to transform this government so that it delivered for the people who have been left behind, the people who have been forgotten in this country. And there's still time to do that," Talarico continued.

Talarico, who Trump has frequently mocked and criticized in the months leading up to the Texas state representative's crucial midterm contest against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, explained that he'd love to work with Trump on issues like healthcare and housing.
Texas state Rep. James Talarico, who is running for U.S. Senate, speaks during a town hall on Saturday, July 11, 2026, at the Plaza Theatre in El Paso, Texas. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"If the president wants to work with me or with any Democrat to expand healthcare access, I'm there. If he wants to make sure that every single kid in this country gets high-quality, accessible childcare, I'm there. If he wants to tackle the housing problem — Donald Trump is a builder — if he wants us to slash the red tape in this country so we could build millions of new homes and ensure everyone in this country has a place to call home, that I'm there. I'll work with him to do it. I would love to do that," Talarico said.
BATTLEGROUND DEM TOUTS BIPARTISAN RECORD, BUT CAN’T NAME SINGLE ISSUE SHE’D WORK WITH TRUMP ON
Talarico also indicated that a successful midterm election for Democrats could be a "rebirth" for Trump's presidency.
"If the people of Texas, if the people of this country elect leaders who are going to check the president, I think it could be a rebirth for his presidency," Talarico said.

State Representative James Talarico, a Democrat from Texas and U.S. Senate candidate, speaks during a campaign event at the University Of North Texas in Denton, Texas, on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Talarico added that he hoped a Democratic victory Tuesday could be a "wake-up call" for Trump and his administration, claiming that he felt the administration should "reverse course" if faced with a Democratic supermajority in Congress.
Talarico's willingness to reach across the aisle comes despite months of Trump badmouthing him on social media and the president campaigning in person for Paxton.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump has taken to frequently referring to Talarico as "TalaFREAKo" in posts on Truth Social, calling him "unelectable" in Texas and disparagingly referring to him as a vegan, a charge which Talarico denies.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, left, was mocked by President Donald Trump during his remarks at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt cast doubt on the authenticity of Talarico's intentions during a Tuesday morning appearance on "FOX & Friends."
"I don't buy it for one second," Leavitt said.

"This is exactly what the Democrats do in every election cycle. They are incredibly disingenuous. In fact, it's the one thing they are good at. They talk like the radical leftist that they are until they win their Democrat nomination. And then they try to fool voters by appearing moderate so that they can win their votes. But when they are elected, God forbid, if Talarico is elected, and we pray that he isn't after polls closed tonight, he will govern as a far left extreme liberal that he truly is," she continued.

"Just listen to his own words. Some of the things he said in the past, he said he's a Christian who hates Christianity. He said God is non-binary. He said he believes there are six genders. He said that the United States southern border in the great state of Texas should be like a front porch where everybody is welcomed, while James Talarico, we have that for four years under the Biden administration, and it resulted in the worst border crisis in American history. He wants to abolish ICE. He wants to open our prisons. This is not somebody who is going to work with President Trump to secure our border and continue deporting illegal aliens," Leavitt added.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt speaks onstage during the second day of the 2026 Republican National Convention at American Airlines Center on Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas, Texas. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"This is somebody who would join the ranks of the extremely liberal Democrat Party to engage in lawfare and obstructionism of all of the common sense policies that the Trump administration is continuing to pursue. And that's exactly why the great people of Texas need to get out and vote," Leavitt concluded.
The Talarico campaign and the White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment.

title: Alaska voter 'disgusted' by reported 'decoy Dan' plot switches from Peltola to Sullivan
summary: An Alaska voter who considered voting for former Rep. Mary Peltola, said he "switched" and would vote for incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
story: A woman in Alaska noted that a man she was with had thought about voting for Mary Peltola, but the man explained that he had "switched." Both individuals said they would vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

As the Senate race in Alaska makes headlines over an alleged Democrat-linked election scheme, Fox News spoke with voters heading to the polls on Monday, including one man who said he is voting for incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, despite having previously considered voting for the Democratic Senate candidate, former Rep. Mary Peltola.

The Senate race, which is a ranked-choice voting contest, has been the subject of significant national attention due to the inclusion of a candidate with nearly the same name as the incumbent GOP lawmaker.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES
The male voter, who did not provide his name, explained that he "thought it was sketchy from the get-go."

A New York Times report published last week detailed the alleged scam that involved Democrats seeking to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to run in the race against the incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan.
"When The New York Times article came out, and I found out how that transpired, I was disgusted by the whole thing, so sleazy," the voter noted.
ELECTION DAY 2026: VOTERS CAST BALLOTS WITH CONTROL OF CONGRESS ON THE LINE

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, a Democrat from Alaska and U.S. Senate candidate, right, raise paddles during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate in Kodiak, Alaska, on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
A woman who was with the man in Alaska noted that he had "thought about voting for Mary Peltola."
"I switched," he said.
The woman said she believes it is "unethical, and I don't think [Peltola] should be elected."
The man agreed.
They both confirmed they would be voting for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.
DOJ FACES 'HEAVY LIFT' IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES

President Donald Trump shakes hands with U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, during a campaign rally at Curtis D. Menard Memorial Sports Center in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)
The Peltola campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday.
In a rally speech last week, Peltola denied being involved in the alleged scheme.

"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said. "I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan."
Sen. Sullivan said during a speech on Monday, "We all knew that the decoy Dan guy was fake, but the extent of the corruption, the extent of the cheating."
DEMS' DIRE WARNINGS ABOUT THREATS TO DEMOCRACY FACE AN UNCOMFORTABLE RECKONING AFTER ALASKA ELECTION REPORT
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump is backing the senator in the race.

"Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Best Senator in the History of Alaska, and one of the Best in the Country, should be running his Senatorial Race in Alaska, 'UNDER PROTEST,' for the FRAUD that has been committed against him in putting another Dan Sullivan on the Ballot. Dan Sullivan against Dan Sullivan — How ridiculous is that? Thank you for your attention to this matter!" Trump posted to Truth Social on Monday night.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: The economy is on the ballot. 3 charts reveal the reality voters face as they head to the polls
summary: Inflation outpacing wages, gas prices above $4, and mortgage rates past 7% are squeezing voters even as the S&P 500 surges over 26% under Trump.
story: Trump’s escalating trade war with Canada could raise costs for businesses and consumers in key battleground states before voters head to the polls.
Voters who have already cast ballots and those heading to the polls on Tuesday are weighing an economy shaped by rising everyday costs, surging home prices and strong gains in the stock market.

President Donald Trump vowed a better economy and a brighter financial future in his 2024 bid for office. But nearly two years into his second term, fuel prices have surged, inflation has accelerated and buying a home remains expensive — all pressures that put Republicans' affordability promises to the test in this midterm election cycle.
Three charts help exhibit the economic forces shaping voters’ choices as control of Congress hangs in the balance and the future of Trump's agenda is put on the line.
HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS

Customers shop for groceries at a Target store in Salt Lake City, Utah, on Friday, July 31, 2026. Target has been overhauling its grocery aisles since the spring, hoping the upscale Tarzhay success it once had with stylish apparel and home goods in the early 2000s can be revived in food. (Kim Raff/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Everyday costs keep climbing

The latest inflation report showed consumer prices rose 3.7% over the year through September and 0.6% from August. The Consumer Price Index tracks prices across a broad range of household expenses, including food, housing, medical care and transportation.
Trade policy has added to some of those costs.
A New York Federal Reserve study found that Trump's tariffs added about 2.9 percentage points to prices across the consumer goods researchers examined.
Roughly one-third of the increase came from U.S.-made products, as domestic manufacturers faced higher costs for imported materials and components under Trump's agenda.

The impact varies by household, but these figures offer a snapshot of the price pressures voters may weigh ahead of the midterms. They show how costs have changed, though not how voters will assign responsibility.
Diesel costs ripple through the economy

A semi-truck driver replaces a diesel fuel pump at a Love's gas station in Eloy, Arizona, on Wednesday, March 18, 2026. U.S. diesel rose above $5 a gallon for the first time since December 2022, the latest sign of surging fuel price pressures menacing the global economy as the war in Iran continues to disrupt energy supplies. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Higher energy costs are putting pressure on households and businesses, as the wars in Iran and Ukraine disrupt global fuel supplies.
Diesel prices have climbed sharply, rising from about $3.45 per gallon in early 2025 to a peak of $6.53 in October 2026, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
The increase matters beyond the pump because trucks, freight trains and farm equipment rely on diesel.
AMERICAN-MADE GOODS ALSO GOT MORE EXPENSIVE UNDER TRUMP TARIFFS, NEW RESEARCH FINDS
Higher fuel costs can raise expenses for businesses moving groceries, packages and building materials, which may absorb some of the increase or pass it along to customers.
Gasoline prices are also adding to household costs. They jumped 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of that month’s overall increase in the Consumer Price Index.
A tougher path to homeownership
Housing remains a major affordability challenge, particularly for prospective buyers.
Housing industry leaders say states that have prioritized homebuilding have been better positioned to accommodate population growth and economic expansion. (Joshua Lott/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
Freddie Mac’s 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.24% as of Oct. 29, while the latest median price for an existing home was $417,500 in September, according to the National Association of Realtors.
Mortgage rates shape buyers’ monthly payments, and home prices determine how much they need to borrow, making it harder for many households to enter the market.
TRUMP’S HOUSING CHIEF PAINTS A GRIM PICTURE FOR HOMEOWNERSHIP IN ONE MAJOR AMERICAN CITY

Rising home values can benefit people who already own property, but that wealth is difficult to access without selling or borrowing against a home. For renters and first-time buyers, the costs are more immediate.
The data offer a snapshot of the costs voters have faced, but the charts alone cannot show how they will weigh the economy — or which party they will hold responsible — as results come in.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Michigan voters weigh in after Dem Rep Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate
summary: Michigan Republican Mike Rogers' campaign touted Haley Stevens' endorsement as a breakthrough with Black and Jewish voters before Election Day.
story: Will Republicans' Haley Stevens gambit pay off?

OAKLAND COUNTY, MICHIGAN — Michigan’s Republican ticket had a clear message for voters preparing to vote in the midterm elections: Their path to victory relies on winning over voters who typically don’t align themselves with the GOP.

That prospect appeared to be buoyed by Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th-hour endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her primary rival, Abdul El-Sayed. Early Monday afternoon, Republican operatives in Michigan blasted out a press release advertising an event just hours later intended to tout Stevens’ endorsement and its purported impact on Black and Jewish voters.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES

In front of a throng of press at the Michigan GOP’s headquarters, six community leaders representing African Americans and Jews criticized what they saw as El-Sayed’s excesses and lauded Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers. Broadly, they argued that El-Sayed had insufficiently distanced himself from some of his radical associations, that Stevens' endorsement had real significance for the race and that they were seeing an unprecedented groundswell of support for Republicans among their peers.
MIKE ROGERS DISHES ON HOW SHOCK HALEY STEVENS ENDORSEMENT UNFOLDED HOURS BEFORE ELECTION DAY

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and U.S. Senate candidate, and Rep. Haley Stevens, a Democrat from Michigan, speak to members of the media following a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit, Mich., on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, formally backed Rogers, sealing her rupture with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In addition to the community leaders, close to two dozen others — many of whom were Black or Jewish — attended the event as well. While some political observers have cast doubt on the impact of Stevens' endorsement and the degree to which African Americans and Jews are defecting from the Democratic Party, members of those communities told Fox News Digital the shift is happening.

"I believe it's going to make a big difference that she came out," Michelle Nard, an African American former Democrat running for state Senate, told Fox News Digital. "She had a big following. She's a great congresswoman, a great state representative for the United States."
BLACK VOTERS RIP DEMS OVER TAKING THEM FOR GRANTED IN EL-SAYED'S BACKYARD: ‘HUSH US UP’
Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens appears alongside GOP rival Mike Rogers at a Detroit church on Nov. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Rogers for Senate)

Nard recounted how she had recently spoken to a Black woman who highlighted that her community makes a big deal of going to the polls on Election Day, a point she used to stress that Haley’s endorsement, though late in the cycle, could still influence last-second voters.

"You have strong Haley Stevens supporters in our community that will support her to the end, and then you have some that feel betrayed," Marcus Bowman, a metro Detroit school board trustee, told Fox News Digital.

Bowman, who says he knows Stevens personally, said: "True supporters of Haley Stevens, they know her as a person and they know what she represents. I think they will follow her and respect her for her decision based off some of the radical things we've heard about Abdul El-Sayed."

While those who spoke were handpicked for a Republican news conference, there is some data to back up Black voter defection. Between August and September, El-Sayed’s support among African Americans held steady at around 75%, well below the party's typical benchmark.
FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS

Rep. Haley Stevens of Michigan, right, and former Wayne County Health Department Director Abdul El-Sayed are facing off in the August 4, 2026, Democratic Senate primary in the Great Lakes battleground state. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The Arab American community in the Detroit metropolitan area has historically been at odds with African Americans in the areas across a number of issues, a theme that has come up occasionally during El-Sayed’s campaign.

While comparable polls have not found similar trends among Jewish voters, who are a much smaller part of Michigan’s electorate, a number of high-profile members of the communities, including top donors, have flocked to the Rogers camp.

"Haley, what she did was give a lot of Jews permission, hardcore left-wing Democrats, permission to now say, you know what, if Haley can endorse him, I can vote for him," Aaron Tobin, a conservative Jewish community leader, told Fox News Digital in reference to Mike Rogers. "Now I think she's broken that wall down, and now they can see that a hardcore Democrat — and she was very successful and very popular in Michigan — if she said Mike Rogers is good enough for her, I think a lot of Jews are going to say, 'I'm going to vote for him because Abdul just says the worst things.'"

Ezra, another Jewish voter, told Fox News Digital that he believes Jews have increasingly been abandoned by the Democratic Party and, even if Stevens’ endorsement doesn’t move the needle, he’s grateful that she took a stand.

"The [March 12] terrorist attack in [a] West Bloomfield [synagogue], I believe was the starting point of the Detroit Jewish community being afraid and that fear was not alleviated over the next [six months]. That fear has not been alleviated by Abdul El-Sayed in any sort of way, which is why I think you're seeing this," he said. "We're waiting for something and it's not coming. And so that's why I think you're seeing so many in the Jewish community moving for Mike Rogers because they're like, you know what, that guy's going to keep my family safe. The other guy's not."
MAMDANI, HASAN PIKER AMONG RADICAL LEFT-WING VOICES ERUPTING OVER HALEY STEVENS' ENDORSEMENT SWITCH

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, announces support from Democrats as he launches a 'Dems for Mike' coalition, on August 20, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

"I think in some ways, it's, it's more brave because it's at the last minute. In some ways, you know what, who knows, even if it, if it's 100 votes or 1000 votes, then it makes a difference," he added.

These alleged breakthroughs with traditionally Democratic constituencies took center stage at Rogers’ closing rally on Monday night. At one point, the campaign invited six Black and Jewish voters, most of them former Democrats, to take the stage where they explained why they believed El-Sayed to be too extreme for their support. Rogers himself praised the group during his final campaign speech, invoked the need for unity and thanked Stevens at length for her endorsement.

Conservatives at the rally were clearly grateful to Stevens for her endorsement, with nearly every mention of her name being met with cheers or chants of her name. Republicans are even optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement could trickle down to their down-ballot races.
MICHIGAN DEM CLAIMS STEVENS SHOT DOWN ROGERS ENDORSEMENT RUMOR HOURS BEFORE TURNING ON EL-SAYED
Detroit voters at the polls inside Central United Methodist Church on Nov. 5, 2024 in downtown Detroit, Mich. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

"I was on the ground last week in Michigan and Ohio, and the momentum in Michigan is real. It was real before Haley Stevens endorsed Mike Rogers, even more real now," Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association, told Fox News Digital.
Piper said he "absolutely" believes Stevens’ endorsement will move the needle for Michigan Republican attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd.

"You know, around the Detroit area, Grosse Pointe, Detroit, elsewhere, I saw homemade yard signs in the yards of Black churches that said African Americans and Jews stand together. And that was powerful."
Lloyd said he is optimistic that Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers could give him a boost.

"Well, I saw something today in the news that basically said 50% of the available voters have voted through absentee and early voting. We still have one day left. And as we've said, you know, the race isn't done until 8 o'clock tomorrow night when the polls close," he said. "So, if this made a difference for someone who had been sitting on the sideline and they decided they were going to get out and vote because of it, I'm excited for that."

Democrats have argued Stevens’ endorsement could strengthen, rather than weaken, El-Sayed’s support. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said he expected the episode to galvanize Democrats, while El-Sayed’s campaign reported raising $2.4 million Sunday, its largest fundraising day of the campaign.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While cutting into the Democratic Party’s margins by successfully pulling away Black and Jewish voters could prove valuable to the GOP, a reversion among Arab voters — who swung toward Republicans in 2024 but strongly favor El-Sayed — could erase such gains. Fox News’ final power ranking rated Michigan’s Senate race as a toss-up, meaning that, as voters head to the polls, neither party holds a clear edge.

title: 9th Circuit block on California noncitizen voter probe lifted, then restored in legal boomerang
summary: A 9th Circuit panel briefly lifted a block on DOJ noncitizen voting investigations in California, but the full 11-judge court reversed course overnight.
story: Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter discusses federal subpoenas issued to California election workers, a dispute over more than 20,000 flagged mail-in ballots and the Justice Department's possible Supreme Court appeal ahead of the midterms.

A federal appeals court briefly lifted a block on the Trump administration’s efforts to investigate alleged voting by noncitizens in California, then reversed course hours later, sending the dispute to the full 11-judge 9th Circuit for rehearing.

Earlier Monday night, a three-judge panel granted the Justice Department’s request to pause a temporary restraining order issued by a San Francisco federal judge. That order had barred the administration from making further requests to set aside ballots under the warning of prosecution of state and local election officials who declined.
The panel said the government was likely to prevail in arguing that its requests and criminal investigations were core executive functions.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS

Hours later, the full 9th Circuit vacated the ruling and ordered the case reheard by all 11 active judges, according to the court’s order. The move restored the district court’s restrictions while the full court considers the dispute.

"The TRO issued by a San Francisco judge purporting to restrict DOJ investigations into election officials has been appropriately lifted," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on X before the temporary restraining order was restored. "Conducting criminal investigations is a core function of the executive branch, not the judiciary."

The case against the investigation of alleged noncitizen voting was brought by labor unions and civil rights groups, including the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens. They argued that DOJ and Homeland Security letters to election officials, which warned of potential criminal liability over ballots linked to suspected noncitizens, amounted to intimidation.
CALIFORNIA ELECTION WORKERS HIT WITH CRIMINAL SUBPOENAS AS TRUMP DOJ TURNS UP HEAT IN VOTING SHOWDOWN

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli (right) is warning the state of California's election officials that refusing to obey federal law about not allowing the counting of legal votes could bring potential prosecution against them. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg; Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times)
The Trump administration argues that allowing illegal voting and halting investigative work could lead to prosecution for those involved.

"Americans deserve to have confidence in their elections," Essayli wrote late Monday night. "The courts have made it clear that the preferred remedy for election law violations is criminal prosecution. Building on Operation Protect the Vote, we will continue investigating and charging those who violate election laws or assist in their violation."

The appeals court whiplash followed a separate Supreme Court rejection of the Trump administration's effort to protect the vote Monday. The justices denied an emergency request to require California to set aside mail ballots from roughly 20,000 registered voters federal officials flagged as likely noncitizens.
BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD
"We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent ​McCotter wrote on X.

The administration had demanded that California separate any alleged unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be U.S. citizens through investigations that the state has rejected without review.
"Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the Justice Department wrote in its request to the Supreme Court.
DHS OFFICIAL VOWS TO PROSECUTE AND DEPORT NONCITIZENS CAUGHT ILLEGALLY VOTING AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The DOJ has been forced into a legal Catch-22 where it has to watch votes be cast in California, even if they have alleged evidence of them being noncitizen voters, and then pursue legal action afterward.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that 63 people were charged with election crimes Monday.

"Today's announcement marks the largest surge of voter-fraud arrests since President [Donald] Trump returned to office," Blanche wrote in a statement. "These foreign nationals allegedly took advantage of the trust of the American people and flouted the laws that govern our nation’s elections. This Department of Justice will continue investigating and prosecuting voter fraud to restore confidence in our electoral system."

The DOJ has charged 195 illegal immigrants across 25 states with illegal voting and voter registration offenses in the past nine weeks. There have been charges against 239 people with voting fraud offenses since Trump returned to the White House, according to the DOJ.

title: Trump says Israel will stop receiving $4B in US aid by year's end, can still buy weapons
summary: President Donald Trump says Benjamin Netanyahu raised the idea of ending $4 billion in U.S. military aid to Israel by the end of the year.
story: President Donald Trump joins 'Fox & Friends' to deliver a final Election Day message as voters cast their ballots in the high-stakes midterms. Trump discusses his record, the state of the Middle East and other top issues.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that U.S. aid to Israel would end at the close of the year, arguing that the country no longer needs the assistance and can purchase its own weapons.
"We were giving them $4 billion – we are – but it gets cut off at the end of the year," Trump told "Fox & Friends" on Tuesday in an Election Day morning announcement.
Trump acknowledged the political nature of the news, pointing to Michigan's battleground Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu brought a zero aid proposal to President Donald Trump, who makes the stunning announcement on midterm Election Day morning on "Fox & Friends." (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it?" Trump said. "It's a bad talking point."

The support included "things and money," according to Trump, calling it military aid, cash or "barter." He said he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had discussed ending the assistance for years, adding that Netanyahu raised the idea.
NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'
"They don’t need it," Trump said. "Israel's our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it."
"Israel is a very thriving country," he added.
NETANYAHU DETAILS 'FINAL' CONVERSATION WITH LINDSEY GRAHAM, SAYS SENATOR CHALLENGED HIS PUSH TO END ISRAEL AID

The current U.S.-Israel security assistance agreement provides about $3.8 billion annually through 2028. Netanyahu has previously said he wants to phase out Israel’s reliance on U.S. military aid, though the timing and terms of any change to the agreement have not been detailed.
Trump said the assistance had become a political target, adding that Netanyahu understood "this is one of their points of contention."

"If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen because America has changed," Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in October.
The $4 billion referred to military hardware or cash, according to Trump.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's aggressive anti-Israel aid stance against Republican Mike Rogers might have been a factor in President Donald Trump's Election Day-timed announcement Tuesday. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images; Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"I’m going to put it in any way you want to define it," Trump said. "You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash. It’s what we give them — $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it."

Trump negotiated the new deal with Netanyahu, who is also facing a difficult election season with his future still up in the air as the balance of power in the Knesset tries to settle on a coalition government amid multifront wars with terrorists and Iran.

"I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money," he said. "He brought it up. He said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.’"
EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY
Congress passed a law in 2020 authorizing the funding for Israel, but the Senate and House must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.
Israel can still buy U.S. weapons, Trump stressed.
"They can buy whatever they want," he said.
SEN RAND PAUL: OUR BUDGET DEFICIT IS OUT OF CONTROL. CONGRESS MUST PASS MY SIX PENNY PLAN

Trump pointed to his administration's 2024 campaign vows to curb free foreign aid and cut government spending, just hours before the balance of congressional power will be determined for his final two years in office.
"We've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money," Trump said. "You know, somebody that wants to have a balanced budget. I'd love to be able to balance our budget."

"If we had a fed that got interest rates down," he added, "we would have a balanced budget quickly. It's a shame, the interest rates. We have a fed that's, you know, populated by Obama and Biden people, and they don't want to do the right thing."
Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Florida polling places in 7 counties are moving locations due to flooding
summary: Midterm election voters in seven Florida counties face temporary polling location changes after heavy rainfall triggered flash flood warnings.
story: Fox News' Griff Jenkins and Charlie Hurt report live from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Election Day to speak directly with local voters at a diner. Voters share their thoughts on the state's gubernatorial race, economic concerns and key midterm issues.

Florida voters in seven counties are being directed to temporary polling locations Tuesday, after widespread flooding prompted Gov. Ron DeSantis to issue an emergency order allowing election officials to relocate voting sites ahead of the midterm elections.

The Florida Department of State confirmed polling-place changes in Brevard, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties, according to its website, which was updated on Election Day.

DeSantis signed Executive Order 26-227 on Monday after a low-pressure system brought heavy rainfall across parts of Florida from Oct. 31 through Nov. 2, triggering flash flood warnings and threatening roads, schools and other critical infrastructure.
ELECTION DAY 2026: JOIN AMERICA'S CONVERSATION HERE!
Residents and vehicles navigate a flooded Pace Dr. in Palm Bay, Florida, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Craig Bailey, FLORIDA TODAY via USA TODAY NETWORK)

The order declared a state of emergency in Brevard, DeSoto, Hardee, Highlands, Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties. It also allows county election supervisors who cannot meet certain polling-place requirements to seek approval from Florida's secretary of state for alternative voting arrangements.
A view of homes during flooding along Pace Dr. in Palm Bay, Florida, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Craig Bailey, FLORIDA TODAY via USA TODAY NETWORK)
The Florida Department of State published a list of temporary polling locations for affected voters.
In Brevard County, several precincts have been reassigned to New Shiloh Christian Center and Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne, as well as Palm Bay City Hall.
In Highlands County, voters assigned to Precinct 20 at Springlake Community Center in Sebring are being redirected to the Penny Ogg Operations Center.
Multiple vehicles are stranded due to flooding along U.S. 192 in West Melbourne, Florida, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Craig Bailey, FLORIDA TODAY via USA TODAY NETWORK)
Indian River County voters assigned to Precinct 7 at Sebastian Church of God are being directed to Sebastian Elks Lodge No. 2714.
In Martin County, voting at Grace Presbyterian Church has been moved to the county supervisor of elections office in Stuart.
ELECTION DAY 2026 LIVE UPDATES
Okeechobee County voters assigned to Precinct 10 at Fort Drum Community Church are being directed to High Point Church.
In Palm Beach County, voters assigned to Casa Rio Clubhouse and Ironhorse Country Club are being directed to RB Preparatory and Achievement Academy and North County Senior Center, respectively.
Parts of Brevard County, also known as the Space Coast, were flooded due to heavy rains on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

St. Lucie County has reported multiple changes, with affected voters being redirected to locations including the Port St. Lucie Community Center, MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, Tradition Town Hall and Havert L. Fenn Center.
The state cautioned that relocations remain subject to change as additional information becomes available.
Voters can check the Florida Department of State's emergency election resources page or contact their county supervisor of elections to confirm their assigned polling place.

Polls in Florida are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time Tuesday. Voters in line when polls close will be permitted to cast their ballots.

title: Federal judge tosses Trump admin Harvard admissions lawsuit, leaves door open to future challenge
summary: A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit against Harvard University over admissions records, citing procedural deficiencies.
story: A federal judge dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking Harvard admissions records, citing procedural deficiencies while leaving open the possibility of another case.

A federal judge on Monday dismissed the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to force Harvard University to turn over admissions records as part of an investigation into whether the Ivy League school continues to consider race in its admissions process.
U.S. District Judge Myong Joun ruled that the Justice Department had not adequately established that it followed required procedures before suing Harvard to obtain applicant-level admissions data.
The dismissal was issued without prejudice, leaving the door open for the administration to file another lawsuit if it addresses the procedural deficiencies identified by the court.

"The Government may be able to identify a qualifying determination or cure the procedural deficiency, but it has not supplied a sufficient basis for the judicial relief currently sought," Joun wrote in his 10-page decision.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACCUSES PRESTIGIOUS LAW SCHOOL OF FAVORING BLACK APPLICANTS OVER WHITE, ASIAN PEERS
Students walk through Harvard Yard on the campus of Harvard University in Cambridge, Mass., on April 27, 2022. (AP Photo/Charles Krupa)

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit in February, alleging that Harvard had failed to cooperate with a federal civil rights review examining whether the university's admissions practices comply with the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling limiting the use of race in college admissions.
The Justice Department alleged that Harvard repeatedly delayed producing requested documents and failed to provide individualized admissions records despite multiple requests and extended deadlines.
JUDGE’S HARVARD ANTISEMITISM RULING SENDS TRUMP JUSTICE DEPARTMENT BACK TO DRAWING BOARD
In announcing the lawsuit in February, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi accused Harvard of withholding information necessary for the government's review.
"Harvard has failed to disclose the data we need to ensure that its admissions are free of discrimination," Bondi said at the time.

Pam Bondi speaks during a news conference at the Department of Justice (DOJ) in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Feb. 12, 2025. Bondi said Wednesday that the Justice Department has sued the state of New York and several officials over its immigration policies. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Joun acknowledged that federal officials had made repeated requests for records and warned Harvard of potential enforcement action. But the judge found that the government's court filings failed to adequately demonstrate that officials had followed the required procedures before seeking judicial intervention.

In particular, Joun noted that the Justice Department's complaint did not allege that officials had notified Harvard of their intent to pursue litigation if the university failed to comply or adequately identified the specific compliance failure at issue.
HARVARD, NYU AMONG 30 UNIVERSITIES HIT WITH PENTAGON FOREIGN-TIE AUDIT DEADLINE

Joun also found that the Department of Education had not sufficiently demonstrated that it followed its own required procedures before referring its separate admissions investigation for judicial enforcement.

Harvard's attorneys argued that the lawsuit was part of a broader retaliatory campaign by the Trump administration after the university resisted demands for changes to its governance and academic policies, according to Reuters.

The Trump administration announced it was freezing over $2 billion in grants and contracts after Harvard University said it would not comply with federal demands regarding antisemitism. (Reuters/Nicholas Pfosi)
The judge did not rule on Harvard's retaliation claims, stressing that his decision addressed procedural deficiencies rather than whether the university had violated federal civil rights law.
"Nothing in this decision converts the Government's request for information into an accusation of present discrimination or resolves Harvard's underlying Title VI compliance," the judge wrote.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Justice Department, Department of Education and Harvard University for comment.

title: Federal judge orders DOJ to ensure poll monitors are not law enforcement officials
summary: The NAACP failed to block Justice Department poll monitors, but a federal judge barred armed officers and anyone with arrest power on Election Day.
story: During an appearance on FOX Across America, co-anchor of "America's Newsroom" Bill Hemmer assesses a few of the key Senate races that will determine which party will control the upper chamber of Congress after Tuesday's midterm elections.

A federal judge denied the NAACP’s request to block the Justice Department from sending election monitors to polling places, but ordered the department to ensure they are not sworn law enforcement officers and cannot make arrests.

U.S. District Judge Reggie Walton, in an order Monday night, said the DOJ must also ensure its monitors are unarmed, out of uniform and do not display insignia identifying them as federal employees. The order applies to the department’s poll monitoring program for Election Day, Nov. 3.
ELECTION DAY 2026 LIVE UPDATES
A Washington, D.C., judge ruled the Justice Department's 1,000 poll monitors can move forward, but they cannot be armed or able to make arrests. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

"The Court is therefore unpersuaded by the plaintiffs' assertion that a person who is simply ‘project[ing a] command[ing] presence, scan[ning] crowds, and more’ – without any outward indications of law enforcement authority – would generate objectively reasonable fear in a voter," according to Walton, who was nominated to the Washington, D.C., court by former President George W. Bush. "Thus, the Court finds that in conjunction with the defendants’ public statements regarding voter fraud and election integrity, the deployment of these individuals as election monitors would not place the average voter 'in reasonable fear of harassment and interference with their right to vote.'"

The NAACP had sought a temporary restraining order barring the DOJ from deploying personnel from agencies including the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Prisons. The group argued their presence could intimidate voters and violate the Voting Rights Act.

Walton denied the motion without prejudice, finding that the current record did not show the NAACP was likely to succeed on its claim. He said the DOJ’s representations at a hearing addressed his concerns: the monitors would be administrative or clerical employees, not sworn officers, and would not carry firearms.
TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE SLAMS DOOR ON DOJ AS COURT LOSSES PILE UP DAYS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

"The Court will order that the defendants comply with their counsel’s concession that they will take action to ensure that the monitors participating in the DOJ’s Poll Monitoring Program are indeed administrative or clerical personnel and not law enforcement officials, will not be in uniform or display any other insignia indicating their affiliation with a federal agency, will not be armed with a firearm, and will not have the power to effectuate arrests," Walton wrote.

Walton also ordered monitors not to interfere with voters or election officials, to follow state and local rules, and to avoid speaking with voters inside polling places. They may speak with voters outside only after they have cast a ballot. Monitors must introduce themselves to election officials and carry federal credentials in case they are asked to verify their employment.
Walton ordered the DOJ to file a status report by 7 a.m. ET on Tuesday explaining how it confirmed that none of the monitors would be law enforcement officials with arrest powers.

"Though there is no prohibition on the use of sworn law enforcement officers as civil rights election monitors, CRT (Civil Rights Division) undertook reasonable efforts to avoid using sworn officers," the DOJ wrote in the Tuesday morning filing."These efforts included excluding the use of Federal Bureau of Investigations personnel, Department of Homeland Security personnel, and consulting the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, the U.S. Marshal Service, and the Drug Enforcement Administration to ensure no sworn agents from those agencies participated in the monitoring program."

The ruling followed allegations that the DOJ planned to send more than 1,000 personnel, including law enforcement agents and investigators, to polling locations. The department’s attorneys told the court that sworn agents and officers would be excluded from the program.
Fox News’ Jake Gibson contributed to this report.
