title: DOJ faces ‘heavy lift’ in Alaska election appeal as separate criminal probe continues
summary: DOJ faces an uphill battle appealing the dismissed Alaska Senate ballot lawsuit over two Dan Sullivan candidates before Election Day polls close.
story: Fox News contributor Josh Ritter joins 'Fox & Friends First' to sound off on the legal implications of the Justice Department's plans to appeal a court ruling dismissing its challenge to Alaska's Senate election certification.

The Justice Department faces an uphill legal battle in its bid to overturn a federal judge's dismissal of its Alaska Senate election lawsuit, according to legal experts who questioned whether the government can secure meaningful relief before voting ends Tuesday — even as a separate criminal investigation continues.

DOJ filed a notice of appeal after Obama-appointed U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed its lawsuit Sunday over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot. The judge ruled that federal officials lacked standing because they had not demonstrated how their proposed remedy could address potential voter confusion without compromising ballot secrecy.

With voting ending Tuesday, attorneys told Fox News Digital that even a successful appeal could leave the government scrambling to obtain an injunction or return to district court, while a defeat would leave the civil case dismissed without necessarily affecting potential criminal charges arising from the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES

"The federal judge dismissed on a procedural issue — standing," election attorney Jason Torchinsky of Virginia-based firm Holtzman Vogel told Fox News Digital. "So if the government were to prevail, it would either have to seek injunctive relief from the appeals court in the first instance, a very high bar, or go back down to the district court to seek relief."
"Given the time available between now and close of polls [Tuesday], this is a heavy lift for the government," Torchinsky added.
A reversal would not automatically change Alaska's election results. DOJ would still need to obtain specific judicial relief, potentially requiring further proceedings in district court.
Former federal prosecutor and ex-Pentagon official Cully Stimson similarly said that DOJ will have difficulty securing any immediate relief in its effort to pause the Sullivan-Peltola contest.
While Gleason was appointed by Obama, Stimson suggested the ruling did not appear partisan and said uncertainty remains because voting had not yet concluded.
"I'm not surprised that the judge did this. I don't think it would matter whether an Obama judge or any other judge appointed by any other president," Stimson told Fox News Digital.
"Asking for injunctive relief way before anything even happens is a reach," he said, adding Alaska falls under the San Francisco-based Ninth Circuit, which will hear any appeal.

But Stimson suggested DOJ may have a longer-term objective beyond winning an immediate injunction: establishing a legal record that could support further proceedings after the election, once the votes are counted.
TRUMP PROSECUTIONS UNDER BIDEN SET PRECEDENT FOR DOJ’S ALASKA ‘DECOY DAN’ PROBE, EX-FEC CHAIR SAYS
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images | Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"They may be filing these suits to establish a record and force Alaska and others supporting the status quo to defend what's happening, knowing that there's some level of confusion, and they have the legal wheels churning," he said. "So after the vote is [over], they've started the legal wheels rolling."
Former Assistant U.S. Attorney for North Florida Zack Smith added that if the Ninth Circuit does not hear the case promptly, DOJ could seek emergency review from the U.S. Supreme Court.
While the Alaska case is considered unprecedented, according to the experts, the idea of a Supreme Court expedition at election time is not.

On Dec. 9, 2000, one day after the Florida Supreme Court ordered a manual recount of disputed ballots in the Bush v. Gore presidential election dispute involving "hanging chads," then-Texas Gov. George W. Bush’s legal team successfully sought emergency intervention.
The court ultimately decided in Bush’s favor within a week.

Since the disputed 2000 election, which featured "hanging chads" on hole-punched paper ballots and the Brooks Brothers Riot at the Miami-Dade elections office, DOJ has become well-accustomed to the expedited-review process, the experts said.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP DOJ'S THREATS AGAINST ELECTION WORKERS AHEAD OF 2026 MIDTERMS
Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)
"DOJ is familiar with kind of working quickly, getting things to the Supreme Court, and so I wouldn't be completely surprised if you were to see something like that," Smith said.
Bush v. Gore offers a procedural parallel because federal courts were asked to intervene in the administration of a state-run election.

"Florida was conducting the election in the manner under Florida law, under this time, place and manners set out by Florida law even though it was a federal election," Stimson said. "They used a particular type of ballot, which had those so-called dangling chads, which were punch-holes that didn't come the whole way off, so the hole was left with a little tag, essentially like a skin tag, and eventually the Supreme Court of Florida ruled."

"But because there were federal violations, eventually the Supreme Court weighed in and stopped it. And at no point in time had the vice president’s (Albert Gore) vote count ever surpassed that of the governor (Bush) and because it was a federal interest, the Supreme Court stepped in and stopped this counting at the state level."
Alex Charns, an attorney who has argued in federal court, told Fox News Digital that the clock has run out and DOJ's goal of segregating ballots based on voter intent is no longer possible.

"I've litigated against the USDOJ for over thirteen years in federal court. I've practiced law in Durham, N.C., for 43 years. The USDOJ filed a case without legal merit and its appeal is likely to fail," he said.

"In addition, voting ends [Tuesday]. The relief they seek isn't possible — ballots already cast can't be segregated. Also, one cannot tell why any voter voted in a particular way. The appeal is unlikely to be successful."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, is seen against the Chugach Range. (Getty Images)

In a statement from the DOJ's "Rapid Response" (DOJ-RR) office, a spokesperson said the court "dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."
"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," DOJ-RR said, announcing their appeal.

Stimson cautioned that the outcome of the civil litigation would have little bearing on the separate criminal investigation, which could uncover evidence supporting additional legal action even if DOJ's appeal fails.

"As long as that criminal investigation is going on, you're not breathing easy," he said, adding that evidence uncovered by federal investigators could potentially provide grounds for a separate civil lawsuit.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: The battle for Congress is just the beginning. Here's what's at stake on Election Day
summary: Election Day 2026 sees Republicans defending slim majorities as early voting shatters records with over 54 million ballots already cast nationwide.
story: 'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host Griff Jenkins breaks down the latest Power Rankings ahead of the midterms, highlighting shifts in Kansas and Nebraska, seven toss-up Senate races and the battle for control of Congress.
It's Election Day in America, with voters heading to the polls to determine control of the U.S. House and Senate for the next two years.
Republicans are defending their slim congressional majorities, but President Donald Trump predicts the GOP will hold the House and Senate for the final two years of his presidency.
"We're going to win and let's make the next two years bigger and better and stronger than ever before," Trump told supporters Sunday night at a rally in Kansas.

But Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.
DEMOCRACY 2026: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally at the Salina Regional Airport, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina, Kansas. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo)
The GOP is also facing a potential turnout deficit, with public opinion polls indicating Democrats are more energized than Republicans to cast ballots in the midterms.

Early voting in the midterms has shattered previous records, with more than 54 million people already casting ballots, according to The Associated Press. That's nearly 9 million more ballots cast in early voting than in 2022, the previous midterm elections.

With early voting traditionally favoring Democrats, Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters, pointing to Election Day turnout, recently told Fox News Digital, "If our voters turn out, we win."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

A voter fills out their ballot at a polling location inside Wayne Community College Eastern Campus on the final day of early voting for the midterm election in Detroit, Michigan, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The political climate has the GOP playing plenty of defense on the campaign trail, as the president tries to energize the GOP base.

Trump's event in red-leaning Kansas, which he touted as his 30th rally over the past month, came hours after the Fox News Power Rankings shifted the state's Senate race from Lean Republican to Toss-up. Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, who is challenging GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, is aiming to become the first Democrat in nearly a century to win a Senate election in Kansas.

The Fox News Power Rankings, as well as many of the leading nonpartisan political handicappers, point to Democrats retaking control of the House, with the majority in the Senate a toss-up heading into Election Day.
ELECTION DAY 2026 LIVE UPDATES

"Think of what is possible tomorrow: Democrats can flip the House, take back the Senate, and stop Trump’s harmful agenda," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin spotlighted in an Election Eve social media post.

Also up for grabs in this year's elections — governorships in 36 of the 50 states. Plus, all but four states are holding legislative elections. And voters will also weigh in on 145 statewide ballot measures in states from coast to coast.
The big question with Election Day upon us — have the public opinion polls that point to a potential blue wave undercounted Republican voters?
LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP DEFYING MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS HE BARNSTORMS COUNTRY
The Election Day sign outside town hall in Newfields, New Hampshire, ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
We'll find out in the coming hours.
Until then, here's a closer look at what's up for grabs on Election Day 2026.
SENATE

Republicans currently control the chamber 53-47, which means Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority. The GOP needs to hold at least 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate.

Besides Kansas, Republicans are also playing defense in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Nebraska, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, which are all rated toss-ups in the Power Rankings. They're also defending seats in competitive races in Kansas, which is rated Lean Republican, and Ohio, which is rated Lean Democrat.
Democrats are on defense in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire.
HOUSE
The GOP is hanging on to a razor-thin majority in the House, with Democrats needing a net gain of just three seats to reach 218, which would hand them the majority.

A good night for the Democrats could see them ending up with as many as 240 seats in the 435-seat chamber, according to the Power Rankings. But if Republicans have a good night, they could end up with 212 seats. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party.
The earliest-closing district polls on election night will give some sense of the House’s future.

"Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th District, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle," Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings, said.
GOVERNORS
There are currently 26 Republican and 24 Democratic governors.

The Power Rankings list three states where the GOP controls the governor's office – Alaska, Nevada and Georgia – as toss-ups. Wisconsin, which has an open Democratic-controlled governor's office, is also rated a toss-up.

The gubernatorial races in red states Florida, Kansas and Texas are rated Lean Republican, according to the Power Rankings. Meanwhile, the showdowns in Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Oregon are rated Lean Democrat.
BALLOT MEASURES

Referendums requiring voters to present identification when they show up at the polls, or bans on noncitizen voting, are on the ballot in 11 states: Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Kansas, Nevada, North Carolina, Ohio, South Dakota and West Virginia.

Voters in Alaska will also decide if they want to repeal the state’s ranked choice voting system, open primaries and a campaign finance disclosure rule. Voters approved the current system in 2020 and narrowly kept it in 2024.
But the voting system has come under fresh scrutiny amid the controversy over a potential spoiler candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race.
Voters in Virginia will decide whether the right to vote should be restored to convicted felons upon their release.
Roughly a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
California's Proposition 40 is making national headlines.
The measure, the first of its kind, would slap a one-time 5% tax on wealth for Californians worth over $1 billion, with the vast majority of the revenue generated going to pay for healthcare.

Also in the spotlight is a millionaires' tax in Washington state. If passed, the referendum would repeal a 9.9% tax on income over $1 million a year, which state lawmakers recently approved. Washington state currently does not have a personal income tax.

Voters in Maryland, Missouri and Colorado weigh in on ballot measures on congressional redistricting, as the mid-decade redistricting fight between Democrats and Republicans will be waged again in 2028.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington state have referendums on transgender students’ participation in sports. Colorado also has a referendum on blocking gender transition surgeries for minors and preventing state or federal funding from being used for those operations.

Voters in Missouri weigh in on repealing a right to abortion and banning gender transition medical care for children. Meanwhile, an Idaho initiative would overturn one of the nation's strictest abortion bans, while Virginia and Nevada voters decide on establishing a right to abortion in their state constitutions.
California, Colorado and Arizona hold ballot measures on policy around energy, transportation and development.
POLL CLOSINGS
The first poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET, with the final poll closings happening at 1 a.m. ET.
6 p.m. ET: Polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.
7 p.m. ET: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia. The final polls in Kentucky and Indiana close. And most polls in Florida and New Hampshire close.
7:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.

8 p.m. ET: Polls close in Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee and Washington, D.C. The remaining polls in Florida and New Hampshire close. Most polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.
8:30 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arkansas.

9 p.m. ET: Polls close in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Louisiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The final polls close in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, North Dakota and South Dakota.
10 p.m. ET: Polls close in Montana and Utah. Most polls also close in Idaho and Oregon.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
11 p.m. ET: Polls close in California and Washington state, with the remaining polls in Idaho and Oregon also closing.
Midnight ET: Polls in all of Hawaii and most of Alaska close, with the remaining polls in Alaska closing at 1 a.m. ET.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Ex-Chicago FBI chief sues DOJ, claims he was ousted over failed anti-ICE prosecutions
summary: The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out after being wrongly blamed for failed prosecutions against anti-ICE protesters in the city.
story: ‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss who or what is responsible for a reduction in crime in the second Trump administration.

The former chief of the FBI's Chicago Field Office said he was forced out of his job after he said he was wrongly blamed for the failed prosecution of six people who protested against the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in the Windy City, according to a lawsuit he filed on Monday.

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence, according to the lawsuit. He said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer.
"I saw the writing on the wall," DePodesta told The Associated Press.

DePodesta accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros, of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

Douglas DePodesta sued top Justice Department officials, alleging that federal prosecutors pushed "politically motivated prosecutions" against Chicago demonstrators before gathering evidence. (Anthony Vazquez/Chicago Sun-Times via AP)
Hours after the lawsuit was filed, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed "Broadview Six" case.
"There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court," Perry wrote in the order.

Federal prosecutors brought charges against roughly 30 protesters during the federal immigration enforcement operation in Chicago, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, but many of those charges have since been dropped or dismissed.
DePodesta’s lawsuit alleges that Boutros faced pressure from the DOJ throughout the immigration crackdown to slap protesters with felony charges.

"Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration," DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the complaint.

Boutros often pressured assistant U.S. attorneys to press charges "before investigating the objective evidence," according to the lawsuit, which says he wanted felony charges when assistant U.S. attorneys "favored misdemeanors or no charges at all."

Douglas DePodesta accused U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros of launching a "campaign" within the DOJ to blame him after the so-called "Broadview Six" case fell apart earlier this year. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

Last October, Boutros charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, in connection with their actions during a protest at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.

Grand jury transcripts later turned over to the court showed that grand jurors twice declined to indict the six people as prosecutors sought charges, according to The Associated Press. Boutros dropped all charges against the six people in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.
Boutros "repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington" that the failure was DePodesta's fault "to deflect attention from his own malfeasance," DePodesta's attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.
DePodesta denied Boutros’ claims to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out of his job due to the "political pressure Boutros created," according to the suit.

The complaint alleges Boutros told DOJ leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, "conspired to destroy" the case.
PRITZKER CALLS FOR CRIMINAL INVESTIGATIONS INTO ICE AGENTS OVER ‘MIDWAY BLITZ’ CONDUCT
Douglas DePodesta said his superiors notified him that FBI Director Kash Patel pushed for his ouster before he was forced to resign over the summer. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug," Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to The Associated Press, adding that it is "both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by" Boutros.

In September, one of the prosecutors on the "Broadview Six" case abruptly resigned, writing in a resignation letter that Boutros had "scapegoated and publicly vilified" her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party moving forward.

The former defendants have asked the judge to appoint a special counsel to probe possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further "fact-finding" about communications between Boutros’ office and DOJ leadership.
Boutros has previously denied that politics played a role in charging decisions.
Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ for comment.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump admin over ICE's use of city-owned lots for immigration enforcement
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened legal action against ICE over agents allegedly staging immigration enforcement operations in city-owned parking lots.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday labeled U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "cruel" as Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the city does not "coordinate" with ICE, ahead of this weekend's gatherings.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat, threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) reported use of city-owned parking lots to stage immigration enforcement operations without the city's authorization.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York Field Office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations," which the mayor said is unauthorized and illegal.

"This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property," Mamdani wrote in the letter. "If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property."
DEMOCRAT MAYOR BLASTED BY DHS FOR 'HUNTING DOWN' PROPERTY OWNERS LEASING TO ICE: 'UNHINGED'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani threatened to sue the Trump administration over ICE's alleged use of city property to stage immigration enforcement operations. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

According to the mayor's letter, ICE agents have reportedly parked their vehicles and conducted meetings in several city-owned, unstaffed parking lots, including a parking lot at Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx as well as in parking lots along 111th Street on the west side of Flushing Meadows Corona Park in Queens, which is located next to a city-run preschool and several cultural institutions that welcome hundreds of children and families every day.
"ICE has not secured any authorization from the City to use these lots for immigration enforcement. To be clear: the City does not authorize ICE using its property in this manner," Mamdani wrote.

"Parking lots connected to City parks are reserved for the safe use and enjoyment of New Yorkers and visitors who wish to use our parks," he continued. "Use of these lots for other purposes, including ICE’s reported use of these lots, amounts to unauthorized activity on City property. Accordingly, you must immediately issue guidance to your agents prohibiting them from using any City lots to stage or conduct enforcement operations."

Mamdani added that New York City "deeply values its immigrant communities and will continue to use all available lawful means to ensure their safety, well-being, and ability to navigate the City and its resources without fear."
MAMDANI CALLS ICE A 'ROGUE' AGENCY AFTER NYC SHOOTING, CLAIMS AGENTS VIEW LAW AS 'MERELY A SUGGESTION'
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he is "deeply troubled" by reports of ICE agents "using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations." (Photo by Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
Last month, Mamdani and other New York Democratic leaders pushed for the city’s private parking lot owners to ban ICE from their properties.

"In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations," the mayor wrote in a letter to property owners and operators.
MAMDANI SAYS EVEN IF HE CAN GET ALONG WITH TRUMP, HE STILL DEMANDS THAT 'ICE SHOULD BE ABOLISHED'
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has previously pushed for ICE to be abolished. (Christopher Dilts/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., were among more than 100 elected officials who signed on to Mamdani's October letter.

Mamdani has previously pushed for ICE to be abolished, including after an ICE agent shot and killed Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston in July and after another ICE agent shot and wounded Dominican national Oscar Belgal during an enforcement operation in New York City last month.

title: JD Vance says Haley Stevens' endorsement of GOP's Mike Rogers will 'certainly' help Michigan Senate race

story: VP Vance answered Fox News Digital’s question about whether the Haley Stevens endorsement would boost Rogers’ chances of winning in Michigan.

WASHINGTON, D.C. - Vice President JD Vance addressed Rep. Haley Stevens’, D-Mich., endorsement of GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers over his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, saying that he believes the endorsement will "certainly" help Rogers in the midterm.

Vance spoke to reporters at Joint Base Andrews following two rallies for GOP candidates in New York and Ohio, responding to a question from Fox News Digital about the impact that Stevens’ endorsement will have on the race.

"I certainly think it helps," Vance said. "I mean, the message is whether you're a reasonable Democrat, a Republican, a conservative, an independent or just a liberal who loves the United States of America. El-Sayed is a crazy person and Mike Rogers is a patriot."
MICHIGAN DEM CLAIMS STEVENS SHOT DOWN ROGERS ENDORSEMENT RUMOR HOURS BEFORE TURNING ON EL-SAYED

A split image shows Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Vice President JD Vance, right. EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT

title: How a midterm tie gets settled in the case of the Senate
summary: A tied Senate could leave control of the chamber uncertain after the 2026 midterm elections. Past 50-50 splits in 2000 and 2020 offer clues about how lawmakers could negotiate power sharing agreements in 2027.
story: 'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-host Griff Jenkins analyzes new Fox News Power Rankings and discusses pathways to Senate control ahead of the midterm elections.
In the World Cup, they play overtime, then rely on penalty kicks to settle ties.

The National Hockey League plays a short overtime, followed by a shootout. NHL games used to end in ties. In the playoffs, the teams keep going – until there’s a winner. In the 2020 playoffs, the Tampa Bay Lightning finally topped the Columbus Blue Jackets 3-2 after a staggering five overtimes. In other words. They played nearly THREE total games. That’s the equivalent of 26 innings in baseball.

Speaking of Major League Baseball, teams play extra innings. And keep playing until one team is ahead and the home team has completed an at-bat in the bottom of the inning. MLB modified its rules a few years ago, introducing a "ghost runner" on second base to start the 10th inning. That’s an effort to end the tie and finish the game sooner.
If only there were a method to settle a tie in the U.S. Senate.
THE NINE KEY RACES THAT WILL DECIDE WHO CONTROLS THE SENATE, AND WHERE THEY STAND
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Yes. In the case of a tie roll call vote, the vice president — who doubles as president of the Senate – can vote to break a tie vote. In fact, the VP doesn’t even have to cast a ballot if it’s a tie and the roll call vote is going the way he or she wants. By rule, tie votes go down to defeat in the Senate.
But what if we wake up Wednesday morning (if not Friday or Saturday morning or sometime in early December, depending on how hotly contested things are) to discover that the Senate is tied at 50-50?

There is nothing in the Senate’s 44 standing rules which serves as a tiebreaker. The Founders didn’t provide a system to bust up a tie and determine which side is in the majority or minority. And no, it’s not written down anywhere that the party of the President is automatically thrust into the majority.
Maybe soccer is on to something with penalty kicks. At least there’s a system. There’s nothing concrete to sort out which party controls the Senate if things are deadlocked at 50-50.

There was a tie was a Senate tie in 1881 after resignations and political maneuvering. The Senate was also tied for a period in 1954. Nearly ten percent of all senators died during the two-year Congress which stretched from early 1953 to early 1955.

However, the Senate featured two ties in recent Senate history. Both instances reflect what the Senate did to sort out which party captured the majority. One tie came after the 2000 election. The other in 2020. Both elections took a while to sort things out.
Democratic Senate candidate, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event at the Georgia Theater on Sept. 13, 2026 in Athens, Ga. (Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images)
In 2026, Alaska, we’re looking at you.
It took until early December, 2000 to determine that Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., defeated then-Sen. Slade Gorton, R-Wash., establishing a 50-50 Senate.

In fact, the tie for the Senate from the 2020 election wasn’t even established until two days into the new Congress on January 6, 2021. Yes. That was the day of the Capitol riot. Sens. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., both won runoffs to set the 50-50 split.

In early December, 2000, the Supreme Court finally settled the Florida election dispute between President George W. Bush and Vice President Al Gore. Republicans had held the Senate. But then Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, R-Miss., and Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-S.D., engineered a power-sharing agreement between the parties. This aligned with the election of Vice President Dick Cheney.

Lott would serve as the Majority Leader and the GOP technically had the "majority." But the bipartisan pact granted Daschle some special floor powers. Republicans chaired each committee. However, there was equal representation by both parties on each panel.
The full Senate had to ratify this agreement. And it did just that.

Such a process is subject to two filibusters requiring 60 yeas. One to bring up the proposal for debate. Another to terminate the debate. Then a simple majority to pass it. But none of that was a problem. The Senate greenlighted it with all 100 senators signing on.
Why such smooth sailing?

Republicans feared Democrats would stall the agenda of President George W. Bush. So they got on board. Democrats agreed because they knew they were kinda, sorta in the majority. Otherwise, they were relegated to an outright minority.

Former Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., was well aware of those same dynamics in 2001. He insisted that Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., propound – word-for-word – the same accord in 2021 which Lott and Daschle hammered out.

Which brings us to a potential tie in 2027. Is there the political will in the Senate – let alone the votes – to agree to such a compact? President Trump is still president. And Vice President JD Vance is still President of the Senate. What would they say about that? Unclear.

Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump and Republican vice presidential nominee Sen. JD Vance joined family members and others at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2024, in New York City, to honor those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks at the World Trade Center. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

The Senate isn’t compelled to present a dedicated "majority" or "minority." The concept of a "Majority Leader" is relatively new – only dating back to the early 20th Century. The Senate is a body of "equals." Thus, the Founders didn’t expect one senator to wield operational control of the Senate. You won’t find the words "Majority Leader" anywhere in the Constitution. Just Speaker of the House and President of the Senate.

If there’s a 50-50 Senate and an impasse, could Vance suddenly have more power? Maybe. As President of the Senate, he can’t debate. He can only preside over the body and break ties. Moreover, would Vance even want to assert more authority? It’s unclear what that could be. And what would all of this do to his plans to run for president in 2028?
EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In fact, a deadlocked Senate with no power sharing agreement could potentially hamstring Vance. It wasn’t that long ago that the Vice President spent much of his time presiding over daily Senate debates. But not anymore. If there’s no set majority, those responsibilities either fall to Vance, current Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, or the possible Democratic Senate President Pro Tempore Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash. The latter two are the most senior senators from their respective parties. The President Pro Tempore is third in line to the presidency, following the Vice President and House Speaker. A power sharing agreement is what helps determine who presides over the Senate. Otherwise, Vance may be moored in the Senate.

So there is precedent for settling a "tie" in the Senate. But it hinges on the political will of senators. And if there are disputes about seating Members – say the Alaska Senate race or another contest becomes a conflagration – one can anticipate a toxic climate on Capitol Hill. Few may be willing to sign on to anything.

The Senate relies a lot on history and precedent to do things. But absent political will, senators may just resort to rock, paper, scissors.
Or maybe, penalty kicks.

title: 7 holiday shopping scams to watch for this season
summary: Black Friday deals are already drawing scammers who use fake delivery notices and gift card payment requests to steal your personal financial information.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion.

Black Friday is still weeks away, but the holiday shopping season is already picking up. Stores are promoting early deals, our inboxes are filling with sales emails, and chances are you're already thinking about gifts for family and friends. Scammers are getting an early start, too.

Holiday shopping scams are designed to blend in with legitimate promotions and messages. A tempting discount could lead to a fake online store. A delivery alert might ask you to confirm your address or pay a small fee. And an email about a problem with your order could be an attempt to steal your payment information.

The tricky part is that these messages often arrive when you're already looking for deals or expecting packages. Before you click or enter your credit card information, here are seven holiday shopping scams to watch for and simple ways to protect yourself.
DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. Holiday shopping scams are targeting consumers with fake online stores, fraudulent delivery alerts and deceptive discounts ahead of Black Friday. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
Why holiday shopping gives scammers an opening

During the holidays, it is normal to receive messages from unfamiliar stores. You may also be expecting several deliveries at once. Meanwhile, sales and shipping deadlines create pressure to act quickly. Scammers take advantage of those distractions. A fake message becomes more convincing when it matches something you are already expecting. That's why one of the best ways to avoid holiday shopping scams is to verify unexpected messages through a company's official website or app rather than responding directly.
The deal that's too good to be true

You see a social media ad for a name-brand coat, popular gadget or designer handbag at 80% off. The photos look professional, and a countdown clock warns that the deal is about to expire. Big discounts happen during the holidays. However, unusually low prices on popular merchandise can signal a scam. Some fake stores collect your payment and send nothing. Others deliver cheap counterfeits or products that look nothing like the advertisement.

The copycat online store

Fake shopping websites can look remarkably convincing. Scammers copy brand logos, product photography and website layouts to make their stores appear legitimate. Sometimes, the biggest clue is hiding in the website address. A fake store might add words such as "outlet" or "sale" to a familiar brand name. Others use subtle misspellings or unfamiliar web addresses.

Suspicious website addresses: Look for misspellings, unexpected words or unusual domains.Missing contact information: Be cautious if you cannot find a reliable way to reach customer support.Unusual payment demands: Avoid sellers requiring gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.Questionable reviews: Look beyond testimonials posted directly on the retailer's website.Unclear return policies: Review refund terms and shipping charges before purchasing.

Unclear return policies: Review refund terms and shipping charges before purchasing.

One important detail: A padlock icon or HTTPS connection does not guarantee that a shopping website is legitimate. It means the connection is encrypted. Scammers can use encrypted websites, too. When in doubt, type the retailer's official address into your browser or open its trusted app.
The fake delivery notice

"Your package could not be delivered. Please confirm your address." Messages like this appear through text messages and emails, often claiming to come from the U.S. Postal Service, UPS or FedEx. Because you may have packages on the way, the message can seem believable. Scammers frequently direct you to a fake tracking page. There, they may ask you to enter your address, credit card number or other personal information. Some demand a small redelivery fee.

The Postal Service confirms that it does not charge a fee for redelivery. If a text claims you must pay USPS to receive your package again, treat it as a warning sign.
The problem with your order email

Another common scam involves an email claiming that your payment failed, your shopping account has been locked or a purchase needs immediate confirmation. Some messages go further. They claim someone made an expensive purchase using your account and provide a phone number to call if you want to cancel it. That number may connect you directly to a scammer. Once you call, the person may request your credit card information, ask for a one-time verification code or pressure you into installing remote-access software.

The gift card payment request

Gift cards make convenient holiday presents. Unfortunately, scammers also like them because the money can be difficult to recover once the card numbers and PINs are shared. A scammer may pretend to be a seller, employer or family member who urgently needs financial help. Some even claim to represent government agencies or utility companies.

A legitimate company might sell gift cards or accept its own gift cards for purchases. However, demands to buy gift cards and send someone the card numbers or PINs are strong signs of fraud.
The charity appeal that pulls at your heart

The holidays are a popular time for charitable giving. Scammers know that emotional appeals can encourage people to donate quickly. Fake charities may use names that resemble familiar organizations. Others take advantage of natural disasters or heartbreaking stories to solicit donations. Some scammers impersonate legitimate charities and direct donations to fraudulent payment pages.

The marketplace bargain that disappears

Online marketplaces and local resale groups can be useful places to find holiday bargains. However, they also attract scammers posing as legitimate sellers. A seller might advertise a popular item at an unusually low price, then demand payment before you can inspect it. Others try to move conversations away from the marketplace to avoid its protections. Fake payment confirmations and requests for additional shipping fees are other warning signs.

Safer checkout habits for the holiday season
Avoiding holiday shopping scams starts with a few simple habits. These precautions can help protect your finances and personal information.

How security software can help protect holiday shoppers

Good habits are your first line of defense, but nobody spots every scam every time, especially during the busy holiday season. That's where reliable security software can provide an extra layer of protection. I recommend using strong antivirus software that helps detect suspicious websites, phishing attempts and malicious links before they put your personal information at risk.

Look for software that offers real-time protection against viruses, malware, spyware and ransomware. Some security solutions also include scam detection tools that can help identify fraudulent text messages, fake shopping websites and suspicious links. These features are particularly useful when scammers impersonate familiar retailers or delivery companies.

A built-in password manager is another valuable feature. It can generate and securely store strong, unique passwords for your shopping accounts. That helps reduce the risk of someone accessing multiple accounts if one password is compromised.

AI-powered scams are also becoming more convincing. Fake celebrity endorsements, manipulated videos and fraudulent holiday giveaways can make questionable offers appear legitimate. Some security products now include AI-powered scam detection and deepfake detection tools to help identify certain types of manipulated content. However, these capabilities vary by product, device and platform.

While security software cannot stop every scam, combining it with secure payment methods, account alerts and careful shopping habits can help protect your money and personal information throughout the holiday season.

Kurt's key takeaways

I love finding a great holiday deal as much as anyone. But I've learned that the best way to avoid getting scammed is to be a little skeptical when something looks unusually attractive or demands an immediate response. Scammers are getting better at copying familiar stores and creating convincing messages. They're also using AI to make fraudulent offers look more believable. That's why I recommend checking purchases directly through retailers you trust and using security tools that can help flag suspicious activity. title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
summary: Apple's iPhone Duo reportedly outlasted the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 by over three hours in battery tests, but its weight and repair costs raise concerns.
story: Apple's newly unveiled foldable iPhone Duo sparks significant consumer interest despite a hefty $1,999 starting price tag. On 'Varney & Co.', Taylor Riggs explains the premium device's unique dual-screen capability and ultra-thin design. Host Stuart Varney admits he plans to purchase the high-end smartphone, which can cost up to $3,000 for the two-terabyte storage model.

How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone.

The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less.

Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, takes on Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 with longer battery life, a glare-reducing display and a higher price tag. (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
Apple enters the foldable phone race seven years late

Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology.

Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing.
iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 price: Prepare for sticker shock

Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions.

However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them.
Apple's folding iPhone has a weight problem

One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone.

If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more apparent when you're holding the phone open for extended periods. Samsung also wins on thickness. Its Fold 8 measures about 0.38 inches thick when closed, while the Duo measures 0.44 inches. Apple counters with a rounded titanium design that may feel more comfortable in your hand. Samsung uses sharper edges and a flatter appearance.

There's also something worth thinking about. Both phones have relatively small outer screens. Apple's measures 5.4 inches, while Samsung's comes in at 5.5 inches. Those screens are perfectly usable for everyday tasks. However, they're considerably smaller than the displays on many conventional flagship phones. You could end up spending $2,000 on a device that requires an extra step whenever you want a bigger screen. That's why I'd recommend trying both in person before buying. The phone that feels exciting for five minutes in a store needs to feel comfortable after five hours in your hand.
The iPhone Duo display has a clever trick

Both folding phones open to reveal 7.6-inch OLED screens with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Each also offers peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. The real difference comes down to how those displays handle reflections.

Apple developed a nano-texture finish for the Duo's inner screen. It creates a matte appearance that helps reduce glare and makes the fold crease harder to see. Anyone who has struggled to read a glossy screen near a sunny window might appreciate this approach.

Samsung's screen has a more traditional glossy finish, which can make colors appear richer. Some early iPhone Duo reviews suggest Apple's matte display sacrifices a little contrast and vibrancy to achieve its reduced reflections. Neither approach will appeal to everyone. However, Apple has another interesting feature coming.
Apple Pencil support could give the Duo an edge

The iPhone Duo now supports the Apple Pencil (USB-C) through iOS 27.2, which Apple released on Oct. 26. That means you can sketch or annotate documents directly on the folding screen. The feature already works in the software's release candidate.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 does not support the S Pen. Samsung removed the feature as it pursued thinner folding designs. There is one catch with Apple's approach. The Duo works only with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Even if you already own an Apple Pencil Pro, you won't be able to use it with this phone.

The USB-C version also lacks the pressure sensitivity available on more advanced Apple Pencil models. Still, this could be useful for someone who regularly signs documents or prefers handwritten notes.
Samsung still understands multitasking better

Here's where those seven years of Samsung experience become apparent. Let's say you're on a video call and someone sends you an important document. You want to review it without interrupting the conversation. Then you need to check your calendar. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 can handle several apps on its larger screen. You can run three apps in split-screen mode, and Samsung also offers pop-up windows for additional flexibility. The Fold 8 supports Samsung DeX, too, giving you a desktop-style experience when connected to compatible external displays.

Apple has introduced Split View on the Duo, allowing two apps to run side by side. That's a first for the iPhone, and it should make the larger screen far more useful. However, Apple's approach remains more restrictive than Samsung's. Split View uses a fixed arrangement, and you don't get the same floating-window flexibility. There's another issue that early iPhone Duo owners are discovering.
Some iPhone apps aren't ready for the bigger screen

Apple redesigned iOS 27 for the Duo, which ships with iOS 27.1. Its own apps have been adapted to use the folding display. However, some third-party apps haven't caught up. Early reviewers found that certain apps display large black bars or awkward layouts when opened on the bigger screen. That could be frustrating when you've paid so much for additional screen space.

Fortunately, developers can update their apps to support the Duo's design. Some popular apps have already received updates, and more are expected. For now, though, Samsung has a more established folding software experience. I would also pay attention to which apps you use most. A larger screen loses some of its appeal when your favorite apps still behave as though they're running on a much smaller phone.
Apple's battery life delivers a welcome surprise

Folding phones have a difficult job. They need enough battery power to run a large display without becoming too bulky. Apple's iPhone Duo uses two internal batteries and an A20 Pro processor designed for efficient performance. Samsung equips its Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a 4,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

Both processors offer plenty of power for demanding apps. However, early independent testing suggests Apple has a surprising advantage when it comes to battery life. In one battery test involving continuous web browsing over 5G, the iPhone Duo reportedly lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, compared with 10 hours and 6 minutes for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's more than three additional hours for Apple.

Another independent test produced encouraging results for the Duo. While streaming video over Wi-Fi with the larger screens at maximum brightness, Apple's foldable reportedly lasted 18 hours and 15 minutes, compared with 16 hours and 30 minutes for Samsung. Although the tests used different methods, both suggest Apple has managed to squeeze impressive battery life out of its first folding phone.

Apple officially claims up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display. However, that figure comes from controlled laboratory testing, so everyday results will vary depending on how you use the phone.

Charging is another consideration. Apple says the Duo can reach 50% in about 20 minutes with a compatible wired charger. Samsung supports 45W wired charging and fast wireless charging. For anyone who spends long days traveling or regularly finds their battery running low before dinner, Apple's early results are encouraging.
THE IPHONE DUO IS OFFICIALLY HERE — GET IT FOR NO MONEY DOWN AT T-MOBILE
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, roughly $100 more than Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, as Apple enters the foldable smartphone market. (Jung Yeon-je/AFP via Getty Images)
A $2,000 folding phone still comes with camera compromises

For nearly $2,000, you'd expect a phone with an incredible camera. And while both of these foldables take excellent photos, there's a catch. Apple's iPhone Duo has two 48MP rear cameras, while Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 has two 50MP cameras. Neither has a dedicated telephoto lens, which means you're giving up some of the zoom capabilities found on other premium phones.

Think about trying to get a close-up shot of your child playing soccer or capturing something interesting in the distance while on vacation. Apple's Duo offers 2x optical-quality zoom by cropping into its main sensor. Samsung uses a similar approach, with digital zoom for subjects farther away. Both can handle everyday photos, but if you love getting those close-up shots, an iPhone 18 Pro Max or Galaxy S26 Ultra may be a better choice.

Here's where Samsung throws another option into the mix. Its Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99, just $100 more than Apple's Duo at their regular starting prices. For that extra money, you get a 200MP main camera and a dedicated telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. That's worth considering if you want a folding phone but aren't willing to give up a more versatile camera. And with Samsung already offering discounts on some models, you may not even have to spend more.
Apple has some fun camera features Samsung can't match exactly

Ever try taking a group photo and realize you're the one missing from it? Apple's Smart Take could help with that. Just prop open the iPhone Duo, get into the picture and let its AI recognize when everyone is posing. The phone automatically snaps the photo, so there's no racing against a timer or asking someone else to take the shot.

Then there's Duo Preview, which lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outside screen. That could save you from hearing, "Wait, let me see that one," after every picture. Apple also came up with Kid Cue, which plays Peanuts animations on the outer display to get children to look toward the camera. If you've ever tried getting a toddler to cooperate for a family photo, you can probably appreciate that one.

Samsung has a few tricks of its own. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can show people a preview on its outer screen, and you can prop it partially open for hands-free photos. That comes in handy when you want to be in the picture instead of always being the one taking it.
The most expensive iPhone Duo surprise could come after you buy it

Now let's talk about something that deserves far more attention than it usually receives. Repairs. Apple rates the iPhone Duo IP68 for dust and water resistance, while Samsung gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 an IP48 rating. That gives Apple stronger protection against dust under standardized laboratory testing. However, neither rating guarantees that a folding screen or hinge will survive years of rough treatment. These phones also contain more moving parts than conventional smartphones. And if something goes wrong, the repair costs can be substantial.

There's another reason to think carefully about durability. As we reported in our article, Apple confirms iPhone Duo screen problems after launch. Some owners experienced cracks along the inner screen near the hinge within hours or days of purchase, sometimes during initial setup. Apple acknowledged an issue affecting a small number of devices and directed affected customers to contact AppleCare for replacements. The company hasn't identified the cause or disclosed how many phones are affected. An AppleCare+ subscription isn't required to request a replacement for this acknowledged issue. Still, it's something I'd consider before spending nearly $2,000 on a first-generation folding iPhone.

According to Apple's published repair estimates, replacing the iPhone Duo's damaged inner display costs $999 without AppleCare+. That's roughly half the cost of the entry-level phone. Apple also lists an estimated $1,499 charge for certain other damage repairs. There is some relief for minor screen damage. Apple's replaceable inner display cover layer costs $49 to replace without AppleCare+, provided the damage is limited to that layer. AppleCare+ can significantly reduce eligible repair charges. For example, an inner display repair is listed at $99 under the coverage, subject to the plan's terms. Of course, the coverage itself adds to the cost of ownership.

Samsung's folding phones also have specialized displays and hinges that can be expensive to repair. However, repair pricing varies by model, damage and coverage. This is one area where I'd encourage anyone considering either phone to look beyond the advertised purchase price. After all, a $2,000 phone is expensive enough without worrying about what happens if it slips out of your hand and you're suddenly facing a repair bill approaching $1,000.
Another iPhone Duo change could surprise travelers

Apple has made the iPhone Duo eSIM-only worldwide. That means you won't find a physical SIM card slot. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports both eSIM and a physical nano-SIM card, although configurations may vary by market.

For most people in the United States, this probably won't be an obstacle. Major carriers support eSIM, and many international providers offer digital plans. However, if you travel frequently and prefer buying physical SIM cards at your destination, Samsung gives you more flexibility. It's worth checking whether your preferred mobile provider supports eSIM before buying the Duo.
iPhone Duo or Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy?

If you've been waiting years for a folding iPhone, Apple's Duo is an appealing first attempt. It offers excellent early battery performance, an impressive display and the convenience of staying within Apple's ecosystem. However, I wouldn't overlook Samsung. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly lighter, costs a little less and offers more flexible multitasking. Those advantages could become increasingly important once the excitement of owning a new folding phone wears off.

And here's something else to consider. If most of your day involves texting or checking email, you may spend far more time using the smaller outer screen than you expect. The larger display becomes especially useful when you frequently review documents or watch videos while traveling.

Before buying either phone, think about how much time you would realistically spend with it unfolded. Also, if you're considering switching between Apple and Samsung, take a look at our guide on how to transfer data to a new iPhone or Android at CyberGuy.com. It can help make the move considerably easier.
HERE ARE SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE

Apple's iPhone Duo and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 feature 7.6-inch folding displays, but differences in weight, battery life and multitasking could influence buyers. (Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Samsung credit. Seven years ago, folding phones seemed like an expensive experiment, and I wasn't convinced they'd ever catch on. But Samsung stuck with the idea, and now Apple has finally joined the party. I like what Apple's done with the iPhone Duo, especially the display and those impressive early battery results. Still, I keep coming back to the price. Nearly $2,000 for a phone that's heavier than Samsung's and doesn't have a dedicated telephoto camera? That's a tough sell. And the possibility of a $999 inner screen repair would certainly make me nervous.

I also wouldn't count Samsung out just because Apple has entered the race. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably lighter, and Samsung has spent years figuring out how to make that larger screen useful. Being able to run more apps at once is a nice advantage, especially if you're someone who likes getting work done on your phone. And let's face it, a lighter phone is something you'll appreciate long after the excitement of showing everyone how it folds has worn off.

If I were spending this kind of money, I'd want to see how Apple's first folding iPhone holds up after a few months of everyday use. I'd also want to hold both phones before deciding. But here's what I keep wondering. How often would I really open that larger screen? If I ended up using the smaller outside display most of the day, I'd have a hard time convincing myself that spending $2,000 was worth it.
Would you really spend $2,000 on a folding phone, or do you think Apple and Samsung are charging us more to solve a problem we never had? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Florida police unveil $148K flying patrol vehicle
summary: Florida Polytechnic University's Jetson ONE eVTOL police vehicle named Astro still awaits FAA authorization before officers can fly operational patrols.
story: Florida Polytechnic University's Astro flying patrol vehicle takes to the skies above campus as police explore how electric aircraft could support emergency response. (Florida Polytechnic University)

You may be used to seeing police cars cruising through your neighborhood or helicopters flying overhead. But what if an officer could respond to an emergency in a small electric aircraft that looks like a giant drone? That idea is getting closer to reality in Florida. The Florida Polytechnic University Police Department in Lakeland has introduced a flying patrol vehicle that the university has nicknamed Astro. Jetson, the company behind the Jetson ONE personal flying machine, built the single-seat aircraft.

According to the university, it's the first U.S. law enforcement agency to add this type of piloted electric aircraft to its fleet. Jetson calls it a world first. However, Astro still needs FAA authorization before officers can use it for operational police patrols. Here's how Astro works and why police believe this unusual aircraft could change the way they respond to emergencies.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
Astro is Florida's new flying patrol vehicle

Astro gets its name from the dog in the classic cartoon The Jetsons. The aircraft even looks like something George Jetson might have parked outside his house. Astro uses electric vertical takeoff and landing technology, commonly called eVTOL. As a result, it can lift straight into the air without needing a runway. Unlike a conventional police helicopter, Astro has a compact frame that folds for easier transport and storage. The aircraft features an open cockpit surrounded by a lightweight frame.

Eight electric motors power its eight propellers. Meanwhile, a four-axis joystick allows the pilot to control its movement. Florida Polytechnic University selected the Jetson ONE to explore its potential for law enforcement. The aircraft arrived during summer 2026. Since then, police personnel have completed flight training, according to Jetson. That includes Police Chief Aaron Murray. Jetson also identifies the aircraft by its registration number, N911FP. The number references emergency services and Florida Polytechnic University. Jetson tells CyberGuy that Astro is a standard Jetson ONE with police lights added. Officers use a handheld radio, and the aircraft has mounts for action cameras. The company says a pilot-controlled searchlight could be added in the future.
How fast can the flying police vehicle go?

Astro may look compact, but its advertised performance is impressive. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph. That's fast enough to cover short distances across a large campus without following roads or dealing with traffic. However, battery life limits how long it can stay airborne. Jetson estimates approximately 20 minutes of flight time per charge, making Astro better suited to short missions than extended patrols. Jetson tells CyberGuy that the aircraft takes approximately 90 minutes to recharge using a 240-volt connection. Charging through a standard household outlet takes about three hours. However, officers can swap batteries between flights. This allows them to return to the air sooner if fully charged replacements are available. Each flight still lasts approximately 20 minutes.

Jetson confirms that the 210-pound maximum includes the pilot, police gear and any emergency supplies. The company says this is a hard limit, which could restrict how much equipment an officer can carry. Jetson also advertises several safety features. The company says Astro can continue flying even if one motor fails. It also has an automatic landing system and a ballistic parachute designed for emergencies. Jetson lists the vehicle at $148,000 before taxes and additional fees, making it a significant investment for a police department.
How police could use Astro during emergencies

Florida Polytechnic University wants to explore whether Astro can help officers respond when roads become difficult to navigate. Consider what happens after a major Florida storm. Roads may flood, debris can block access and emergency crews may struggle to reach certain locations. Once weather and flying conditions allow, a small aircraft that takes off vertically could help officers survey the damage.

Police Chief Aaron Murray believes Astro could help officers monitor the campus and reach places that traditional vehicles cannot easily access. The department also wants to investigate using it to deliver emergency supplies. "Advanced air mobility is a technology on the rise, and we can either choose to be proactive or reactive as it develops," Murray said.

The university also plans to collaborate with regional law enforcement agencies on potential emergency-response missions. However, Astro carries only its pilot. It cannot transport an injured person or bring someone back from a rescue mission. Because the 210-pound limit includes the officer and everything onboard, the amount of emergency supplies Astro can carry depends on the pilot's weight and equipment.
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
The single-seat Jetson ONE aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph and stay airborne for approximately 20 minutes per charge. (Florida Polytechnic University)
The FAA hurdle facing Florida's flying police vehicle

There's an important regulatory issue before Astro can become a regular part of police operations. Jetson developed the ONE as a recreational aircraft designed around the FAA's Part 103 ultralight rules. Those rules allow qualifying ultralight vehicles to operate without traditional aircraft or pilot certification. However, Part 103 limits their use to recreational or sporting purposes. Police patrols fall outside those permitted uses. FAA guidance specifically identifies aerial surveying and patrolling as activities that cannot operate under Part 103.

Jetson says Florida Polytechnic University needs additional federal authorization involving FAA Part 91 rules to use Astro for public-safety missions. When the university announced the aircraft in mid-October, it said the approval process was in its final stages. At that time, officials expected approval in November or December. The university has not publicly confirmed when regular operational police patrols will begin.
Students will help develop the flying police aircraft's future

Astro has another role beyond its potential police duties. It will serve as a hands-on research platform for Florida Polytechnic University students. The university launched an aerospace engineering degree program in fall 2026. As a result, students will have an opportunity to study electric aircraft technology while learning about the challenges of operating it.

Faculty members and students plan to use Astro's flight data for research and senior engineering projects. Reports also indicate that the university is exploring virtual training simulations for police officers. This could provide useful information about how small electric aircraft perform during specialized missions. It may also help future engineers identify limitations that need attention before wider adoption.

Florida is also expanding its involvement in advanced air mobility. The nearby SunTrax transportation testing facility in Auburndale has a dedicated aerial test track for emerging aircraft technology. Testing under Florida's participation in a federal advanced air mobility pilot program is expected to begin by the end of 2026. That statewide testing effort is separate from Astro's pending authorization for police operations.
Could more police departments start using flying vehicles?

Astro raises an interesting possibility for law enforcement agencies looking for alternatives to traditional helicopters. Police helicopters require significant resources to purchase and maintain. A smaller electric aircraft could eventually offer another option for certain missions, especially when an officer needs a quick view of an area from above.

However, Jetson's aircraft also has substantial limitations. Its short flight duration means officers would need to plan missions carefully. Swappable batteries could support repeated flights, but officers would still need to land between missions to replace them. Weather conditions and airspace restrictions could further affect operations. There's also the question of whether a single-seat piloted aircraft provides enough benefits compared with a drone, which can conduct aerial surveillance without putting an officer in the cockpit.

Even so, Jetson sees the police department's purchase as an important step toward expanding personal electric aircraft into professional use. The company says its entire 2026 and 2027 production is sold out. It is now accepting orders for 2028, with a listed price of $148,000. Jetson also expects Astro to appear at the public UP.Summit event at Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 7 and 8.
A closer look at Astro reveals its compact design, open cockpit and police markings, with eight electric motors powering the $148,000 aircraft. (Florida Polytechnic University)
What this means to you

You probably won't see flying patrol vehicles operating above your neighborhood anytime soon. However, Astro offers an early look at how public-safety agencies might use small electric aircraft. After a major storm, an officer flying over blocked roads could potentially assess damage and help emergency crews understand where assistance is needed. The same technology might eventually support searches for missing people, although Astro's usefulness still needs to be demonstrated during actual police operations.

There's another side worth considering. As police departments explore aerial technology, questions about privacy will become increasingly important. People may want to know when officers can fly above their property and whether aircraft will collect or record information. Those questions deserve attention alongside the aircraft's potential benefits. For now, Florida Polytechnic University has an opportunity to study a new approach to emergency response while working toward the necessary federal authorization.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've been following Jetson's flying aircraft for several years, and seeing one enter a police department's fleet is an interesting development. When I first covered the Jetson ONE, the attraction was the idea of people being able to fly their own electric aircraft. Now we're seeing a possible use beyond recreation. I can understand why a police department would want this technology, especially in Florida, where storms can leave communities cut off from emergency services. But I'm also interested in what happens after the excitement wears off. Twenty minutes of flight time leaves little room for unexpected delays, and there's still the question of whether an officer flying overhead offers enough advantages over a drone to justify the expense. I'm encouraged that the university plans to study those questions before putting Astro into regular service. And I think communities should have a say in how police use these aircraft, particularly when it comes to privacy.

Would seeing police officers flying above your neighborhood make you feel safer, or would you worry about having another set of eyes watching from the sky? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
