Down the homestretch, Jeffries crisscrossed the country, stumping with candidates in California, Texas, Florida, Ohio, Michigan, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., trying to protect his paper-thin majority, campaigned in many of the same battleground districts.

The speaker, a close Trump ally, warned that a Democratic victory would lead to nonstop investigations and a rollback of the signature piece of legislation the Republicans passed during the first two years of Trump’s second term, the “big, beautiful bill.”

“If this crazy group of Marxist Democrats took over, you can kiss your freedom goodbye. … They would spend every waking hour for the next two years investigating the president, the Cabinet, leaders in business and industry. It would be retribution,” Johnson said at a campaign event for Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., one of the cycle’s most vulnerable Republicans who represents a Harris-won district.
“We cannot go down that road,” Johnson added.

title: GOP fights to hang on to Senate majority
summary: Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal and alleged ballot shenanigans.
story: Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal, alleged ballot shenanigans and President Donald Trump’s incessant swooning over the backside of one Republican candidate.
Close races are expected in the traditional battlegrounds of Michigan and North Carolina — but also in states that have become more reliably red since Trump’s rise in politics, such as Ohio and Iowa.
NBC News projects that Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won re-election in swing state Georgia, defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
There are also closer-than-expected races brewing in even redder states such as Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

Underscoring the high stakes: In the most expensive election cycle ever, more than $3.4 billion has been spent on television and digital advertisements in Senate races across the country, according to tracking firm AdImpact.
Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber, meaning Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to regain control.
Follow live election coverage here.
A Democratic takeover would require them to flip at least two states that Trump won by double digits in 2024.

The most likely targets are Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Kansas and South Carolina. More than 50% of voters in each of those states disapprove of how Trump is handling his job, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.
In Kansas, for example, where Trump won by 16 percentage points two years ago, 57% of voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance, according to the survey.

The consequences for Trump are significant. For the past two years, his own Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress, allowing him to pursue his agenda largely unchecked. But if the Republicans lose the Senate, he’ll need Democratic cooperation to move forward on legislation and appointments. Democrats will have increased power to pursue investigations into the administration.

The NBC News Exit Poll found midterm voters with decisively negative opinions on how Congress is handling its role as a check and balance on Trump — 71% of voters, including 41% of Republicans, said there is not enough congressional oversight of the presidency.

Alaska has emerged late as a closely watched contest. Democrat Mary Peltola is under scrutiny after a New York Times report that her campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate into the race — Dan J. Sullivan — with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The “ballot-stacking” tactic is seen as a way to sow confusion among voters in a state that uses ranked choice voting and has four Senate candidates on the ballot.
Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied allegations that they recruited the lesser-known Sullivan.
For Subscribers
Polls close in Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.
For Subscribers
Clarity about the fight for the Senate will come much earlier in states such as Ohio, where polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET, and Michigan, where the last polls close at 9 p.m. ET.

In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted faces a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the race to serve the remaining two years on JD Vance’s unexpired Senate term. Husted was appointed to fill the seat temporarily last year after Vance was elected vice president.

Polls have shown a close race in Ohio, and the president held three rallies in the state in recent weeks — as well as one in the Cincinnati media market, in neighboring Kentucky — in an effort to boost Husted. Trump used the rallies not only to promote Husted’s work as a senator, but also to compliment his physique. Trump, who often gives the impression that he is casting for a movie, repeatedly praised Husted’s “ass” in Ohio and elsewhere down the stretch.
“If Husted wins,” one senior Republican official told NBC News last week, “it’s because Trump literally dragged his ass over the finish line.”

Then there’s the Michigan race, which is ending on an explosive note. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, scored a surprise last-minute endorsement Sunday from Rep. Haley Stevens, who in August lost the Democratic nomination to challenge him.

Stevens had vowed as late as Saturday, publicly and privately, to not break her promise to vote for Abdul El-Sayed. The Democrats had long clashed over his criticism of Israel, but Stevens’ criticism had intensified in recent days, prompting the El-Sayed campaign to signal that she was no longer welcome at his events. Stevens cited that in her decision to defect to Rogers, sparking outrage and accusations of betrayal from House Democratic colleagues.
Other key races to watch Tuesday include Maine, where polls close at 8 p.m., and where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is up against Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

And at 9 p.m. ET, the last polls will close in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator in 33 years. The race took on a heightened energy after the Republican incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, lost a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after a heavy push by Trump in favor of the latter.

Democrats are excited about their candidate, state Rep. James Talarico, who has maintained steady leads in polls, though within the margin of error. Trump ally and tech billionaire Elon Musk, meanwhile, has spent at least $150 million to back Paxton.

title: Routine voting issues fuel conspiracy theories and confusion
summary: Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online.
story: SLEEPY HOLLOW, N.Y. — Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online.

The issue was discovered early in the morning, after ballot tabulators failed to scan voters’ hand-marked paper ballots in 44 out of 45 of the county’s municipalities. State election officials said in a post on X that the issue was due to a programming error.
Election officials directed voters to put their ballots in secure orange ballot bags, following standard contingency plans.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections

The news has raised alarm among voters and onlookers. In text chains and Facebook posts viewed by NBC News, Westchester voters discussed the issue, with some expressing concern over whether their votes would be counted.

Tensions are high in part because Westchester is home to a key House race in the battle for control of Congress: In the 17th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a close race. The district narrowly leans blue, but Lawler has held it for four years by maintaining high popularity and campaigning aggressively on crime and affordability issues. Conley, a veteran and former Biden cybersecurity official, hopes to capitalize on President Donald Trump’s sagging approval ratings in her challenge.
In social media posts, both candidates urged voters not to be dissuaded by the tabulator issues.

Ken Jenkins, the Westchester County executive, said Tuesday afternoon that alternate tabulators are being rolled out, and that the ballots stored in secure bags will be counted after polls close at 9 p.m.

“Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” the New York State Board of Elections said in a Tuesday statement posted on X. “While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, told reporters that the ballots would be counted.

“Every vote will be counted; I think I need to say that three times. Every vote will be counted, every vote will be counted,” she said in Queens on Tuesday morning. “It’s being resolved in a bipartisan way that it’s supposed to. The backup plan is in place, so voters in Westchester should feel very confident.”

Isolated ballot scanner issues are routine, though the problems have been been particularly common in New York state. In 2018, scanners jammed across New York City, while Queens reported tabulator issues in 2024.

This year, ballot tabulator issues also occurred in other states including Florida and Oklahoma, while other issues like power outages and flooding shuttered some polling sites, including some in Maricopa County.

Online influencers supportive of the Republican Party and some officials saw an opportunity in the malfunctioning machines and polling location closures, framing them as a conspiracy against party candidates.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“The Democrats are already cheating,” posted Loomer Unleashed, a podcast associated with close Trump ally Laura Loomer, about power outages in Maricopa County. In reality, heavy rain and flooding have caused polling location issues across the county. The ballot counting issues in New York have sparked similar accusations, including from an elected official.
“The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat,” posted Rep. Claudia Tenner, R-N.Y., the chair of the House Election Integrity Caucus.
“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” Loomer wrote on social media, her post garnering over 100,000 views.
“This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, conservative podcast host and wife of White House adviser Steven Miller.

The nascent accusations echo similar narratives Trump and his supporters raised in past elections. The most famous of these false narratives claimed machines stole votes away from Republicans, costing them the 2020 presidential election. Yet technical failures are common, officials have warned, as are conspiracies about those malfunctions.

Researchers studying false online information have been worried about the potential for such accusations to recirculate as normal glitches get misrepresented. Such narratives could pave the way toward challenging the results of the election, several researchers told NBC News ahead of the midterms.
In Oklahoma City, the county’s top election official said normal issues were getting far more attention than usual.

“It’s not uncommon to have some voting machines cause us a few problems early in the day. It’s a common occurrence,” said Doug Sanderson, the county’s election board secretary. “Many times we wouldn’t hear about it other than from our precinct officials. I just think perhaps the climate and the sensitivity everyone has around this election causes people to be a little bit more on edge than they normally would be.”

Offline in Westchester County, voting at a Sleepy Hollow polling site at a social club called the Fraternal Order of Eagles appeared to be proceeding smoothly. A regular flow of voters trickled in and out through the lunch hour in the Hudson River Valley town, most having already heard via text message or from friends and neighbors that the scanners were not functioning.
As of 12:30 p.m. ET, of the 225 people who had voted at that location, only two walked away on account of the tabulators being down.
“One was pretty disrespectful,” a poll worker named Dennis told NBC News, declining to share his last name. “The other said maybe they’d come back later.”

title: Floods and severe weather beset parts of the U.S. on Election Day
summary: Flash flooding, heavy rain and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the U.S. to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races.
story: Flash flooding, heavy rain and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the United States to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races.

At least 21 polling locations were moved across eight Florida counties — including Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties — after intense rain caused flash floods Monday and into Tuesday morning.

Roads were impassable in several parts of the state’s Atlantic coast after a storm dumped as much as 22 inches of rain in 24 hours in a storm that “exceeded everyone’s expectations,” as one forecaster put it.
Severe storms were moving across Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas overnight. Forecasters issued a tornado watch that lasted until about 2:45 a.m. local time Tuesday.

Forecasters were also predicting possible flash flooding in parts of Alabama, Tennessee, Arkansas and Mississippi on Tuesday, as that storm system continued to travel east. A flood watch remained in effect in some parts of Florida, though rainfall rates were slowing.
“Areas affected by catastrophic flooding remain extremely sensitive to any additional rainfall,” forecasters wrote in a Tuesday morning discussion.

In Oklahoma, a tornado Sunday forced Cimarron County officials to change one of its polling locations. The tornado, which had peak winds of about 100 mph, snapped tree branches, damaged the roof of the Keyes Community Center and collapsed a wall, according to a damage survey report from the National Weather Service.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
In an emergency request, county election officials said the tornado caused “considerable structural damage” to the community center “rendering the polling location unsafe.”

And after historic flooding in the Four Corners region, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre M. Henderson declared a state of emergency and issued a special accommodation that will allow voters registered in San Juan County who are isolated by floodwaters to request and return ballots electronically.
The Colorado secretary of state is allowing a similar measure for voters — allowing votes online — in La Plata and Archuleta counties, according to 9 News.
In Florida, Port St. Lucie resident Jessica Rendon said she spent hours trying to cast her ballot after the weekend’s severe flooding led to waterlogged highways and closed polling locations.
“I personally did not see one officer out in public helping any of us out,” Rendon said. “Voting or not voting.”

She said she learned that her polling location had changed only from another resident who was also out trying to vote. Other residents who have located their polling stations are sharing the information via social media.

“Unfortunately, many by me are still stuck in their homes,” Rendon said, noting that the only reason she is been able to get around is that she owns a truck. “Frankly, I don’t think a lot can vote because of this.”
More Election Day surprises could be in store.

Experts say inclement weather has suppressed voter turnout in past elections. In research of elections from 1948 to 2000, researchers observed a modest drop in turnout during unusually intense rainstorms.

“What we found was that for every inch of rain that a county received above its average amount of rainfall, voter turnout went down about eight-tenths of 1 percentage point,” said Brad Gomez, an associate professor of political science at Florida State University.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

But experts said the effect of rain on turnout is diminishing over time as more people choose to vote early or vote by mail, and they said it’s hard to predict what effect the inclement weather will have, if any, on key races.
In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in seven counties along the Atlantic Seaboard that are being hit with flash flooding and extreme precipitation.
Damage in parts of Colorado remains widespread after heavy rain and flooding, with first responders searching for people who may be stranded across the area, including by helicopter.
People with homes along the Animas River in southwestern Colorado were also facing evacuation.
Record rainfall was also reported in usually dry Arizona, causing deadly flooding and power outages.

The brief closure of two voting centers in Maricopa County sparked a chorus of conspiracy insinuations online Monday. Two out of the 254 polling locations in the county had to be temporarily shuttered “due to power related issues,” election authorities announced on social media.
The two polling locations have since been reopened, authorities said, but some online used the shutdown to allege impropriety in the competitive swing state.

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs issued a statewide emergency declaration Monday after recently issuing an emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties. The governors of New Mexico and Colorado also asked President Donald Trump to declare a major disaster to receive federal funding assistance.

title: In top Senate race states, gas and grocery costs are rising faster than the national average
summary: From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation say the economy is their top issue this Election Day.
story: From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.
In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.
But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters.
These frustrations aren’t confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections

This has created an opening for Democrats to win majorities in both the House and the Senate. And while the House majority is widely expected to shift to Democrats after Tuesday night, the Senate is still very much a jump ball.
Veteran election data analysts are quick to remind the public that as Tuesday’s voting and later counting unfolds, any one of the competitive Senate races could tip either way.
Pain at the pump
In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period.

Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof.
Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16.
In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more,  nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%.

All three states broke for Trump in 2024. But two years later, they are in play, and Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, will be very closely watched Tuesday night.

title: Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?
summary: Americans might be waiting awhile. It all depends on how states count their votes and how close the races will be.
story: In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant most Americans went to bed Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks’ having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.

Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term.
Follow live election coverage

Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s likelier that determining the winners in important races will take time.

Of course, no one, including the Decision Desk, will know what will unfold until election night, but we will have a good sense possibly early in the night of how the contests are trending. The answer of when we could call control in both the House and the Senate depends not only on how states count their votes, but also on how close the races will be.
When we could know Senate control
Senate control is likely to come down to the eight races NBC News rates as either toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas) or lean Democratic (Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire).

Assuming Democrats win the states NBC News rates as “Likely” Democratic (which includes flipping North Carolina’s Senate seat from red to blue and keeping Georgia in their column), Democrats still need to win five of those eight contests.

Some of those states are quick to count their ballots, and others are perennially slow. If some of those Senate contests are as close as we expect, calling control of the Senate as a whole could take us into early Wednesday, regardless of who wins those individual races.

It’s also a real possibility that Americans will wake up at a slightly more reasonable hour Wednesday without a majority decided, even if we have a good sense of who will ultimately win. And if Senate control comes down to the outcome in Alaska, we’ll all be here awhile.

In that case, it will take a couple of weeks to know who won the majority thanks to the state’s ranked choice voting system. Past elections offer a useful guide to how quickly we expect to see votes counted in each of the states, even if the timing Tuesday night isn’t exact. Let’s look more closely at each of those categories — the fast-counting states, the slow-but-steady states and the ranked choice wild cards.

Votes in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas were counted fairly quickly in 2024. We expect over 80% of the vote in those states to be counted by midnight ET. If those historical patterns hold, there is a good chance that those Senate races will be called. And some of the calls may come in before midnight if there is some spread in the races, as some recent polls suggest.

But remember, Democrats must win five of those eight Senate races we listed above to take a majority, which means that even if they win all four states in the fast-counting list, NBC News would still not be able to project control of the Senate.

In two of the key battleground states, New Hampshire and Michigan, nearly all votes will be counted over the course of election night, but more steadily and slowly than in the fast counters. Here, elections are administered by towns and municipalities, not by counties. That results in a more decentralized and variable counting process that lasts until early morning or even midday Wednesday. How quickly those races are called really depends upon the margins of the races.

Earlier in the election cycle, polls suggested both those races would be close. Recent polls favoring the Democratic candidates and what appears to be a Democratic advantage in the early vote in Michigan mean there’s a wide range of timing possibilities there.

If the nationwide Democratic momentum translates to results, New Hampshire could be called before midnight. But that seems to be highly unlikely in a place like Michigan, where Wayne County, home to Detroit, often releases large batches of votes between midnight and 3 a.m. ET. That is such a significant source of ballots that statewide races in Michigan often cannot be called without Wayne County’s results.

The takeaway here is that if the Senate races in those states are close as the polls have indicated all along, it’s unlikely that calls will come before early morning. But it all depends upon how far apart the two candidates are in the state, and we won’t know that until tonight.

Maine and Alaska are the slowest counters of the group. As in New Hampshire, Maine’s elections are administered by towns, each with its own schedule for tabulating ballots and releasing results. In Alaska, mail ballots from remote corners of the state can arrive up to 15 days after the election. If those historical patterns hold, there won’t be enough votes counted on election night to call a close race in either state.

In 2024, the presidential race in Maine was called at 4:40 p.m. ET Wednesday and in Alaska at 10 a.m. ET Thursday. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 percentage points, while Trump won Alaska by 13 points. It’s possible the margins in this year’s Senate contests could be much closer.

There is a second complication in Maine and Alaska that could cause even more delay in knowing which party will control the Senate. Those states use ranked choice voting for their Senate races, in which voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of more than 50% of voters, the winner will be determined by ranked choice tabulation, in which the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and his or her votes are reallocated based on voters’ next-most-preferred candidates.

In Alaska, the ranked choice tabulation occurs 15 days after Election Day. Maine doesn’t provide official guidelines about when its ranked choice tabulation will occur; in June, the ranked choice results were released 10 days after the primary election.
In either case, if one or both of those seats are needed to win a majority, we may not know until the next day, or even for several weeks, which party will control the Senate.
What about the House?

Democrats need a net gain of only three seats to flip control of the House, and they’re heavily favored to succeed. But the size of that majority depends on how much voters shift their support toward the Democrats and away from Republicans.
For Subscribers

A recent NBC News Decision Desk analysis found evidence that the nationwide shift could be big enough to produce a historically large majority for the Democrats — or it could be sufficiently small that either party could end up with a razor-thin majority. (The House is made up of 435 seats, all up for re-election every two years, and 218 seats are needed for control.)

The size of that majority for either party matters significantly to our ability to project control of the chamber. The smaller the final size of the majority, the longer it will take for the Decision Desk to be certain who will control the House.
If current polls are overestimating Democratic support and the size of the House majority for either party is small, the 2022 and 2024 elections provide some idea of timing.

During the 2022 midterms, it took the NBC News Decision Desk eight days after Election Day to project that Republicans would win a slim majority. That call came as the Decision Desk projected the Republicans would win California’s 27th District, their 218th win. The ultimate size of their majority was nine seats.
For Subscribers

In the 2024 election, the Republicans won an even smaller majority — just five seats. That election also took until the second Wednesday after Election Day for the Decision Desk to project the 218th seat for the Republicans.
If the size of the Democrats’ or Republicans’ majority this year is a single-digit number of seats, we expect it to take days or weeks for either party to reach 218 seats.

Just like the Senate elections, the House elections in Maine and Alaska use ranked choice voting to determine winners. If control of the House hinges on Maine’s 2nd District or Alaska’s lone district, we may have to wait until ranked choice tabulation occurs 10 to 15 days after Election Day.

On the other hand, if current polls end up being close to accurate, Democrats would be poised to win at least 230 seats, according to the recent Decision Desk analysis. That could speed up when we know control.

Throughout the night, the NBC News Decision Desk uses a statistical model to estimate the total number of seats the Democrats and Republicans will end up winning. It’s possible that NBC News will report the estimate on election night. The House model relies on past and current vote counts; it doesn’t use any polling, including exit polls, in its estimation.

Elections in states with early polling close times or states that count their ballots quickly can also indicate where things might end up. Kentucky’s 6th District, which Trump won in 2024 by 15 points, is a good example of an early bellwether district. The Republican-held district’s polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and in 2024 it reported nearly 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m.

While the Democrats don’t need their candidate, Zach Dembo, to win the district to earn a majority, a low-single-digit win by the Republican candidate, Ralph Alvarado, would be a favorable signal for the Democrats’ chances of winning the House. If Dembo were to win this district, it would most likely foretell a Democratic tsunami, as there are 267 districts nationwide where Trump performed more poorly on his way to the White House. And if Alvarado were to win by a margin close to or in the double digits, it might suggest that neither party will end up with a large majority.

Florida, which tends to report its votes quickly, also has several congressional districts worth paying attention to early in the night. One of them is the 25th, where Democrat Jared Moskowitz seeks re-election in a district that Florida Republicans redrew to favor Trump by 9 points. If Moskowitz loses to Republican Scott Singer, it would be a major victory for Republicans and may foreshadow the party’s holding on to House control. If Moskowitz wins comfortably, it may signal a large Democratic wave.

Florida’s 14th and 22nd districts are also Democratic-held toss-ups that Republicans redrew to be districts Trump would have won by 10.5 points. Given how quickly Florida counts its ballots, those two districts may be the first toss-ups NBC News can project. If one party were to win both of them early in the night, it could very well end up with the majority.

title: NBC News Exit Poll: How it works and how we use the results on election night
summary: Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.
story: Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.

An exit poll is a survey of voters taken as they leave (or exit) their voting location. Unlike public opinion polls ahead of elections that predict whether respondents will vote, exit polls capture the views of voters in person on Election Day. The exit poll also reflects the views of people who voted early or by mail — we take steps to reach those voters by phone and by mail, as well as online.
Here’s how exit polls work, where they are conducted and how NBC News will be using the results on election night and in the days after.
Who conducts the exit poll?

For this year’s midterm election, exit polls are being conducted by SSRS, a survey and market research firm, on behalf of a group of news organizations: NBC News, ABC News, The Associated Press, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and MS NOW. The companies receive the same data, and NBC News then independently analyzes and reports on the exit poll results.
What questions are asked?

The national exit poll asks respondents whether they voted for the Democratic or Republican House candidate in their district, and in many states the poll also asks which candidates voters supported in Senate and governor’s races.
In addition, the poll usually includes a number of questions about voters’ views, such as, “What is the most important issue facing the country?”
Follow live election coverage
The other key component of an exit poll is asking about voters’ demographics, such as age, gender, race and education level.

These types of questions help illustrate how different groups of people voted and what mattered to them. Demographic data is also used to weight the exit poll — that is, to make sure the poll reflects the demographics of the electorate as well as the election results.
The national and state exit polls include some different questions, to capture voters’ views on local issues and candidates.
The news organizations jointly determine how the exit poll will be conducted and develop the questionnaire together.
How are exit polls conducted?
The in-person Election Day exit polls are surveys that voters in scientifically selected precincts are asked to fill out as they leave their polling place. The paper forms have about 25 questions.
This year, interviewers will be stationed at over 450 polling locations in 15 Senate battleground states. Each interviewer follows local rules about where they can stand outside the polling location.

The exit polls also include a pre-election survey to capture voters no matter how they participate, whether early, by mail or on Election Day. Before Election Day, respondents are surveyed through methods including mailed invitations, telephone and text interviews and online surveys. Interviewers then follow up with respondents to confirm that they voted and whom they ultimately voted for.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Respondents can complete the poll in English or Spanish.

On Election Day, interviewers count the people coming out after they have voted and are instructed to offer questionnaires to every third person or every fifth person, for example, from the time polls open until polls close.

Interviewers phone in the results from the questionnaires to a data center three times during the day. Those results are tabulated with the pre-election survey results, and the exit poll is updated throughout the day as new data is collected.
Are exit polls anonymous?

Yes. In person, voters fill out the questionnaires themselves and deposit them in boxes, so their answers, like their actual ballots, are secret. Interviews conducted by mail, by phone and online do not retain any personal information about the voter who was interviewed.
Which states will have exit polls?
In addition to a national exit poll, which captures voters in all 50 states, there are also state exit polls this year in 45 states that have consequential Senate and governor’s contests.
How many people are interviewed?
The national exit poll sample will include over 75,000 voters at voting locations, online and by telephone.
In 15 states, interviewers will be stationed outside at least 30 randomly sampled voting locations. In the remaining states, interviews are conducted via phone, online and mail.

The sample size in each of these states will be about 4,000 voters: Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin.
The sample size in Alaska will be about 3,000 voters, and it will also include interviews from voters at early-voting locations before Election Day.
All other states with exit poll results for Senate and governor’s races will include between 500 and 3,000 voters.
How do we use exit polls?
The NBC News Decision Desk uses some exit poll data to help project race outcomes on election night, but the exit poll is primarily used to help tell the story of the election.

The data gives viewers and readers real-time insight into what motivates voters and how they feel about the country. It’s the nation’s first look at who is turning out to vote this year and what is driving their choices.
What does NBC News report and when?

NBC News does not report any exit poll results before 5 p.m. ET on election night, and no exit poll results that may indicate the outcome of a race are reported until after all the polls are scheduled to close in that state. As election night goes on and interviewers on the ground call in more exit poll results, the data is updated and reweighted in real time.

title: Google to shut off search for schools that opt out of AI
summary: The company said AI-enabled products would be shut off by default for schools, which would also cut off their access to Google Search.
story: Google announced Tuesday morning that it would switch off AI products by default for students in schools that use the technology giant’s education software. But those schools that forgo its AI services would also be cut off from Google Search.

The move comes after mounting criticism from advocacy groups and senators about the spread of Google’s AI services available in classrooms. Until Tuesday, its AI products — branded under the Gemini moniker — were automatically activated for schools using Google Classroom.
Google said Tuesday’s move would also cut off students’ access to Google Search if schools do not enable Gemini, given AI’s growing integration into the company’s search products.

Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post announcing the change that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search “will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.

Some education and technology advocates immediately slammed the decision, painting the move as a punishment for schools that don’t use Google’s AI. “It is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of our children,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, a national educators union.

“Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether,” she told NBC News in written comments.
Josh Golin, executive director of advocacy group Fairplay, said in a statement that Google is attempting “to strong-arm schools into using its AI products.”
“Schools should use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click,” Golin said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In a statement posted to social media after this article was published, Google said the announcements “give schools more choice, not less,” and that schools can turn on Google Search individually without enabling Gemini products. But Search will still have AI features built into it, which the company said have been updated “to make it better for learning. Specifically, AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”
Earlier this year, Google turned on Gemini in its Classroom app, allowing children — regardless of age — to access AI products unless districts disabled it.

Parent advocacy groups and experts on the use of technology in schools denounced Google for providing AI products to children — raising concern that students would outsource their work to AI systems on school devices — and lobbied school districts to disable Gemini products. In an open letter in early October, 13 leading parent advocacy organizations — including the Digital Childhood Institute and Schools Beyond Screens — called on school districts to turn off access to Gemini and YouTube, which is also owned by Google.

Google has established a dominant role in education technology over the past 15 years. The vast majority of Chromebook laptops are purchased by school districts to provide to students. Nearly two-thirds of assignments use a Google product, according to a 2023 report by the firm Schoolytics. This year, the company began offering multiday AI training sessions for educators, featuring sessions that focused on how they could mitigate pushback by teachers who don’t want to use AI.

Research on AI in educational settings has not established a long-term benefit for students. There are no high-quality causal studies into student use of AI, according to the SCALE Initiative at the Stanford Graduate School of Education. Researchers have also warned that many of the studies conducted so far on AI in education didn’t measure whether it boosted learning and often did not test whether AI-assisted learning was superior to other teaching methods.

In Tuesday’s blog post, Google said that for schools that enable its AI products, it will now detect when a student is trying to use them just to get an answer on an assignment. A redesigned version of Google Search will instead walk students through the topic or problem and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer, the company said.

title: Supreme Court sympathetic to Catholic plea to participate in Colorado preschool program
summary: The justices heard arguments in the latest in a line of cases pitting religious rights against LGBTQ rights.
story: WASHINGTON — Tackling the latest in a series of cases that pit LGBTQ and religious rights against each other, the Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared to lean toward Catholic entities that are seeking an exemption from Colorado’s antidiscrimination rules so they can participate in a taxpayer-funded preschool program.

In the Election Day session, the court’s conservative majority seemed inclined to see Colorado’s refusal to grant an accommodation as a violation of the religious rights of the Archdiocese of Denver and other plaintiffs under the Constitution’s First Amendment. A ruling is due by the end of June.

It is the latest in a series of cases in which Christian plaintiffs have pushed back against antidiscrimination measures aimed at protecting LGBTQ rights. Most such cases considered by the Supreme Court in the past decade have arisen from Colorado.
The court has a 6-3 conservative majority that regularly favors religious rights in cases brought by Christian groups.

At issue is a provision of state law that bars preschools from participating in the state-funded program if they refuse admission to children based on the sexual orientation or gender identity of the child or parents.

As Catholic doctrine does not recognize same-sex relationships or transgender status, the plaintiffs say the rule conflicts with their religious rights. The Trump administration supports the challengers.

Several conservative justices indicated during the two-hour session that the refusal to give the Catholic preschools an exemption had echoes of past discrimination against religious groups even if the law did not expressly single them out.

Justice Neil Gorsuch cited a line of rulings over the last decade in which the Supreme Court has paved the way for taxpayer money to flow to religious entities, including schools, despite long-standing prohibitions driven by the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause, which bars government endorsement of religion.
He wondered whether “we were just wasting our time for the last 10 years.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett also seemed skeptical that the state would not have known that certain religious entities would refuse to comply with a blanket LGBTQ rights provision.

“I’m not assuming animus” on the part of the state, she said. But, she added, “if you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with a contrary belief, how is that different?”

Another conservative justice, Brett Kavanaugh, questioned why there was any need to enforce compliance with the antidiscrimination provision, noting that LGBTQ families have many other preschool options.
The state could have taken a “win-win” by accommodating both religious and LGBTQ rights, he said.

“There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools an appropriate fit for their children,” he added.
The court’s three liberal justices expressed concern that the Catholic entities want to be given broad leeway to refuse to comply with any law they object to.
“It seems to me like you are asking for a special rule for religious schools,” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told the Catholic challengers’ lawyer, Nicholas Reaves.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
On the flip side, by refusing to accommodate LGBTQ families, the preschools effectively want to “discriminate by exclusion,” she added.
The preschool program, approved as part of a statewide referendum in 2020, provides taxpayer funds for parents to send their children to their preferred preschool.

The case before the justices on Tuesday focuses on the long-running question of whether excluding religious groups from certain government programs violates the Constitution’s First Amendment, which protects the free exercise of religion.
In a 1990 ruling called Employment Division v. Smith, the Supreme Court stated that religious exemptions are not required when a law applies equally to everyone.

The court has stopped short of overturning that ruling in recent cases, even as it has ruled in favor of religious plaintiffs. In a notable ruling in 2021, the court ruled that a Catholic group could not be barred from a Philadelphia foster care program because of its views opposing same-sex couples.

The Catholic challengers in the Colorado case argue, among other things, that the state program already contains some loopholes that allow for schools to apply some discretion when accepting children. They are allowed, for example, to prioritize children with disabilities and those from low-income families. Those allowances “expressly conflict” with the state’s equal access requirement, the challengers wrote in court papers.

Colorado argues that its allowance for specialized services for disabled children and low-income families is consistent with its equal access approach because it “advances Colorado’s interests” in ensuring that disadvantaged people are not denied entry to the preschools, the state’s lawyers wrote.

Separately, preschools operated by Catholic Charities do participate in the state program. That organization has a different mission from the preschools run directly by the church and does not require attendees to comply with Catholic teachings.

The other plaintiffs in Tuesday’s case are St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton and Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood, plus two parishioners at St. Mary, Daniel and Lisa Sheley. The Sheleys have seven children, with one in preschool and another soon to follow.
The Sheleys have not been able to benefit from more than $12,000 in tuition assistance because they chose to send their children to the church’s preschool, their lawyers said.
The archdiocese operates 34 preschools in the state in total.
The challengers sued in 2023 but lost in lower courts before asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

title: Escaped Tennessee inmate captured, authorities say
summary: Jacob Allen Morley escaped from prison in the small town of Tiptonville and is alleged to have stolen a truck. He was convicted last year of killing a co-worker in 2022.
story: Jacob Allen Morley, the convicted murderer who escaped from a Tennessee prison, is in custody, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said Tuesday.

He was captured more than a week after he escaped on Oct. 25 from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville — a town of about 3,500 people roughly 100 miles north of Memphis — and, according to authorities, stole a truck that was later found abandoned in Illinois.
The TBI announced that Morley was captured near Kansas City, Missouri, and was in custody Tuesday.

The Missouri State Highway Patrol said in a statement that it received information from the TBI at around 9:30 a.m. Tuesday that Morley may have been traveling west on Interstate 70 near Independence. Morley’s vehicle was located by Flock Safety cameras, the statement said.

Officers from multiple agencies moved into the area, as it “was believed the suspect was armed with multiple weapons,” the statement said. A police helicopter then spotted Morley’s car and followed it.
Morley’s car “attempted to travel off the roadway and became stuck, at which time a trooper with the Patrol confronted Morley and took him into custody without incident,” the statement said.
He was taken into custody around 11:34 a.m., police said.
Prison officials discovered Morley, 28, was missing around 11:30 p.m. Oct. 25. Security video showed he had breached a perimeter fence, the Tennessee Correction Department said in a statement.
“He has been added to the Tennessee Most Wanted list and should be considered dangerous,” it said.

Morley was convicted in 2025 of murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary in the killing of co-worker Cody Birchfield, 34, in 2022, according to court documents shared by the Carter County Clerk’s Office in Tennessee.
In an interview with NBC News, Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, called her brother’s killer “a very dangerous man.”
“And if he gets ahold of any kind of weapon, he will kill somebody,” she said.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
In a statement Tuesday afternoon after Morley was taken into custody, Norman thanked authorities and everyone who followed the case.

The white Ford F-350 truck Morley is accused of stealing had passed the Hornbeak Fire Department in the town of Hornbeak, Tennessee, shortly after the theft early Monday. Hornbeak is 12 miles east of Tiptonville.
The fire department posted timestamped still images on its Facebook page from security video showing the truck driving by.
The TBI said Tuesday that the truck was found abandoned in Marion, Illinois, about 123 miles north of Hornbeak. It was left behind a business, police there and in Tennessee said.
Morley was accused of shooting Birchfield in the back of the head. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence in northeast Tennessee, court documents say.

A motive was unclear, and Morley claimed self-defense at his trial. He reported that he had been hospitalized multiple times for mental health issues, including bipolar disorder, and he had no previous felony offenses, according to the records.
Morley was convicted and sentenced to life in prison.

title: Exit poll: Voters cast ballots against Trump
summary: The president’s approval rating dropped among voters, who have big concerns about the economy, according to early polling results.
story: Nearly half of voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.
Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — far higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election during his first term.
The early results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating.
A key frustration voters cited? The economy.

Most voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families, with the affordability of gas, food and utilities being a significant concern. Voters blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse.
The poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
Trump’s sagging job approval rating
Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll.
Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).
Trump’s dismal approval ratings have dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.
Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.
Voters have negative opinions of both parties

Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 voters said they don’t have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.

Fifty-four percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 46% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters today said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views. Voters expressed more unfavorable views toward both parties than they did in the last two midterms.

Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.
On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.

Voters also expressed negative opinions about Congress. Three-quarters said they disapproved of the way Congress is handling its job. Republicans were far more likely than Democrats to approve of Congress, 46% to 9%.
Economic pessimism
The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.

An overwhelming majority said the nation’s economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About half of voters casting ballots said the cost of living was crucial to their votes. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018 — a wave election for Democrats during Trump’s first term. That year, 68% of voters said the economy was in good shape.
Voters are driven by the economy

Voters rated the economy as the most important issue facing the country today (39%), followed by the state of democracy (32%), according to the poll. They voiced significant concerns about the prices of gas, groceries and utilities, blaming Trump for affordability problems.

Forty-four percent of voters said their finances are worse today than they were two years ago when Trump returned to office. Just 18% say they’re better off. These numbers are in line with the way voters characterized their finances during the 2022 midterms but much worse than in Trump’s first midterm election in 2018.

Driving voters’ financial concerns: the cost of living. Top issues include the cost of gas and diesel fuel (87% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned), food and groceries (88% concerned), utilities (86%) and healthcare (85%). All told, just under 8 in 10 voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families.
More than half (65%) say Trump’s policies have made the economy worse; 62% said he’s responsible for high prices.
Other key issues for voters: immigration, corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence

More than half of voters (57%) said Trump’s immigration enforcement actions have gone too far, according to the poll. Twenty-three percent said the crackdowns have been about right, and 21% said they have not gone far enough. Fifty-nine percent of voters said they disapproved of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency carrying out much of the enforcement actions; while 41% said they approved.
For Subscribers

Corruption was also a key issue. Ninety percent of voters said it was a crucial or major factor in their vote, but they were divided on which party was better positioned to fight it. Thirty-six percent said the Democratic Party, while 31% said Republicans. The remaining third of voters said they didn’t believe either party would be better.

The war in Iran was largely unpopular among voters, with 62% saying the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. Forty-five percent of voters who backed Democratic candidates for the House said the war was crucial to their vote, compared with 21% of voters who supported Republican candidates.

Concerns about AI were also high on voters’ minds: 57% said AI will do more to hurt society than help, the poll showed. A large majority, 76%, said they opposed the construction of a new data center in their community. Voters split almost evenly on which party was better able to handle AI.
Groups we’re watching closely as the night unfolds
We’ll closely watch several groups that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 — but with particular interest in Latino voters and voters under 30.
For Subscribers
After having fallen in every national election since 2018, the share of Latino voters who identify as Democrats ticked up this year to 43% from 39% in 2024, the poll showed.
The share of Latino voters calling themselves independents dropped slightly, to 30% from 32%. The share identifying as Republicans also dropped slightly, to 27% from 29% in 2024.

The results halted a steady erosion of the Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters in party identification, which narrowed from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024. This year, Democrats hold a 16-point edge.
Young voters also seem to be shifting back to the Democratic Party after Trump shrank the margin among them in the 2024 presidential election.

title: Everything you need for election night: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to a special Election Day edition of the From the Politics Desk newsletter, where we’re putting all the links and information you’ll need when the vote tallies start rolling in tonight in one place.
story: Welcome to a special Election Day edition of the From the Politics Desk newsletter, where we’re putting all the links and information you’ll need when the vote tallies start rolling in tonight in one place.
And keep an eye on your inbox tomorrow morning for a post-election edition of our Morning Rundown newsletter wrapping up the results from all the key races.
— Adam Wollner
Everything you need for election night
Election Day is finally here! Voting is underway across the country, with control of the House and the Senate — and the direction of the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency — at stake.
As a reminder, Democrats would need to gain a net of three seats to win the House and four to win the Senate.
